title: Haiti Protection Analysis Update - September 2026
content:
Haiti has been experiencing a deepening political, security, and humanitarian protection crisis since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, with escalating armed violence and civil unrest, particularly in the West, Artibonite, and Centre departments. Weak rule of law institutions, constrained resources, and endemic corruption hinder the State’s ability to protect and promote human rights. Armed violence exacerbates pre-existing humanitarian needs and vulnerabilities stemming from socio-economic inequalities and frequent natural disasters.

The Haitian population faces serious protection risks arising from the actions of armed groups, self-defence groups, and security forces. From 1 January to 31 July 2026, the Human Rights Service (HRS) of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) documented 3,373 killings and 1,494 injuries. During the same period, 176 people were kidnapped for ransom by armed groups, compared with 433 in 2025.

These patterns of violence intersect with other protection risks and disproportionately affect people facing heightened vulnerabilities. Gender-based violence (GBV) remains alarmingly high and underreported, with 6,337 incidents, primarily affecting women and girls, reported between January and 31 July 2026. Children are exposed to violence, family separation and trafficking, including recruitment by armed groups, increasing their vulnerability to abuse and exploitation. Restrictions on freedom of movement further compound these risks, limiting access to food, safe drinking water, healthcare and education, disrupting the transportation of goods and constraining humanitarian access.

Continued violence and restrictions on movement have also contributed to more than 1.47 million people being internally displaced since 2022. Many live in increasingly overstretched host communities, while others remain in overcrowded and unsafe displacement sites with limited access to basic services. Repeated displacement has disrupted family and community networks, education, livelihoods and access to social protection, eroding existing coping capacities.

These internal displacement dynamics are compounded by forced returns of Haitians from countries of destination. Haitians returning from the Dominican Republic and other countries may face return without adequate safeguards or due process, often into areas where insecurity, limited services and weak institutional capacity constrain opportunities for safe and sustainable reintegration. The termination of U.S. Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians on 27 July 2026, which had protected 350,000 Haitian nationals and the arrival of the first deportation flight in Cap-Haïtien on 20 August, further underscore the potential for increased return-related protection pressures.

Mass displacement forced returns and weakened State presence in areas affected by violence are aggravating barriers to legal identity and access to justice. Loss of documentation limited civil registration services and restricted access to legal assistance and remedies particularly affect internally displaced persons and forcibly returned Haitians. These barriers undermine fundamental rights and compound risks, including restrictions on freedom of movement, exposure to violence and exclusion from essential services.

Against this backdrop, the Humanitarian Reset provides an opportunity to move beyond responding to incidents and delivering assistance to address the underlying drivers of protection risks – by reducing threats, mitigating vulnerabilities and strengthening the capacities of affected populations, through prevention, community-based protection and multisectoral interventions. Such an approach is critical to strengthening community leadership and resilience, preserving social cohesion and ensuring that humanitarian interventions contribute measurably to reducing protection risks.

The priority protection risks requiring immediate attention in the period covered by this analysis are:
1. Attacks on members of the population and other unlawful killings, and attacks on public and private objects
2. Unlawful impediments or restrictions to freedom of movement, and forced displacement
3. Gender-based violence
4. Forced recruitment and association of children in armed forces and groups
5. Impediments and/or restrictions to access to legal identity, remedies and justice

title: Colombia: Flash Update 014 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - September 23, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia with inputs from humanitarian partners and official reports. Information is current as of 23 September at 6:30 p.m. This document will continue to be issued on a weekly basis through the end of September.

  • More than one month after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake, approximately 487,000 people have been affected across 500 municipalities in 16 departments, with the most severe impacts reported in Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Chocó, Quindío and Caldas. The potential onset of a severe El Niño event could further exacerbate humanitarian and recovery needs.
  • Communities are facing multiple, simultaneous crises. In addition to the impact of the earthquake, people continue to experience pre-existing effects of the armed conflict, including displacement, confinement and restricted access to essential services. These factors increase population vulnerability and place additional strain on institutional response capacities.
  • The Government and international partners continue to deliver a coordinated response. Institutions within the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD) are providing sectoral assistance in coordination with territorial authorities. United Nations agencies and humanitarian partners continue to work together to deliver health care, water, sanitation and hygiene services, food security support, shelter, protection and early recovery assistance. To date, 31 organizations have supported more than 137,000 people in 53 prioritized municipalities.
  • Significant needs and funding gaps persist. While recovery efforts are advancing through the development of the Specific Action Plan for Recovery (PAE), the humanitarian response still faces a 52 per cent funding gap against the US$619 million required to address the multisectoral needs of affected populations through the end of 2026.

title: Eswatini | Drought - Early Action Protocol Activation, 9th September 2026 (EAP2023SZ01/MDRSZ005)
content:
Early action protocol Activation

Activation Overview

Baphalali Eswatini Red Cross Society (BERCS) has activated its Early Action Protocol for drought following National forecasts indicating a high probability of an El Niño-induced drought season in Eswatini. Seasonal outlooks and forecast monitoring conducted through the Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG), National Meteorological Services and Regional climate information systems indicated an elevated likelihood of below-normal rainfall in the October to December season (Figure 1). This is expected to lead to reduced water availability and worsening food insecurity conditions across drought-prone areas, particularly in the Lubombo, parts of Lowveld, parts of the Highveld and Middleveld.

The trigger threshold in the Drought Early Action Protocol was reached when the OND forecast issued in early September indicated below normal rainfall was expected. Early actions will be implemented before peak drought impacts occur during the January-March lean season.

Implementation will focus on vulnerable households who will potentially be exposed to food insecurity, loss of livelihoods and reduced access to water. Priority will be given to households headed by women, older persons, persons with disabilities, child-headed households, smallholder farmers, and households dependent on rain-fed agriculture.

Target geographical areas include drought-prone chiefdoms across the Lubombo and Shiselweni identified through EAP risk analysis, vulnerability assessments and drought monitoring systems.

title: Middle East Situation Lebanon - Operational Update (August 2026)
content:
Lebanon remains among the countries most affected by forced displacement globally, hosting one of the largest refugee populations per capita while almost 334,353 people remained internally displaced at the end of August. Despite ceasefire agreements, repeated violations and persistent insecurity continue to drive humanitarian needs and repeated displacement, hinder safe and sustainable returns and recovery of conflict-affected areas, and place additional stress and strain on families and affected local communities.

Around 136,000 refugees who had been living in areas directly impacted by the escalating hostilities became internally displaced and faced difficulties finding safe and dignified shelter and livelihoods in displacement. Nearly 29,700 displaced Syrian refugees were directly identified as being in need of protection and assistance and referrals to services. The volatile situation, repeated displacement and uncertainties continue to affect people’s safety, dignity and psychological well-being.

title: Lebanon Crisis Response Plan 2026 (update)
content:
In 2026, IOM aims to support and empower Lebanon’s most vulnerable populations, including migrants, refugees, internally displaced persons, and host communities, amid ongoing socioeconomic challenges and the lasting impact of the 2024 conflict escalation, and the renewed hostilities which started in March 2026. IOM will continue delivering essential humanitarian aid and protection services, while strengthening community recovery and resilience, reducing tensions, and promoting safe, dignified, and regular migration. Through integrated efforts across the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, IOM seeks to foster stability, inclusion, and renewed hope for all communities in Lebanon.

This plan has been updated to reflect renewed hostilities resulting in a fluid mix of active displacement, fragile returns, and secondary displacement. It outlines IOM's efforts to save lives and protect people on the move, drive solutions to displacement and facilitate pathways for regular migration. In 2026, IOM now requires USD88,564,750 to support 1,159,200 individuals, including internally displaced persons, local populations / communities, international
migrants and a range of stakeholders.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 19, Data as of 20 September 2026
content:
Event description
The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé Province, bordering South Sudan, being the latest affected, bringing the total number of health zones affected to 63 since the start of the outbreak. This latest geographic expansion heightens concern about further spread towards international borders, while transmission within the country remains increasingly heterogeneous across affected provinces and health zones. Since External Situation Report #18, a further 475 confirmed cases and 222 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 7733 confirmed cases, including 3732 deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR 48.3%)], as of 20 September 2026. Ituri remains the principal focus, although its relative contribution continues to decline, accounting for 76.9% of cumulative confirmed cases, while substantial transmission continues in Nord-Kivu and persists in Haut-Uélé.

At the national level, daily incidence remains high and fluctuating, with the seven-day moving average rebounding in early September before declining in the most recent days. This national pattern masks divergent provincial trajectories. Ituri continues a gradual decline from its late-July peak but remains at a high level, while Nord-Kivu experienced a marked increase, reaching its highest incidence in mid-September, followed by an apparent decline in recent days. Transmission in Haut-Uélé remains sustained but below its August peak, while Tshopo shows renewed activity from a low baseline. Bas-Uélé continues to report sporadic transmission, with no recent transmission evident in Sud-Kivu. Overall, the epidemic remains geographically heterogeneous, with recent declines in the principal transmission areas occurring alongside persistent low-level transmission and continued geographic expansion to new areas.

title: WFP Guinea Bissau Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Guinea-Bissau is one of the world's least developed countries, with a population of approximately 2.2 million people, nearly half of whom live below the national poverty line. Ranked 174th out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index, the country faces persistent development challenges that perpetuate intergenerational vulnerabilities.

• Food insecurity and malnutrition remain widespread, particularly in inland regions. An estimated 146,000 people face acute food insecurity, while nearly one in three children under five suffers from chronic malnutrition, with stunting rates surpassing the 30 percent threshold of a serious public health burden in the Oio, Gabú, and Bafatá regions.

• These outcomes are driven in large part by limited access to affordable and healthy food. While nearly 30 percent of the population cannot afford even an energy-only diet, almost 70 percent are unable to pay for a nutritious diet, estimated at USD 4 per day for an average household of seven people.

• In this context, since 1974 WFP has been supporting the Government of Guinea-Bissau in addressing immediate food and nutrition needs while strengthening resilience, livelihoods, and national capacities. Through an integrated food systems transformation approach, WFP contributes to improved food security and nutrition outcomes, enhanced resilience to shocks, and progress towards sustainable and inclusive development

title: IOM Yemen Dispatch August 2026: Updates on the humanitarian crisis, people on the move and IOM's response in Yemen
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security situation deteriorated markedly throughout August, with escalation in active conflict since the collapse of the 2022 truce in July. On August 6, deadly Ansar Allah (AA) strikes targeted the Government of Yemen (GoY) key positions in Hadramaut and facilities in Ma’rib, resulting in around 45 fatalities, marking one of the deadliest days on record. Over 119 operational incidents were reported in the first week of August alone as ballistic missiles, UAVs, and heavy artillery focused heavily on the Ma’rib, Hadramaut, and Red Sea coastal fronts. Ground fighting expanded toward the end of the month, as the AA forces launched concentrated offensives in western Ta’iz and southern Hodeidah, aimed at seizing strategic positions overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Maritime insecurity in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb has escalated freight costs and introduced critical supply delays for international relief goods. On the ground, flash floods have created additional challenges to road access, affecting emergency assistance delivery to displaced populations. Furthermore, the dual shock of conflict-driven displacements and extreme weather events has overwhelmed Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) and emergency stock pipelines, requiring an urgent, multisectoral scale-up to prevent further loss of life and mitigate acute food consumption gaps.

The severe cooking gas shortage in Aden and surrounding governorates like Abyan deepened in August, due to scheduled summer maintenance at Ma’rib Safer facility, which temporarily reduced gas production by 6,000 barrels per day. The supply disruption heavily impacted daily life by driving black-market prices for a 20-liter gas cylinder up to YR 18,000 (official rate is YR 8,500), rendering cooking gas unaffordable for poorer households and threatening already fragile food security. Beyond home kitchens, the crisis has paralyzed public transportation by stranding converted gas-powered buses, and brought local businesses, bakeries, and restaurants to the brink of shutdown.

Cholera transmission remains heavily concentrated in the same governorates that have consistently reported the highest caseloads since the beginning of the year. Abyan remained the epicenter of the outbreak, accounting for over 2,070 suspected cases, followed by Lahj with over 1,060 cases. Together with Ta’iz and Aden, these four governorates account for approximately 82 per cent of the national caseload.

UN Special Envoy Hand Grundberg and the USG for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, briefed the Security Council on 13 August, during which they underscored the dire situation that millions of Yemenis face and the heightened risk of Yemen getting entangled in complex regional confrontation. The humanitarian situation also has not improved, with the 73 UN staff still detained along with dozens of civil society staff. Despite the challenges, however, humanitarians reached 3.4 million people across Yemen with lifesaving assistance and protection in the first half of 2026.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 5 – 11 September 2026
content:
Russia increasingly targets border crossings in Ukraine, while Ukraine doubles down on striking Russian oil infrastructure.

Author

Tetiana Gaviuk

1863 conflict events

225 incidents of violence targeting civilians: 9% increase compared to last week

At least 92 civilians killed by targeted violence:19% increase compared to last week

1132 air- and drone strikes: 4% decrease compared to last week

276 shelling events: 48% increase compared to last week

444 armed clashe: 9% decrease compared to last week

221 Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure: 9% decrease compared to last week

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

Education: 15 events (21% decrease)

Healthcare: 12 events (9% increase)

Energy: 41 events (5% decrease)

Residential: 186 events (8% decrease)

Key trends

  • Russia has expanded its targeting of Ukraine’s transport infrastructure beyond passenger trains and railway hubs to drone attacks on or near border crossings in an attempt to further degrade Ukraine's connection to the outside world. Following a series of disruptive strikes on three Ukraine-Moldova border crossings in August and a ferry crossing to Romania on 6 September, Russia launched a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing on 8 September. This is significant as the border crossing connects Ukraine with Moldova and wider Europe. These kinds of attacks on border crossings risk hindering the movement of goods such as grain and military supplies and putting additional pressure on Ukraine’s economy.
  • In an attempt to further reduce Russia’s revenue sources and hinder its military production, Ukraine carried out its deepest strike inside Russia to date against two Arctic gas facilities on 9 September. Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces also resumed attacks on Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea, targeting 13 vessels on 8 September alone, including the Malta-flagged Seaviolet tanker at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s mooring point near Novorossiysk while it was loading Kazakh oil. Despite United States President Donald Trump’s claim on 14 September that Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, Ukraine is likely to maintain such strikes until a formal ceasefire is reached and Russia halts its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in turn

title: UNHCR Ecuador: Operational Update No. 8 | August 2026
content:
Operational context

UNHCR Ecuador operates in a complex and evolving environment shaped by security, humanitarian and environmental considerations. In August 2026, Ecuador received 1,441 new asylum applications, including 766 from Venezuelans and 675 from Colombians. Applications increased sharply compared to August 2025, rising by 72% and 239% respectively. Venezuelans accounted for 62% of all asylum claims processed in 2026, while Colombians represented 40%, underscoring the continued demand for international protection despite increased border restrictions and reduced mobility. Security-related incidents continued to affect several coastal areas, including Guayas, Manabí, Esmeraldas, and Santa Elena, including targeted killings in public spaces such as beaches during national holidays, reflecting the continued security challenges affecting the country. Also, the northern border remained an area of particular attention given developments involving transnational criminal and armed groups operating in the wider Colombia-Ecuador area. These dynamics continued to require close monitoring of protection risks and their effects on communities, including refugees, asylum-seekers and other people in need of international protection.

In light of these developments, national authorities maintained efforts to address organized crime and strengthen public security including the extension of the state of exception for 30 days across several provinces and cantons. In parallel, legislative developments further strengthened the framework for security operations through enhanced coordination between the Armed Forces and the National Police, and international cooperation.

Environmental risks added a further layer of complexity during the reporting period. National authorities maintained a high level of preparedness in anticipation of the potential impacts of the El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to affect the country over the coming months.

Rising sea levels and changing weather conditions have increased concerns of flooding, coastal erosion, and potential impacts on livelihoods and infrastructure, particularly in vulnerable coastal areas where forcibly displaced people reside. Authorities also expressed concern about the possible effects on energy production and essential services due to reduced water inflows affecting the country’s hydroelectric generation capacity. The 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia was felt across several Ecuadorian provinces. In a demonstration of regional solidarity, the Government of Ecuador established humanitarian aid collection points to support affected populations in Colombia.

Additionally, UNHCR continued to contribute to national and technical discussions on protection and internal displacement. UNHCR participated in the dialogue “Reflexiones sobre el desplazamiento interno en Ecuador” , organized by FLACSO Ecuador and 3iS, with the participation of the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights of Internally Displaced Persons. The exchange contributed evidence-based analysis and fostered academic reflections on internal displacement, supporting ongoing efforts to strengthen understanding of displacement dynamics and protection responses in Ecuador.

Overall, the August operational context required continued flexibility, risk monitoring and coordination with national and local authorities, partners and other humanitarian actors. UNHCR maintained its focus on ensuring access to protection and assistance for refugees, asylum-seekers and other people in need of international protection as well as host communities, while adapting its operational approach to the country’s evolving security and humanitarian environment.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, September 24, 2026 – September 30, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is strengthening. Abnormal heat continues to threaten parts of northern and eastern Africa, Hispaniola, and northern South America. Dry parts of Central America to receive heavy rain. South Africa sees flooding.

Africa Weather Hazards

Hot, dry conditions continue in northwestern Africa, the eastern Sahel, and much of eastern Africa. Meanwhile, flood risk remains high in North Africa, far western West Africa, eastern Africa, and southern Africa.

1) The Sudd wetlands of South Sudan continue to experience inundation.

2) Severe rainfall deficits across Chad and large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have led to abnormal dryness. As a result, conditions have been upgraded to "Drought" across western Sudan, southern and southeastern South Sudan, northern Uganda, and parts of Ethiopia’s northern, eastern, and central regions.

3) Southeastern Mali and central and eastern Liberia remain under abnormal dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall.

4) Persistent heavy rainfall continues to pose elevated risks of flooding across southern and southeastern Nigeria, and the western part of Cameroon. The forecast heavy rainfall elevates flood risk in northern Libya, Senegal, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea-Conakry, western Mali, Sierra Leone, western Liberia, central Angola, and western, southern, and eastern South Africa during the next week.

5) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected in western Morocco, Western Sahara, eastern Niger, central Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, northern Uganda, northwestern Kenya, and northeastern Ethiopia.

title: Bangladesh Dengue 2026 DREF Operation (MDRBD041)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

14-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Dengue continues to be a major public health challenge in Bangladesh. Every year, seasonal outbreaks put many lives at risk and place extra pressure on the healthcare system. Bangladesh is facing an escalating dengue outbreak in 2026, with cases rising sharply since late August following heavy monsoon rains according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Until mid-August 2026, the number of dengue cases was lower than during the same period in 2025. However, heavy monsoon rains in late August led to a rapid increase in infections. As a result, the total number of cases quickly surpassed the figure recorded during the same period last year.

According to DGHS, In September 2026, more than 15,000 new dengue cases and 52 deaths have been reported up to 13 September. Between 8 and 13 September 2026, more than 8,000 new dengue cases were reported, with 16 deaths recorded during this six-day period. During the first 13 days of September, the country recorded an average of more than 1,200 hospital admissions per day, indicating a continued sharp increase in dengue transmission and the pressure on health facilities. August recorded 20,536 hospital admissions and 43 deaths; more than double the 9,206 admissions recorded in July 2026.

Moreover, according to some popular news portals, hospitals are currently managing a dual caseload of measles and dengue admissions, placing additional pressure on an already stretched health system. Health authorities report that measles patients require strict isolation owing to the disease's high transmissibility and cannot be co-located with dengue admissions. This is constraining ward capacity and complicating patient triage and management across affected facilities.

A further rise in dengue cases is expected to compound this pressure. Health experts anticipate a sharp increase in dengue infections over the coming two months, driven by continued wet weather conditions and gaps in vector control coverage.

The current surge has affected all eight divisions, with Dhaka Division the hardest hit. From 1 January to 13 September 2026, Dhaka Division (including its two city corporations) reported 20,177 cases approximately 40% of the national total. Khulna (8,096), Chattogram (7,391) and Barishal (7,313) reported the next-highest numbers, followed by Rajshahi (2,915) and Mymensingh (2,788). Sylhet and Rangpur reported the lowest numbers.

Camps in Cox’s Bazar: By Epidemiological Week 35 (30 August–5 September 2026), 2,698 dengue cases had been reported across the 33 Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar. During EW35, 135 RDT-positive cases were identified, including 116 (86%) among the Rohingya population and 19 (14%) among the host community. Although this represented a 37 per cent decrease from the previous week (214 cases), the outbreak continues to pose significant public health concern in the camps. In 2026, 10 dengue-related deaths have been reported, resulting in case fatality rate (CFR) of 0.42 per cent, with six deaths occurring among children under 10 years of age. Overall, the dengue cases are lower during January–August 2026 in comparison to the same period of 2025. A total of 1,496 cases were recorded during January–August 2026 compared with 2,963 during January–August 2025.

In response to the escalating dengue outbreak, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) activated its volunteer network to support community awareness, health promotion, and clean-up activities in affected areas. As the outbreak continued to intensify and critical gaps emerged in diagnostics, case management, blood services, and community-level prevention. BDRCS requested support from the IFRC through the Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) to scale up its response. Throughout the outbreak, BDRCS has been maintaining close coordination with the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), IFRC, and in-country Participating National Societies (PNSs) to monitor the situation and identify priority needs. Following ongoing technical discussions, DGHS formally requested support from BDRCS on 16 September 2026 for critical dengue response commodities and community awareness materials, reinforcing the need for additional surge capacity to address the growing humanitarian impact of the outbreak.

content:

  • Nutrition: Malnutrition treatment and prevention activities supported 271,200 children under 5 and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls.

  • Resilience and education: Cash transfers and capacity strengthening supported around 14,000 people, while take-home rations reached more than 10,000 schoolchildren.

title: Situation Update No. 3: Escalation of hostilities and displacement across Yemen | Update No. 3 | as of 21 September 2026 | Reporting period: 1 August –20 September 2026 | Countrywide
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • A total of 128,382 people (21,397 households) were displaced between 1 August and 20 September 2026. The Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) figures, which also serve as the alert baseline for the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM), show that 98 per cent of this displacement was recorded from 31 August onwards, following the intensification of hostilities on 3 September. Ta’iz governorate hosts 57 per cent of the displaced, followed by Lahj (26%), Aden (7%) and Al Hodeidah (6%) governorates. The increase compared with earlier updates reflects both continued new arrivals and the consolidation and verification of earlier reports.
  • New arrivals continue. DTM recorded 31,482 newly displaced people in the week of 14–20 September. Around 68 per cent of displaced people remain within their own governorate, while 32 per cent (40,692 people) have crossed into another governorate, mainly from Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah into Lahj and Aden.
  • Civilian casualties continue to be verified across affected governorates. Between 1 August and 22 September, OHCHR verified 128 civilian casualties across 37 incidents, including 32 civilians killed and 96 injured; of these, 73 were verified in September alone. Women and children account for more than half of the verified casualties. In Marib, hits on Asdas settlement (Raghwan) and Al-Hamma hosting site destroyed or damaged at least 19 shelters, causing temporary secondary displacement.
  • A total of 90,600 IDPs (12,956 households) have been assisted. The implemented response, covering ompleted and under way assistance, is highest for WASH and RRM and lower for cash and shelter, while food security partners assisted 6,882 households. RRM stocks are critically low. Access constraints continue to impede the response. Humanitarian movements into several west coast locations have been suspended since 10 September, leaving 533 RRM kits inaccessible. Telecommunications outages in Ta’iz are delaying verification, assistance delivery and cash distributions. DTM has had no access to Al Hodeidah since 9 September, therefore, displacement in this area is likely under-reported.
  • Food assistance faces critical pipeline pressures. WFP has pre-positioned emergency food assistance for 20,000 households in Ta’iz, Aden and Lahj using stocks diverted from the regular pipeline, which must be replenished urgently to avoid gaps for existing IPC Phase 4 caseloads.

This update consolidates information from IOM DTM, the RRM, clusters and partners. All figures are provisional and subject to verification, reconciliation and deduplication. Individual figures from DTM are estimated at six persons per household. Because the same households may receive assistance from more than one sector, figures cannot be added across sectors or sources.

For each of these events, a brief description, followed by public health measures implemented and an interpretation of the situation, is provided. A table is provided at the end of the bulletin with information on all new and ongoing public health events currently being monitored in the region, as well as recent events that have been controlled and closed.

Major issues and challenges include

Diphtheria in Nigeria:

Diphtheria remains a significant public health concern in Nigeria, with transmission highly concentrated in northern states, particularly Kano, Bauchi, Katsina, Borno and Sokoto, which account for most cumulative cases. Persistent immunity gaps, including large zero-dose and undervaccinated populations, continue to drive transmission. Inadequate primaryseries and booster vaccination coverage leaves susceptible populations among older children, adolescents and adults. Surveillance and reporting backlogs, alongside data-quality limitations, hinder accurate assessment and targeted response efforts. The situation is further exacerbated by insecurity, population displacement, disruptions in vaccine and essential supply availability, and substantial subnational inequities in immunization coverage and access to health services, complicating outbreak control efforts across affected communities.

title: Somalia: IPC Acute Food Insecurity and Malnutrition Snapshot | July - December 2026
content:
Overview

Somalia continues to face a volatile and complex food and nutrition crisis, with the risk of Famine identified for the second consecutive IPC analysis. Previous droughts, erratic rainfall, insecurity, and above-average food prices are driving high levels of need, while the impacts of El Niño are expected to further aggravate conditions. At the same time, humanitarian funding and response capacity have declined sharply since January 2026 and are likely to reduce further in the coming months despite increasing needs.

Nearly 5.1 million people are facing high levels of acute food insecurity— IPC Acute Food Insecurity (AFI) Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse)—from July–September 2026. While an improvement from the April 2026 analysis, it is a 50 percent increase from the same period in 2025. Close to 1.4 million people are facing IPC AFI Phase 4 (Emergency), which is characterised by large food gaps and high acute malnutrition.

Food security conditions vary significantly across the country. Pastoral, agropastoral and riverine areas are experiencing improvements in southern Somalia in the current period due to near-average rainfall during the Aprilto-June 2026 Gu season. However, Gu rains performed poorly in pastoral livelihoods of the northeastern region and adjacent areas in northwest and central Somalia.

During the October–December 2026 projection period, the population in IPC AFI Phase 3 or above is expected to increase by 6 percent, to 5.4 million people, driven largely by flooding from El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole. This includes 1.5 million people in IPC AFI Phase 4 (Emergency) and, alarmingly, close to 26,000 people in Bay Region among Baidoa internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Catastrophe (IPC AFI Phase 5), facing starvation and the collapse of livelihoods. In a plausible worst-case scenario in which El Niño flooding and associated displacement are worse than expected, Baidoa IDPs face a risk of Famine from October–December 2026.

Acute malnutrition has also deteriorated, with an estimated 1.92 million children aged 6–59 months suffering or expected to suffer from acute malnutrition from July 2026 to June 2027—a 4 percent increase from 2025. Approximately 157,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women are also facing or expected to face acute malnutrition during the same period.

From June–September 2026, 19 areas are classified as IPC Acute Malnutrition (AMN) Phase 4 (Critical), reflecting a significant deterioration compared to historical trends. The situation is expected to further deteriorate in the projection period as El Niño rains heighten disease burden and outbreaks in IDP settlements, compromise access to safe water and hygiene practices, and severely limit access to health and nutrition services. Beletweyne IDPs are expected to deteriorate to Phase 5 (Extremely Critical), which is characterised by high disease prevalence and widespread deaths. Substantive deterioration towards the upper limit of IPC AMN Phase 4 is expected in seven areas: Bari Urban IDPs (Bossaaso), Bay Urban IDPs (Baidoa), Nugaal Urban IDPs (Garoowe), Beletweyne District, North Gedo Riverine, Bay Agropastoral and Shabelle Riverine livelihoods.

While conditions remain severe, the acute malnutrition situation among agropastoral populations in Burhakaba District has shown a significant improvement since the April 2026 analysis, which identified the area as at risk of Famine through June 2026. This is largely attributed to the scale-up of a targeted and integrated humanitarian response.

Urgent action is critical to save lives and mitigate the high levels of need forecasted for October to December. This includes an immediate and targeted scale-up of humanitarian food security assistance as part of an integrated humanitarian response and alongside anticipatory action.

title: VNM: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall (2026-09-23)

Description

According to local authorities and online sources, heavy rainfall has caused flooding across northern and north-central Viet Nam. The Department of Dyke Management and Disaster Prevention and Control reported on 21 September 2026 that three deaths remain confirmed in Phu Tho. Eight houses had collapsed and 144 were damaged. title: UNHCR Ukraine Operational Update - 14 September 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS:

• Since late August, the Russian Federation (RF) has significantly intensified frequency of attacks, damaging infrastructure and civilian sites, disrupting daily life and causing growing casualties. One of the deadliest attacks occurred on 28 August in Kyiv region, where a Russian strike triggered explosions that killed at least 37 people. According to the UN HRMMU, at least 372 civilians were killed and 2,349 injured in Ukraine in August 2026 - the second highest monthly figure in 2026, after July, with 448 killed and 2,675 injured.

• Strikes on Kherson on 27 August damaged the city’s combined heat and power plant, prompting the authorities to urge residents to evacuate. The situation reflects a broader trend across frontline areas, where escalating insecurity and damage to energy and water systems are driving new displacement, mostly within affected regions but also towards western Ukraine.

• Humanitarian operations faced growing security risks. RF strikes repeatedly hit warehouses contracted by various UN entities, including UNHCR’s, damaging stocks of critical relief supplies. The increased frequency of attacks also made emergency response efforts more complex and dangerous.

• Given security challenges, to ensure continuity of assistance, UNHCR is adapting its operational modalities, including through decentralizing humanitarian stock and exploring additional protective measures such as mobile bomb shelters for war-affected communities.

• In the fifth year since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and more than 12 years since the war began, UNHCR’s programme in Ukraine increasingly aims to help war-affected people and communities to recover, and displaced people to find durable solutions, particularly through housing and strategic protection advocacy.

title: UNICEF Djibouti Humanitarian Flash Update No. 2 (Refugee influx from Yemen), 21 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of 18 September 2026, according to the Ministry of Social Affairs and Solidarity, just over 3,100 people have arrived in Djibouti from Yemen. Nearly half of them are children, including 523 children aged five and under.
  • The pace of arrivals has slowed down since 16 September, reportedly due to fuel shortages in Yemen. However, authorities anticipate a possible new surge, and partners continue to plan for up to 10,000 people, in line with the Government appeal launched on 16 September.
  • UNICEF and the Djiboutian Red Crescent (CRD) have established five water points in Markazi village, with a total storage capacity of 37 m³. The response also included the installation of 10 emergency latrines reserved for women and girls and the connection of the Markazi health post to the water supply.
  • Public health risks remain high. Contributing factors include overcrowding, confirmed scabies cases and a high risk of waterborne disease. Health authorities report a high proportion of acutely malnourished and zero-dose children among those screened at the Markazi health post.
  • One unaccompanied child has been identified to date. He has been placed in a vetted family-based care arrangement, and the family was jointly assessed by UNICEF and the Ministry of Women and Family (MFF).
  • UNICEF requires USD 3 million to respond to the needs of up to 10,000 people over 6 months.

SITUATION UPDATE

Following the sharp acceleration of arrivals between 11 and 14 September, the rate of new arrivals has declined, reportedly due to fuel shortages in Yemen limiting sea crossings. As of 18 September, according to the Ministry of Social Affairs and Solidarity (MASS), 3,106 people have arrived from Yemen. This includes refugees identified through ongoing door-to-door registration in host communities. Nearly half of them are children, including 523 children aged five and under.

The situation nevertheless remains fluid. According to the Prefecture, a significant number of Yemenis are gathered in Al Arah, the closest point of the Yemeni coast, and arrivals could resume rapidly should fuel become available. Partners therefore continue to plan for up to 10,000 people, in line with the Government appeal launched on 16 September.

Living conditions in Markazi remain especially harsh for children. Many families, including those with young children, continue to stay in the overcrowded transit hangar because of high temperatures in the tents. This increases the risk of waterborne diseases and skin infections such as scabies. Health authorities report a high proportion of acutely malnourished and zero-dose children among those screened at the Markazi health post.

In parallel, around 600 migrants wishing to travel to Yemen are waiting in Obock, and at least 120 Ethiopian migrants have returned from Yemen through Djibouti in recent days. Their presence adds pressure on already limited services in the region.

The Government of Djibouti has been at the forefront of the response since the outset of the arrivals, coordinating the response and providing life-saving assistance.

On 19 September 2026, UNICEF Djibouti, led by Representative Ms. Ramatou Touré, joined national authorities and partners in Obock to assess the urgent needs of newly arrived Yemeni refugees and reinforce the coordinated response. The situation of unaccompanied and separated children is of particular concern, as timely action can make the difference between risk and safety.

title: Yemen - Displacement Caused by Escalation in the West Coast — Update #10 (22 September 2026)

Additional displacement was recorded in Al Hodeidah, with 8,244 individuals (6%); Abyan, with 3,324 individuals (3%); Hadramawt, with 1,008 individuals (less than 1%); and Ma’rib, with 594 individuals (less than 1%).

title: Nigeria Situation Report - August 2026
content:
Nigeria has recorded more than 65,000 suspected cholera cases across 35 states and about 195 Local Government Areas (LGAs) since the start of the year, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC). Borno State remains the epicenter, with Maiduguri, Monguno, and Jere being the hardest hit.

Severe violence and herder-farmer conflicts across Northwest and North-Central Nigeria caused widespread civilian displacement, hitting women and children hardest. An estimated 724,543 people are displaced across Zamfara and Benue states only , with women and children among those most affected by ongoing violence, herder-farmer conflicts, and disruptions to livelihoods. UNFPA and partners provided 150 emergency dignity kits, alongside sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and gender-based violence (GBV) services, to support affected women and girls.

Heavy seasonal rainfall in mid-to-late August triggered severe urban and riverine flooding across non-BAY states (such as Nasarawa's Lafia LGA, Anambra, and Ondo States), destroying property, inundating health infrastructure, and amplifying displacement risks. In August, UNFPA and partners reached 8,769 people with SRH services and 5,993 people with GBV prevention, mitigation, and response services across 60 health facilities and 34 safe spaces.

title: Violence and Displacement in the Commune of Kenscoff – SitRep #2 (As of September 21, 2026.)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

On the night of 23 to 24 August 2026, armed groups launched new attacks on several localities in the 3rd communal section of Sourcailles, within Kenscoff commune (including Centre-Ville, Vilier, Tête de l’Eau and Morne Jean Jacques). According to the United Nations, at least 47 people were killed, including 22 people executed inside a church where they had sought refuge. Municipal authorities further reported the abduction of 50 people, multiple incidents of gender-based violence (GBV) and property destruction. Through negotiations supported by UNICEF and local community partners, six abducted children and seven women have since been released., and over 4,238 people (1,159 households) were displaced following the attacks. Approximately 80 percent of the displaced populations are sheltered with host families, while 20 per cent are currently housed across six displacement sites (four pre-existing sites and two newly established ones) in response to this surge. These recent escalations underline the continuous deterioration of security in Kenscoff, following similar attacks in July 2026 that displaced nearly 6,000 people. The humanitarian community is putting in place a coordinated multisectoral response for affected and displaced populations.

title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #6 (September 22, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • As of September 20, 447 cholera cases and four deaths have been reported in Minawao Refugee Camp, which currently is home to more than 81,000 refugees and operating at about 325% of intended capacity. In Cameroon, there have been 2,753 cases and 77 deaths across 11 health districts.
  • This cholera outbreak has a case fatality rate of 2.87%, which is nearly three times higher than the internationally accepted target of less than 1%.
  • Multiple transmission chains are suspected within the camp, where heavy rainfall is increasing the risk of rapid spread among vulnerable populations.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps has been operating in Minawao Refugee Camp since 2013, providing refugees fleeing violence in Nigeria with primary, community-based and referred secondary healthcare.
  • In response to the severe outbreak, our team expanded the cholera treatment unit by 45 beds, trained 105 health workers in advanced case management and reached a daily average of 9,486 people through community hygiene sessions.
  • We have directly managed 447 patients—predominantly children under 10—with 438 successful recoveries (98% recovery rate). Working with the Mokolo Health District, teams also monitored 57 new contacts and referred nine suspected cases this period.
  • We are coordinating with national health authorities, United Nations agencies, camp management and humanitarian partners to support a harmonized response.

title: GBV Working Group Response Update for the current emergency - Yemen (September 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

The ongoing fighting that has escalated in southwestern Yemen since the beginning of September 2026 has triggered one of the most rapid displacement surges of the conflict’s twelve-year duration.

According to the latest IOM Yemen Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flash Update, issued on 20 September 2026, 127,032 individuals (21,172 households) have been displaced since the escalation began in June 2026. Ta’iz hosts the largest concentration, with 72,066 individuals (57%), followed by Lahj with 33,660 (26%), Al Hodeidah with 8,244 (7%), Aden with 8,220 (6%), Abyan with 3,324 (3%), Hadramawt with 960 (less than 1%), and Ma’rib with 558 (less than 1%). Approximately 86,262 people have been displaced within their governorate of origin, indicating predominantly localized displacement and intense pressure on already overstretched host communities and services.

The escalation is unfolding amid severe constraints on humanitarian access and response capacity. Road and communication access has been disrupted in affected areas, with humanitarian movements temporarily suspended in some cases, and emergency stocks had already been depleted by the recent flood response further constraining effective response. This has further strained the Yemen's health system where only 60 per cent of health facilities nationwide are fully operational. Hospitals in Marib, Hadramaut and Taiz are recording increased trauma caseloads that are straining emergency, surgical and intensive care capacity.

The pressure on the system is directly affecting the availability of GBV response services. Most newly affected districts lack comprehensive GBV coverage, while existing partners face funding, staffing, access and resource
constraints that limit their ability to expand rapidly into newly displaced and hard-to-reach populations. The combination of rapid displacement, unsafe site conditions, disrupted services and limited referral pathways is increasing GBV and protection risks for women and girls while simultaneously reducing access to life-saving support.

title: Situation Report No.11: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 18 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Nearly three months after the 24 June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela, the response has moved into early recovery while sustaining essential emergency operations. Efforts now center on maintaining continuity of care across mental health, sexual and reproductive health, maternal and neonatal care, NCDs, and rehabilitation, alongside restoring affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and strengthening Health Cluster coordination as Emergency Medical Teams and international partners withdraw.

• Health system recovery is advancing, with 16 ASICs and 356 health facilities assessed (61% operational) and rehabilitation progressing under CERF, CFE and US funding, while fluctuating electricity, medication refrigeration and emergency-generator gaps continue to challenge the safe continuity of essential health services.

• Public health surveillance and prevention remain active, with 47,145 cumulative vaccine doses administered and 556 health professionals trained, while intensified surveillance in La Guaira and Miranda and mounting environmental risks from tropical rains and heatwaves continue to require sustained vector-control and water/sanitation action.

• Contraception remains the most consistent unmet need across assessed shelters, particularly among adolescents and young women, while mental health needs continue to rise across the transitional camps amid limited supplies and specialized personnel.

• PAHO/WHO continues to support the response with critically needed medical supplies and medicines, having shipped 46.6 metric tons to Venezuela to date, benefiting 72 actors and reaching 117,714 people with treatment through PAHO and partner donations, while sustained technical and logistical support to the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) has strengthened the national supply chain and ensured the continuity of health services through the coordination, reception, and mobilization of international donations of essential medical products.

title: World Health Organization - Middle East Escalation of Conflict, Global Situation report #11 - 15 September 2026
content:
ACUTE HEALTH THREATS

Following a period of relative calm since late July, hostilities began to re-intensify on 30 August in Iran, with
additional reported impacts in military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Additional sanctions
announced on 24 August on Iran have had significant effects on the economy, including on health. Currency
depreciation and access restrictions to international financial systems are adding additional complexities to

East, attacks impacting oil infrastructure and shipping raise additional concerns on the continued effects of the
current escalation on oil supplies and prices in addition to the potential environmental health consequences

title: Colombia | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRCO036)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

On 10 August 2026 at 07:34 local time, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near the municipality of San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of 103 km. The earthquake was followed by multiple aftershocks and was felt across much of the country, affecting densely populated urban centres and rural communities alike. The departments most severely impacted include Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío, while significant impacts were also reported in Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Huila, Boyacá, Tolima, Cauca, Putumayo, Sucre, and Santander. As of 14 September, the National Disaster Risk Management Unit (UNGRD) reports indicate impacts across 16 departments and 500 municipalities, while the earthquake was felt across much of Colombia and reported in Ecuador, Panama, and Venezuela.

Search and rescue efforts were concentrated in these departments and, as of this date, operations have concluded. In total, 16 accredited Colombian USAR teams, 4 international support teams from the United States, Ecuador and Israel, as well as 34 other support teams were deployed, comprising a total of 1,849 rescuers. These efforts resulted in a total of 356 people rescued and 259 bodies recovered.

According to the UNGRD report of 10 September, in terms of human impact, 778,281 people were reported as affected (364,672 families), with 4,505 people injured and 331 deaths. In terms of infrastructure, 36,327 houses were destroyed, 758 buildings collapsed, and 6,047 buildings and more than 200,000 houses were damaged. Additionally, essential basic services remain in a critical situation, with 4,316 educational facilities and approximately 400 health facilities reported as affected. Likewise, according to the Ministry of Housing, City and Territory, 137 municipalities reported disruptions to water supply, sewerage and solid waste management services, of which 93 have not been able to restore these services. In addition, 286 Colombian Red Cross Society volunteers were themselves directly affected by the earthquake.

The impacts of the earthquake are estimated to have caused direct physical damage to structures amounting to COP 42.1 trillion (USD 13.2 billion), equivalent to approximately 2.3 per cent of Colombia’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The damage is highly concentrated in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, Caldas and Quindío. (UNDP, 2026)1 . Critical disruptions to electricity, telecommunications, and health services have been reported in several affected areas. Airport closures, damaged roads, communication outages, and continuing aftershocks are affecting access to communities and delaying comprehensive damage and needs assessments, particularly in Chocó, where connectivity remains intermittent and some municipalities remain difficult to reach. Pre-existing vulnerabilities, poor health outcomes, and limited access to health services already constrained the ability of communities to cope with additional shocks. On the day of the earthquake, the Government of Colombia declared a national State of Emergency and activated national and departmental emergency management mechanisms. The Colombian Red Cross Society (Cruz Roja Colombiana – CRC) immediately activated its National Crisis Room and emergency response mechanisms. This response is unfolding against the backdrop of the El Niño phenomenon. The Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM)2 confirmed that El Niño conditions are already present in the equatorial Pacific Ocean and atmosphere, with more than 95% probability of strengthening during the second half of 2026 and persisting into the first quarter of 2027, potentially reaching “very strong” intensity comparable to the most significant events recorded since 1950. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)3 , the phenomenon is expected to act as a multiplier of humanitarian risk nationwide, with an estimated 4.3 million people across 508 municipalities (45% of the country) facing severe impacts, particularly water shortages, increased wildfire risk, and rising food insecurity. For the departments already affected by the earthquake, these compounding hazards risk further straining water, health and shelter systems that remain damaged, delaying recovery, and deepening the needs of already vulnerable households.

title: Syrian Arab Republic — Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update — Round 22 (21 September 2026)
content:
Cross-border movements from Lebanon into Syria have continued to stabilise since the ceasefire announced on 17 April 2026, with recent movement patterns becoming more gradual. Between 2 March and 21 September, DTM identified 128,129 arrivals across 1,185 communities spanning all 14 governorates. Syrian nationals accounted for 99 per cent of recorded arrivals, while Lebanese nationals represented less than 1 per cent.

Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded approximately 813,000 movements into Syria during the same period. Of these, around 98 per cent were Syrian nationals and 2 per cent were Lebanese nationals. A further 4,100 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, indicating that Syria continues to serve as a transit route for onward regional movement alongside arrivals into the country.

Access conditions at the border have also continued to shape observed movement patterns. The Arida crossing has remained closed for more than six weeks following its temporary closure on 6 August for technical works on the Lebanese side, with movement data therefore available only through 5 August. KIs reported that those who previously relied on Arida have had to use alternative crossings located further from Tartous Governorate, contributing to longer journeys and increased travel costs.

title: Syria Protection Sector: Key Findings and Analysis Q2 2026
content:
The April-June 2026 monitoring round consolidated information from 5,094 key informant interviews (KIIs) conducted by 48 contributing partners across all 14 governorates, covering 175 sub-districts and 756 communities. The assessment employed a purposive sampling approach. Geographic coverage was concentrated in Aleppo (34% of KIIs), Idleb (26%), and Ar-Raqqa (13%), reflecting the areas with the highest levels of data collection. As a result, comparisons across communities should be interpreted as indicative rather than representative, with findings considered more robust in locations where multiple key informants provided consistent responses. Findings are limited to the protection risks directly monitored through the harmonised Sector Protection Monitoring Tool.

At the national level, the findings indicate that protection concerns remain widespread across assessed communities. Compared to previous rounds the findings also indicate a gradual improvement across several protection indicators. Rather than indicating a broad normalization of protection conditions, the observed trends point to an increasing concentration of risks in specific locations where returns, documentation barriers, HLP challenges, psychological distress, GBV, and EO contamination continue to overlap.

More than half of assessed communities (55%) reported that community members had experienced psychological or emotional abuse or distress, highlighting significant mental health and psychosocial well-being concerns. Likewise, 50% of assessed communities indicated that incidents of violence against women and girls were frequently reported or commonly heard about within their locations, while Housing, Land and Property (HLP) issues were reported in 46% of assessed communities.

The assessment employed a purposive sampling approach. Geographic coverage was concentrated in Aleppo (34% of KIIs), Idleb (26%), and Ar-Raqqa (13%), reflecting the areas with the highest levels of data collection. As a result, comparisons across communities should be interpreted as indicative rather than representative, with findings considered more robust in locations where multiple key informants provided consistent responses. Findings are limited to the protection risks directly monitored through the harmonised Sector Protection Monitoring Tool.

At the national level, the findings indicate that protection concerns remain widespread across assessed communities. Compared to previous rounds the findings also indicate a gradual improvement across several protection indicators. Rather than indicating a broad normalization of protection conditions, the observed trends point to an increasing concentration of risks in specific locations where returns, documentation barriers, HLP challenges, psychological distress, GBV, and EO contamination continue to overlap.

More than half of assessed communities (55%) reported that community members had experienced psychological or emotional abuse or distress, highlighting significant mental health and psychosocial well-being concerns. Likewise, 50% of assessed communities indicated that incidents of violence against women and girls were frequently reported or commonly heard about within their locations, while Housing, Land and Property (HLP) issues were reported in 46% of assessed communities.

Movement restrictions continued to affect access to services and livelihoods, with 47% of assessed communities reporting restrictions on population movements. In addition, the presence of explosive ordnance (EO/UXO) remained a major protection concern, with 41% of assessed communities reporting contamination within or near their locations. Civil documentation challenges also persisted, with 39% of assessed communities reporting that a significant proportion of community members faced difficulties obtaining, replacing, or renewing civil documentation. Similarly, 39% of assessed communities described the overall environment for children as bad or very bad, pointing to ongoing child protection concerns.

Other protection risks remained evident across assessed locations. One quarter of assessed communities (25%) reported having observed or heard about cases of trafficking, child labour, forced labour, or slavery-like practices. Although poor community relations between host communities, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and returnees were reported less frequently at the national level, localized tensions continued to be identified in specific communities, particularly in areas experiencing returns, housing-related challenges, and pressure on local resources and services.

Several communities presented particularly concentrated protection risk profiles, with multiple indicators reported at high levels by Key Informants. The most notable high-risk communities include Suran in Hama, Eastern Buwayda in Homs, Maskana-Onaiza and Eastern Kwaires in Aleppo, Busra Esh-Sham in Dar’a, and Ghabra in Deir-ez-Zor. These locations demonstrated multiple and overlapping concerns related to movement restrictions, civil documentation challenges, HLP issues, child protection concerns, GBV, EO contamination, trafficking and exploitation, and psychological distress.

Returnee arrivals continue to be reported across a significant proportion of assessed communities, with 73% of communities reporting the arrival of returnees from within Syria or from abroad during Round 3. While slightly lower than in previous rounds, this indicates that return movements remain widespread across the country despite considerable geographic variation. Importantly, many returns are taking place in environments where protection concerns remain prevalent. Across assessed communities, psychological distress, GBV, movement restrictions, HLP challenges, EO contamination, civil documentation barriers, and child protection concerns continue to affect a substantial proportion of locations, potentially limiting the prospects for safe, dignified, and sustainable return.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 4 (15 September 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #1 (22 September 2026)
content:
Highlights

§ Escalating hostilities in Yemen have driven significant displacement within the country and cross-border movements across the Gulf of Aden, with close to 130,000 people internally displaced inside Yemen1 and over 3,000 people crossing to Djibouti2 . Arrivals in Somalia remain smaller but are gradually increasing, including Yemeni refugees and Somali refugee returnees.

§ In response to the evolving situation, UNHCR has declared a Level 1 emergency for Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia for three months and is scaling up preparedness and response across the affected operations.

§ In Yemen, UNHCR is taking part to the inter-agency response under the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). In light of the recent escalation, UNHCR requires USD 25 million to support an estimated 231,000 people with protection services including monitoring, legal assistance and support for people at heightened risk, cash assistance, shelter and core relief items (CRIs) inside Yemen.

§ In Djibouti, UNHCR with the Government of Djibouti, developed an interagency appeal for a total amount of USD 13,27 million. The plan reflects a coordinated inter-agency approach covering activities among agencies (WFP, UNICEF, UNFPA, IOM and UNHCR) in support of 10,000 individuals (2,500 households) over a six-month period.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (01-15 September 2026)
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that between 07 October 2023 and 31 August 2026, at least 3,464 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across the occupied Palestinian territory. 95% of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

  • Gaza: 2,375 attacks on health care were recorded during which health facilities were damaged 455 times, 777 health workers were killed and 399 arrested. Patient access to medicine was obstructed on 303 occasions.
  • West Bank: 1,020 attacks on health care were recorded during which health facilities were damaged 32 times, 13 health workers were killed and 198 arrested. Patient access to medicine was obstructed on 626 occasions.

View the incidents on our interactive map. Download the data. Updated every Monday and includes information on weapons use, perpetrators and effects. For data enquiries, please get in touch. Data is continuously updated and numbers may change if/ when further information is made available. See here for methodology.

Read the full SHCC chapter in Arabic and English. See here for methodology.

Documented incidents

01-15 September 2026

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care between 01-15 September 2026. The incidents below have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open source verification protocol.

Gaza
01 September 2026: In Abu Sharekh area, near Abu Sharekh roundabout, North Gaza governorate, a Civil Defence paramedic was injured in an Israeli strike and later succumbed to his injuries. Sources: Quds News Network, Quds News Network I and Quds News Network II

01 September 2026: In Al-Katiba area, west of Gaza city, Gaza governorate, the American Hospital, which was located near a UN shelter, was ordered to evacuate amid Israeli airstrikes and clashes involving an Israeli special forces unit and Palestinian fighters. The Israeli military reportedly carried out at least 13 air raids in the area. Three Palestinians, including two children and a woman, were killed and eight others injured in the strikes. Sources: Quds News Network and Quds News Network I

03 September 2026: In North Gaza governorate, Kamal Adwan Hospital temporarily suspended operations for a day and was evacuated following the advance of Israeli forces and tanks in the vicinity of the hospital amid gunfire. The decision was taken to protect health workers and patients, with services expected to resume on 06 September 2026. Sources: Quds News Network and Quds News Network I

13 September 2026: In Gaza city and governorate, a vehicle carrying 10 MSF aid workers was damaged by an Israeli airstrike on a vehicle traveling two metres away, injuring one of the workers. The bus was clearly marked as an MSF vehicle, with a large MSF sticker visible on its roof. Sources: MSF, Quds News Network and UN News

As reported on 13 September 2026: Across Gaza, an unspecified number of hospital generators stopped due to the unavailability of oil, fuel and spare parts, disrupting the operation of hospitals and limiting their ability to provide electricity to vital and life-saving departments. Only limited quantities of oils that were allowed to enter the Strip. Source: Quds News Network and Shourouk News

West Bank and East Jerusalem
04 September 2026: Near the Khallet al-Murabba junction, west of Al Mughayir village, Ramallah governorate, an ambulance was attacked by Israeli settlers, injuring a paramedic. Source: Quds News Network

05 September 2026: Near Al Mughayir village, Ramallah governorate, an ambulance was blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers. Source: Quds News Network

07 September 2026: In Qabalan town, Nablus governorate, a PRCS ambulance was prevented by Israeli forces from reaching the site where a person was fatally shot during the raid after allegedly carrying out a stabbing attack against an Israeli settler. The ambulance and an ambulance officer inside it were detained by Israeli forces, who also prevented ambulance crews from approaching the site. Sources: Quds News Network and WAFA

08 September 2026: In Anata town, Jerusalem governorate, an unspecified number of ambulances were prevented from reaching injured people and emergency cases due to a curfew imposed by Israeli forces. Source: Quds News Network

08 September 2026: In Khirbet Al-Fakhit, Masafer Yatta area, Hebron governorate, an unspecified number of health units were destroyed by Israeli forces. Source: WAFA

09 September 2026: In Masafer Yatta area, Hebron governorate, a vehicle belonging to Palestinian Medical Relief Society (PMRS) was chased by Israeli settlers. Sources: Quds News Network and Quds News Network I

10 September 2026: In Khirbet al-Hums village, near Yatta city, Hebron governorate, ambulance health workers were prevented by Israeli forces from reaching people who had been assaulted and injured by Israeli settlers at night. Source: Quds News Network

Other resources

Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 432 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care across Gaza in 2025. At least 190 incidents were recorded in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Health workers were arrested, threatened, or injured; health facilities were damaged, violently raided, or surrounded; and ambulances and emergency medical teams were repeatedly delayed, blocked, or searched amid Israeli military incursions and increasingly restrictive movement and access constraints imposed across the West Bank. Most incidents were attributed to IDF troops armed with guns. Attacks on health care linked to Israeli settlers, typically armed with guns or rocks, more than doubled in 2025, compared to 2024, rising from around 2% to 9% of total reported attacks.

Despite the two ceasefires, incidents continued in Gaza throughout 2025, often increasing in conjunction with IDF military movements and ground operations. On average, 2.8 attacks were reported each week during the January 2025 ceasefire, and 1.9 attacks per week from the start of the October ceasefire through December 31, 2025. During both ceasefires, four health workers were killed and two others injured, and the IDF shelled a clinic in Jabalia IDP camp, injuring multiple people, including a pregnant woman. The IDF repeatedly fired at and bombed ambulances responding to emergencies.

Armed drones are an escalating threat in humanitarian settings, with their use expected to grow. Once rare, they are now a defining feature in modern conflicts. Adapting to the growing threat of drones means rethinking security risk measures in high-risk contexts. This practical guide by Insecurity Insight brings together current best practice and is available in Burmese, English, French and Spanish. Individual resources:

title: UNHCR Türkiye Monthly Operational Update (August 2026)
content:
Highlights

UNHCR in Türkiye is working with 12 RLOs and community-based organizations (CBOs) across the country through grant agreements. UNHCR’s engagements with these RLOs aim to foster consultation, community outreach, participatory assessments, protection monitoring, safe identification and referral of persons at heightened risk, and dissemination of accurate information on rights, services and available referral pathways. UNHCR maintains close working relations with the RLOs, particularly from an accountability perspective, and to increase their participation in decision-making processes.

In 2026, UNHCR's RLO grantees in Türkiye delivered a wide range of protection, empowerment and community-based services for refugees and host communities, reaching thousands of beneficiaries in various provinces including Istanbul, Gaziantep, Adana, Kayseri, Trabzon, Uşak, Mardin, and Şanlıurfa.

Organizations such as ARSA, AHCSA, and ASA led awareness-raising workshops and life-skills trainings for children and youth on child rights, prevention of early/forced marriage, and peer bullying, alongside empowerment sessions for women and girls addressing self-protection, communication, and confidence-building. ULFED and SURIAD focused on institutional strengthening and economic inclusion, training RLO representatives in project management and safeguarding, and planning business-dialogue sessions to reduce fraud exposure and expand Syrian entrepreneurs' access to formal labour markets.

title: UNHCR Returns to Syria Regional Update - (September 2026)
content:
REGIONAL OVERVIEW

As of 31 August 2026, an estimated 1.8 million Syrians had returned from neighbouring countries, alongside over 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) who returned to their areas of origin. Return movements continued across the region, although patterns and volumes varied by operation.

This edition focuses on the role of cash assistance in supporting voluntary return and reintegration. Across host countries and inside Syria, cash assistance helps refugees and returnees address practical barriers before departure, during movement and after arrival, including transportation, documentation, baggage, food, shelterrelated costs and other immediate household needs.

Cash assistance is one part of UNHCR’s broader protection and durable solutions response. It complements counselling, legal assistance, information provision, protection monitoring, in-kind support, referrals and community-based services. It is not designed as an incentive to return; rather, it supports refugees and returnees who have already made, or declared, an informed and voluntary decision to return.
