title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #29 (10 to 16 September 2026)
content:
The Situation Report No. 29 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 10 to 16 September 2026.

Highlights

Between 10 and 16 September, IOM continued its multisectoral response in planned camps and affected communities through interventions in Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), shelter, health, mental health and psychological support, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). IOM maintained co-management of camps in La Guaira, strengthened inter-agency coordination, and supported processes related to housing solutions, returns and relocations.

Heavy rainfall in Campo de Golf caused flooding in Sector C and the collapse of the drainage channel connected to the sea, prompting risk assessments by authorities and consideration of relocation alternatives for the accommodated population. IOM supported community dialogue efforts, population profiling and capacity assessments in Mare Abajo II and Polideportivo José María Vargas in preparation for a possible reception of families from Campo de Golf.

IOM strengthened health and mental health activities through mobile outreach, primary health care services, and the launch of a mental health and psychological support needs assessment in César Nieves, Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II and Polideportivo José María Vargas. IOM also expanded coordination with health authorities and humanitarian organizations for epidemiological surveillance and the introduction of specialized services.

IOM also strengthened inter-agency and community coordination through protection, health and WASH technical working groups, as well as through the introduction of new rehabilitation, education, disability inclusion and psychological support services in planned camps.

IOM Activities

IOM maintained management of the Polideportivo José María Vargas planned camp and continued co-management of César Nieves, Campo de Golf and Mare Abajo II together with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Activities focused on continuity of services, infrastructure improvements, community participation, and support for return, relocation and housing solution processes.

In César Nieves, IOM supported the completion of perimeter fencing around the health area and strengthened follow-up on infrastructure, drainage and sanitation needs. In Campo de Golf, IOM facilitated coordination among authorities, humanitarian organizations and community representatives to address environmental risks and potential relocation scenarios. In Mare Abajo II, IOM strengthened community coordination mechanisms and supported the introduction of rehabilitation, education and disability inclusion services. In Polideportivo José María Vargas, IOM continued coordinating services and preparedness measures related to a potential reception of families from Campo de Golf.

IOM continued distributing essential household items in camps and affected communities. During the reporting period, IOM distributed 400 collapsible jerry cans, 170 kitchen sets and 238 hygiene items. To date, IOM has distributed more than 11,077 plastic tarpaulins, 8,304 collapsible jerry cans, 6,890 kitchen sets, 5,770 tool kits, 4,594 solar lamps and 5,166 hygiene items.

In WASH, IOM continued coordinating and monitoring water, sanitation and hygiene services. In César Nieves, IOM strengthened follow-up on water supply, water quality monitoring and sanitation infrastructure. In Campo de Golf, IOM monitored impacts caused by flooding and the collapse of the main drainage system. In Mare Abajo II, IOM coordinated activities related to diarrhoeal outbreaks reported during the reporting period and assessed WASH service capacity in anticipation of possible population movements.

IOM continued providing mobile health services in César Nieves, Polideportivo José María Vargas and affected communities in La Guaira. During the reporting period, 511 health and psychological support consultations were provided. The most common conditions included hypertension, chronic diseases, musculoskeletal conditions, acute respiratory infections, and sexual and reproductive health needs. In addition, three Primary Health Care outreach activities were conducted at the Centro de Alta Tecnología 10 de Marzo and in the communities of Ana Merlo and Miralejos.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal orientation, case management, referrals and coordination of specialized services. IOM also strengthened coordination with authorities and specialized organizations to facilitate access to protection services, psychological support and assistance for people with specific needs.

IOM continued leading sectoral and inter-agency coordination spaces with authorities, humanitarian organizations and community representatives. Key activities included follow-up on the Campo de Golf situation, coordination of relocation processes, and the Shelter, Land and Settlements Coordination Cluster (SLSC), co-led by IOM and IFRC.

In PSEA, IOM continued integrating Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse principles into camp management and community activities, strengthening awareness-raising efforts and dissemination of reporting mechanisms among actors present in the camps.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue monitoring shelter conditions and supporting return, relocation and other temporary accommodation processes while maintaining community participation mechanisms and updated information to strengthen response planning.

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure and services in planned camps, including activities related to drainage systems, water supply, sanitation and infrastructure maintenance.

In WASH, IOM will continue monitoring drainage systems and greywater management, strengthening hygiene promotion activities, water quality monitoring, and follow-up on sanitation infrastructure, vector control and solid waste management needs.

IOM will maintain mobile health services, strengthen referral pathways for specialized care, continue epidemiological coordination with health authorities, and sustain mental health and psychological support activities in camps and affected communities.

IOM will also continue providing protection services, including legal orientation, case management, referrals, prevention of violence against women and girls, child protection activities, and actions aimed at facilitating access to specialized services. In addition, IOM will maintain information management, population monitoring and inter-agency coordination activities to support evidence-based planning for return, relocation and durable solutions processes.

title: Djibouti: New arrivals from Yemen Flash Update No.2 ( 17 September 2026 )
content:
Highlights

  • More than 2,800 people fleeing conflict in Yemen have arrived in Djibouti, nearly half of whom are children.
  • Newly arrivals continue to be transferred to the Markazi site, where the National Office for Assistance to Refugees and Disaster-Affected People is leading registration.
  • Public health risks are a significant concern due to overcrowding, inadequate living conditions, and the potential presence of communicable diseases.
  • Djiboutian authorities, with support from humanitarian partners, are responding to the influx. However, response capacities remain constrained, particularly in the areas of registration, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, nutrition, and food assistance.
  • Authorities and humanitarian partners are appealing for increased donor support to address the needs of new arrivals and host communities.

title: WFP Chad Situation Report, 30 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP reached 566,354 acutely foodinsecure refugees through general food assistance, with women accounting for 51 percent of the beneficiaries.

• WFP is scaling up its response to the rapidly deteriorating situation in Lake Province, where an estimated 75,210 people have been displaced since May 2026.

• Following the official declaration of a cholera outbreak in N’Djamena by the Ministry of Public Health and Prevention, WFP and other UN agencies and partners stand ready to support the Government’s response efforts.

SITUATION UPDATE

Humanitarian Situation:

• Between June and September, crisis levels of acute food insecurity (IPC 3) are expected in Chad’s eastern provinces that host Sudanese refugees, as well as in the western Lake Province, which has a large internally displaced population due to persistent attacks by armed groups, according to FEWS NET’s latest analysis . The analysis also highlights that refugees – more than 940,610 people who have arrived since April 2023, according to UNHCR – remain with limited livelihood opportunities and sources of income. Many refugees continue to rely heavily on food assistance to meet their basic food needs, and significant investments in livelihoods and agriculture, such as the ones under the Haguina initiative, continue to be required. In Lake Province, which hosts more than 294,800 internally displaced persons (IDPs), recent insecurity has led to the abandonment of arable land, population displacement, and a decline in fishing activities.

title: Republic of Türkiye Fact-sheet September 2026
content: Developments in Syria following December 2024 have led to an increase in voluntary returns to Syria, with 723,000 refugees returning by August 2026 from Türkiye, which hosts one of the largest refugee populations globally. UNHCR supports the national asylum procedures and works in coordination with diverse stakeholders, including government institutions, local authorities, and civil society, in advancing refugee protection, inclusion, access to solutions, including voluntary return. Responsibility-sharing to enhance access to social services remains crucial, with an increasing need for diversified and flexible funding for the refugee response, as well as other solutions, such as resettlement and complementary pathways.

title: Doo Tha Htoo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling, air strikes, and arbitrary arrests harmed local villagers in Kyeh Htoh Township (March to December 2025)
content:
This Short Update describes events occurring in Kyeh Htoh (Kyaikto) Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, during the period between March and December 2025. Between March and December 2025, Burma Army and allied militia forces conducted mortar shelling, drone attacks, air strikes, and arbitrary arrests against local villagers in Kyeh Htoh Township and surrounding areas. In March, frequent shelling in and around Kha Ywel village tract forced over 7,500 villagers to flee and relocate. On 21 March and 24 April 2025, militia soldiers and Burma Army Military Operations Command (MOC) #310 fired mortar shells into Ng--- village, Kha Ywel village tract, the former of which killed one monk and injured two others, and damaged a monastery, and the latter of which injured a villager and damaged villagers’ houses and properties. In addition, the shelling and displacement restricted villagers from accessing their livelihoods, healthcare, and essential commodities. On 10 May 2025, a Burma Army Y-12 aircraft dropped five bombs onto Jz--- village, Win Kan village tract. The bombs landed and exploded in the village, injuring two villagers, burning down four houses, destroying two villagers’ houses, and leading 3,000 villagers from Win Kan village tract to displace. On 17 October 2025, Burma Army aircraft conducted air strikes on Wk--- and Pj--- villages, Kyauk Pya village tract, injuring three villagers and destroying and damaging villagers’ houses. On 12 December 2025, the Burma Army fired mortar shells into Jt--- village, A Lu village tract, killing two villagers and injuring one, before entering the village, where the Burma Army then arbitrarily arrested at least 13 villagers and travellers, five of whom remained detained. These attacks were conducted during ongoing military operations and resulted in local villagers’ casualties, property destruction, displacement, livelihood difficulties, food shortages, and medicine shortages. They also increased insecurity among local communities in Kyeh Htoh Township.[1]

Repeated Burma Army mortar shelling caused casualties and displaced local villagers

On 20 March 2025, six cars and four motorcycles of the SAC [State Administration Council,[2] also referred to as the Burma Army[3]] arrived at Rk--- village, Waw Township, Bago Region (Shwegyin [Hsaw Htee in Karen] Township, Kler Lwee Htoo [Nyaunglebin] District).[4] They brought and unloaded four 4-foot-high boxes, including materials and mortars, at the monastery. Mortar shelling was often conducted by the SAC into Gn---, Zm---, Js---, Kr---, and Rk--- villages, Bago Region [an area under the control of the Burma Army], and mostly it landed and exploded on Ng--- village. Consequently, over 2,000 Ng--- villagers had to flee and relocate frequently. Moreover, over 5,500 villagers in Jn---, Sj---, Ld---, Dl---, Nj---, Ik---, and Ng--- villages, Kha Ywel village tract[5] had to flee and relocate frequently because [the SAC], based in Theinzayet army camp, under Light Infantry Division (LID)[6] #44-controlled MOC [Military Operations Command][7] #310 and LIB [Light Infantry Battalion][8] #207, conducted shelling frequently. Therefore, the villagers faced livelihood difficulties and insufficient healthcare.

On 21 March 2025, at 9:33 am, militia soldiers from the house of Aung Gyi, who is a leader of [Burma Army-affiliated] militia soldiers, indiscriminately fired an 81 mm mortar shell from the front yard of his house [garden] to Rk--- village, Waw Township, Bago Region (Shwegyin Township, Kler Lwee Htoo District) [an area under the control of the Burma Army]. The mortar shell landed and exploded on a monastery’s dining hall, located at the northern part of Ng--- village, Kha Ywel village tract, Kyeh Htoh (Kyaikto) Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District (Mon State). As a result, a monk named U[9] G--- was hit by the shrapnel of the explosion on his head and entire body. He died on the spot. Due to the explosion of the mortar shell, two other monks were also slightly injured. The explosion of the mortar shell caused severe damage to the entire monastery. Ng--- village is located in Waw Township, on the other side of the Sittang River [opposite Rk--- village].

Because the SAC often conducted shelling and drone strikes, the local villagers needed to flee and relocate [where they thought it would be safer for them]. Furthermore, there was no humanitarian organisation that came and provided support, so [the villagers] had to face a difficult situation. Moreover, the extreme increase in commodity prices and the scarcity of job opportunities became huge challenges for the local villagers. Mainly, [the villagers] had to go to Theinzayet Town, which is [distance censored for security] away to buy commodities. Regarding this, if they bought a lot of [commodities], [soldiers] at the SAC checkpoint seized the commodities randomly; [the villagers] were being fined due to the commodities, and [SAC] also threatened them [the villagers]. Because of that, the shopkeepers in the villages faced difficulties to store commodities for selling. So, it caused livelihood problems in the villages.

On 24 April [2025], at 2 pm, SAC MOC #310 fired two 120 mm mortar shells. The mortar shells landed and exploded on In--- part, Ng--- village, and the shrapnel hit 34-year-old Ko[10] W---, who was taking a bath at a well. When Ko W--- was taking a bath at the well, he heard the sound of the mortar shelling conducted by MOC. However, he assumed that it was a usual shelling like previous times [which had landed elsewhere, outside of the village], so he did not flee. When he heard the sound of mortar shelling above his head, he quickly fled into an old bunker near the well, but the shrapnel hit his left foot. Ko R---, the younger brother of Ko W---, came to carry him. At that time, MOC #310 fired another mortar shell, and that mortar shell hit bamboos and exploded not too far and not too near to the first one that had landed: it was only around ten yards away. Regarding the explosion of the mortar shell [shrapnel] that hit Ko W---, it hit branches of a lebbek tree [siris tree] near the well and exploded. The distance between the tree and Ko W--- was around two yards, so if it had landed on the ground, maybe he would have lost his life. The SAC conducted shelling constantly, and when the sound of the shelling stopped, the authorities in Kha Ywel village tract transported Ko W---, who was injured by the shelling, to a [self-funded] clinic that is connected [cooperates] with the NUG [National Unity Government][11] in Kyeh Htoh Township, and he received treatment there. [Ko W--- returned home after receiving treatment, but he can no longer walk comfortably as before.]

The tree that the mortar shell hit and exploded was very close the house of 68-year-old U[12] L---, who is the father of Ko W---. Therefore, the house was also destroyed by the shrapnel, and almost all of the materials inside the house were destroyed. Furthermore, the house of the younger brother of Ko W---, located at the western part of their father’s house, was also hit by the shrapnel. The SAC often conducted shelling, and it frequently caused destruction. SAC LIB #207 and MOC #310, based in Theinzayet Town, are under the control of LID #44. LIB #208 and MOC #310 are close; only a fence separates them. At the other side of Ng--- village and the western part of the Sittang River, there is Waw Township, Bago Region (Hsaw Htee Township, Kler Lwee Htoo District) and the SAC army sheltered in the villages that are located there.

The SAC army, which sheltered on the other side of the Sittang River, often conducted shelling into Kyeh Htoh Township, Doo Tha Htoo District, located at the eastern part of the Sittang River. Most of the mortar shells landed and exploded on Kha Ywel village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township. Therefore, the mortar shells often landed and exploded on Ld---, Jn---, Ng---, and Ik--- villages, and it often caused damage as well. The SAC not only often conducted shelling but also used drones [to conduct air strikes and do reconnaissance].

On 12 December 2025, around 2 pm, the State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC),[13] based in KNU [Karen National Union][14]-controlled Kyeh Htoh Township at a gate [checkpoint] located on Than Ta Tan [Iron Bridge], fired two 120 mm mortar shells into A Lu village tract. The mortar shells landed and exploded in Jt--- village, A Lu village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township and the vicinity of Wp--- village, A Lu village tract. The mortar shells killed two villagers and injured one villager [in Jt—village]. The two villagers who were killed were the primary breadwinners for their families, and their family members faced livelihood challenges and displacement following their deaths.

Right after the SSPC mortar shelling, around 60 SSPC soldiers conducted a military offensive into Jt--- village, A Lu village tract, and they stationed at a cemetery located at the entrance of Jt--- village. At 2:05 pm, they fired around seven 120 mm mortar shells into Jt--- village without any skirmish happening. The mortar shells landed and exploded in the northern part of the village in the front yard of the house of U O---. The shrapnel of the mortar shells hit 58-year-old U Q---, who was visiting U O---, at his right ear, and he died on the spot.

Another 54-year-old named U H---, who was visiting Jt--- village and was the one closest to the place where the mortar shells landed, was hit on his stomach and the whole of his left leg was shattered, [leaving] his whole body severely injured [by the shrapnel]. While U H--- was injured, nearby villagers carried him to a nearby clinic. But while carrying him to the clinic, mortar shells [were fired and] landed continually. So, villagers who carried the victim left the victim in front of a monastery located at the centre of the village, and they ran to hide. A few moments later, the victim was taken to a clinic by car [by other villagers]. However, there was too much bleeding, so he passed away [after arriving at the clinic].

Another injured villager was 58-year-old U K---. He was hit by mortar shrapnel on his right thigh. He was not severely injured, so he was taken to Bilin Hospital [located in Bilin Town, administrated by the SAC] and was receiving treatment currently [as of December 2025].

Burma Army air strikes caused injuries and displacement to local villagers and destruction to villagers’ properties

The SAC army from Bago Region launched drones to Mon State [Kyeh Htoh Township] and conducted drone strikes. The local villagers needed to be afraid, and they could not work to secure their livelihood; they lived their lives full of anxiety. Therefore, they had to face a lot of difficulties for their livelihood. The villages located in Kha Ywel village tract are villages near the Sittang River, so most of the villagers worked as fishermen to secure their livelihood. The main time [the best period] for catching fish and frogs is at night. The SAC arrested and hit the villagers who caught fish and frogs at night, and if they saw light, they threatened [the villagers] by conducting indiscriminate firing [of guns], so the fishermen had to face difficulties.

The civilians in those villages had to face not only the scarcity of job opportunities but also an extreme increase in commodity prices. Most of the villagers were daily wage workers, and they did not have extra foods to store for an emergency. Currently [as of December 2025], there were over 5,000 villagers in Kha Ywel village tract. They had to survive difficultly under the danger of shelling and drones strikes. Currently [as of December 2025], the situation of healthcare was that there were no health workers in SAC clinics, so it was the same as having no healthcare. Even though it is a [partially] KNU-controlled area, KDHW [Karen Department of Health and Welfare][15] health workers could not enter [to provide healthcare, as it is a mixed-control area], so the villagers had to go to Theinzayet Town, which is the nearest place to receive healthcare.

On 20 March 2025, at 4:55 pm, [the SAC] launched two drones from Rk--- monastery located in Rk--- village, Waw Township, and the drones flew to Ng--- village, Kha Ywel village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township (Kyaikto Township, Mon State). The drones dropped one bomb near the Ng--- graveyard and one bomb near Zn--- place; in total two bombs were dropped. Therefore, the villagers from Ng--- village were afraid and fled to safe places.

On 10 May 2025, at 4 pm, a Burma military regime Y-12, which is a small reconnaissance aircraft, dropped five bombs onto Jz--- village, Win Kan village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township. The bombs landed and exploded on Jz--- village. Four houses were burnt down, and two houses of villagers were destroyed by the explosion. More than 80 villagers from Jz--- village and the People’s Defence Force (PDF)[16] from Win Kan village tract participated together to extinguish the fire. So, the fire was extinguished in time, and the other houses were saved from the danger of fire. There were approximately 300 houses and around 350 households in Jz--- village.

In addition, because the SAC conducted an air strike against civilians, houses were destroyed. Moreover, two villagers were hit by the shrapnel: 31-year-old Saw[17] M---, the son of Saw T---, was hit on his thighs, arms, and forehead, and 18-year-old Saw Z---, the son of Saw Y---, was hit on his temple. After, they were transported to Za--- clinic, located in Za--- village, Baw Ka Hta village tract, Ler Doh (Kyaukkyi) Township, Kler Lwee Htoo District, administered by the KDHW. Then they received treatment in the emergency room at the hospital. There was no fighting occurring between the Burma Army and an armed resistance force when the air strike was conducted. So, from the villagers’ perspective, the Burma Army deliberately conducted an air strike to attack the village.

However, at that time, the PDF was conducting an operation to capture the base of LIB #598, located in Shwegyin Township in an area bordering Kyeh Htoh Township. When the PDF conducted an operation to capture [LIB] #598 army camp, they [the PDF] were not led by a local KNLA [Karen National Liberation Army][18] battalion; several battalions of PDF combined together to capture SAC LIB #598 army camp. Because the SAC dropped bombs onto Jz--- village by Y-12 reconnaissance aircraft, four houses in Jz--- village, Win Kan village tract, owned by Saw D---, Saw A---, Saw I---, and Naw[19] J--- were burnt down. Also, two houses owned by Saw B--- and Saw X--- were hit and destroyed by the shrapnel from the bomb explosion. Before the SSPC conducted an air strike in Jz--- village, [the Burma Army] had conducted four rounds [of air strikes] in Pyin Ka To Kon village tract and one round in Kyauk Pya village tract: five rounds in total. As a result, a monastery and a school in Wk--- village, Kyauk Pya village tract, were destroyed. The air strike that was conducted in Jz--- village was the fourth round of the air strikes, and it was the first air strike [of the five] which caused injuries to civilians.

The PDF had to advance through Jz--- village to conduct an inspection operation while they were conducting an operation to capture [LIB] #598 army camp, so some of the PDF set up a temporary army camp. So, villagers from the village suspected that the air strike happened because PDF had conducted activities [in the area]. Due to the SAC air strike, [the civilians in] Win Kan village tract, Zi Pyaung village tract, and Kha Yweh village tract mainly had to flee. Even though they fled, only a few of [the civilians] fled to Theinzayet Town, because the SAC have conducted arrests [there]. There were over 3,000 IDPs [internally displaced persons] in Win Kan village tract, and most of them were hillside farmers and daily wages workers. The school in Jz--- village had to close temporarily because of the air strike. In previous years, they [teachers and students from the village] studied in the school. Since a mortar shell landed near the school [on 23 March 2025], the village’s elders participated and built a temporary school to prevent the danger of mortar shells and so the students would be able to study during emergency situations [the ongoing conflict]. The school is not too far and not too close to the village. They [the village’s elders] had to try so that the children would be educated [would be able to access education]. There was no SAC teacher in Jz--- school, so the volunteer teachers in the village had to teach the children. The KECD [Karen Education and Culture Department][20] also could not provide sufficient support [to the school], so the school was run by the villagers independently [as a self-funded school].

On 17 October 2025, at 10:40 am, a [Burma Army] fighter jet conducted air strikes onto a KNU-controlled area in Kyauk Pya village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township. The fighter jet first dropped cluster bombs onto Wk--- village, Kyauk Pya village tract, where the bombs landed and exploded in the village.

The fighter jet then continued its attack by dropping rockets onto Pj--- village, Kyauk Pya village tract; the bombs landed and exploded in [Pj---] village. One of the bombs landed and exploded on the house of a villager [originally] from Wk--- village, named Saw C--- [living in Pj--- village]. The house was completely destroyed. However, the house owners were able to enter their makeshift bunker in time, so none of them were injured. Another bomb landed and exploded in a garden of Saw E---, located behind Saw C---’s house [garden], causing shrapnel damage to the houses of Saw E--- and Saw N---.

Right at the time when [two other villagers from Pj--- village named] Saw E--- and Saw N--- heard the sound of approaching aircraft, they ran as quickly as possible toward their makeshift bunker, but the bomb was dropped nearby them while they were running. As a result, 31-year-old Saw E--- was mildly injured on his right shoulder and his shoulder was minorly burnt; [the injury] was not life-threatening.

The fighter jet continued bombing Pj--- village. One of the bombs landed in the vicinity of the village on a turmeric farm. The bomb did not cause any casualties or destruction. Then another bomb landed on the peanut farm of Saw S--- and caused mild damages to nearby houses owned by Daw[21] V---, Daw Aa---, and U Ab---. Another bomb landed in the backyard of U Ac--- and caused no casualties or damages. In total, the Burma military regime conducted three [rounds of] air strikes on Pj--- village.

Afterward, the fighter jet flew back over Wk--- village and continued dropping bombs onto the [Wk---] village. One of the bombs landed on the football pitch of the village, another bomb landed at the monastery of the village, another two bombs landed in front of the clinic of the village, and another bomb landed in a house garden [of a villager]. In total, five bombs landed and exploded in Wk--- village during this phase of the attack. There were no casualties or [major] damages from these explosions. Overall, the Burma military regime conducted six [rounds of] air strikes on Wk--- village. None of villagers were severely injured during the attacks.

Burma Army arbitrarily arrested villagers and used the villagers as human shields and navigators

On 12 December 2025, at around 3 pm, after the SSPC fired mortar shells [see incident above], they entered [Jt---] village, A Lu village tract, and when it was turning dark [after sunset], they stationed in the monastery located in the centre of the village. When the SSPC entered the village, they arrested travellers and villagers, then used them as human shield and navigators. There were 13 known villagers in total who were arrested and used as human shields and navigators, and the remaining people [arrested by the Burma Army] were unknown since they were travellers.

Five out of 13 arrested villagers were still detained [as of December 2025], and all the remaining villagers were released. Those five villagers who remained detained are 1) Saw Ad---, 2) Saw Ae---, 3) Saw Ag---, 4) Saw Ah---, and 5) Saw Ai---. The SSPC soldiers who conducted the military offensive operations were under the control of LID #44.

Because the SSPC conducted military offensive operations and fired mortar shells, almost all villagers from A Lu village tract fled to places where it would be safer for them. Some villagers fled to nearby villages, some fled to monasteries, and some fled to rubber fields. They faced difficulties because there was not enough food and medicine.

title: WFP Nepal Situation Report on the Rasuwa Flood Response, 17 September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP has dispatched 160 mt of food rations, sufficient for 15 days, to Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa, including 56 mt via air operations reaching 15,700 people.

• The Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster continues to support partners by facilitating the receipt, storage and onward transport of humanitarian cargo to affected areas through road and air operations.

• Ongoing analysis of household food security, market functionality, supply chains and price trends will be critical to informing the most appropriate mix of cash-based and in-kind assistance and ensuring assistance is delivered efficiently, accountably and in line with evolving needs.

Situation Overview

• The humanitarian impact of the floods and landslides continues to deepen, with widespread displacement, extensive infrastructure damage and significant recovery needs across affected districts. Reported fatalities have risen to 1,403, with 6,150 people still missing and 13,742 rescued, while the floods have caused extensive damage to settlements. Over 2,000 displaced people are staying in 29 holding centers in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

• The Government's Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment estimates USD 5.3 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs, with infrastructure accounting for three-quarters of total requirements. Approximately 1.6 million people are affected, 7,570 homes damaged and 783 MW of energy infrastructure has been impacted.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 85, as of 15 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Persistent insecurity in Ouham is causing new population displacement.
  • Survivors of gender-based violence are receiving assistance in Bamingui-Bangoran and Ouham-Pendé.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Ouham Prefecture – West

  • On 12 September, nearly 2,500 people who had recently returned to their areas of origin fled once again to the bush and surrounding villages following reports of gunfire near Pama, about 20 km from Bowaye, in Nana-Bakassa sub-prefecture. On the same day, along the Nana-Bakassa–Bossangoa road, a child died after delays in reaching hospital care when armed men stole the motorcycle being used to transport him. Two days earlier, three civilians from the Fulani community were killed along the Bodé–Kouki–Pama axis amid recurring tensions related to transhumance movements. On 7 September, along the Dékoa–Bouca road, two children were killed and another injured in an attack attributed to armed men. These incidents highlight the continued protection risks facing civilians. They have triggered new displacement, restricted access to essential services, particularly healthcare, and increased the risk of intercommunal tensions.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

  • Mbomou Prefecture, South-East

From 7 to 10 September, ACTED distributed hygiene kits to 500 of the most vulnerable households from both host and displaced communities in Rafaï sub-prefecture. To support economic recovery, 120 young people received training in bakery production and soap-making. ACTED also monitored food crop and vegetable harvests for 40 vulnerable households. The organization completed the construction of a waste management area and an incinerator in Guérékindo, as well as a borehole in Louété. Funded by the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF), these activities aim to sustainably improve access to essential services and livelihood opportunities in Rafaï sub-prefecture.

Protection

Ouham-Pendé Prefecture, West

  • From 7 to 11 September, the Association des femmes pour la promotion de l’entrepreneuriat (AFPE), Maison d’actions pour le développement (MAD) and Arbre de vie pour une nation (AVN) trained 60 protection actors in Bocaranga. During the same period, 50 survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) received medical care and psychosocial support, while two survivors received legal assistance. The three organizations also distributed dignity kits to 50 survivors in Bohong, Boukayan, Létélé and Koumbam. The activity was funded by the CAR HF.

title: Mozambique: The Cost of Inaction (August 2026)
content:
Mozambique is facing converging humanitarian pressures as conflict, displacement, climate shocks and public health risks compound existing vulnerabilities. In the north, conflict continues to uproot communities, while families affected by severe floods earlier this year are still struggling to recover. At the same time, emerging El Niño conditions could deepen food insecurity and livelihood losses. For communities already affected by repeated shocks, each new crisis leaves fewer resources to cope and recover.

In Cabo Delgado, conflict continues to drive displacement and humanitarian needs. Around 1.38 million people are living with the consequences of displacement—662,000 remain displaced while 722,000 have returned. Behind these figures are families repeatedly forced from their homes, children whose education has been disrupted, and communities whose livelihoods and access to basic services have been shattered. For many, returning home is not a return to normal: insecurity, damaged homes, lost livelihoods and disrupted services continue to shape daily life.

Violence is showing no sign of abating. In the first six months of 2026, more than 400 conflict incidents were recorded—10 per cent more than during the same period in 2025. These have included killings, abductions, destruction of homes and looting, with abduction increasingly being used systematically for ransom and forced recruitment, including of children. Civilians are the target of this violence, not its collateral. Displacement has become a key protective strategy, with many people forced to flee more than once, while insecurity is expanding into districts with little previous exposure to conflict and limited protection capacity. Prolonged insecurity and repeated displacement are eroding family and community protection mechanisms, increasing the risks of family separation, recruitment and use of children by armed groups, abduction, gender-based violence, child marriage, sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA), and other harmful coping strategies. As families struggle to meet basic needs and access assistance, women, girls, children and other vulnerable groups face heightened risks of exploitation. At the same time, shrinking humanitarian resources are limiting community-based reporting, survivor assistance and accountability mechanisms. As the conflict reaches new areas and protection systems are stretched, the likelihood of further displacement and worsening protection risks is growing.

Meanwhile, families affected by the floods earlier this year are still struggling to rebuild. More than 724,000 people were affected countrywide, with over 100,000 displaced at the peak of the emergency. Months later, many households are still struggling to rebuild homes, restore agricultural production and replace lost assets.

Emerging El Niño conditions threaten to compound these losses, with below-average rainfall and drought risks expected in parts of the south and centre, while northern areas remain exposed to flooding and cyclones. For families who have not yet recovered, another shock could be devastating.

Public health risks add another layer of vulnerability. Since September 2025, Mozambique has recorded more than 9,500 cholera cases and 89 deaths in the ongoing outbreak, underscoring persistent gaps in water, sanitation and health services. Acute malnutrition is also a critical concern: an estimated 114,000 children under five and more than 23,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women are expected to require treatment in 2026. When conflict, disease, hunger, and climate shocks converge, the consequences are measured not only in immediate needs, but in lives and futures permanently altered.

Yet the resources available to respond remain far below what is needed. As of August 2026, the HNRP —requiring US$534 million—was 43 per cent funded, with approximately US$227 million received. Logistics, Education and Nutrition were among the least-funded sectors, at 9, 13 and 17 per cent, respectively. In some of the most food-insecure districts, food assistance has been reduced to once every two months, covering only 39 per cent of minimum caloric requirements. For communities already living on the edge with insufficient livelihood support to restore self-reliance, funding gaps are not abstract—they mean fewer meals, fewer services and fewer chances to recover before the next shock arrives.

title: WeWorld Flash Update #38 - From Awareness to Action: Child-Friendly, Community-Led Hygiene Promotion in Gaza, August 2026
content:
Across Gaza, civilians continue to face protection risks as military operations, displacement, and insecurity persist. Between 12 and 26 August, 47 Palestinians were reported killed and 176 injured.

Since the October 2025 ceasefire, 1,303 fatalities and 4,336 injuries have been reported. Access and funding constraints continue to limit the scale and continuity of humanitarian assistance.

Living conditions remain critical. Around 1.98 million people require shelter and non-food assistance, while overcrowded displacement sites face poor sanitation, accumulated waste and pest risks. Around 70% of WASH infrastructure is damaged. On 24 August, damage to a water well and desalination facility in Deir Al Balah disrupted safe water access for more than 4,000 people, including around 2,000 children.

Health services remain under severe pressure, while conflict-related injuries continue to generate significant rehabilitation needs. Food insecurity and poor diets further affect children’s health.
TheAugust Gaza SMARTSurvey found chronic malnutrition among 12.2% of children under five in accessible areas, while 37.1% had experienced diarrhea in the previous two weeks.

Children continue to face the combined effects of violence, displacement, disrupted education, and psychosocial distress. As Gaza prepares for the 2026/27 school year, 613 Temporary Learning Spaces (TLSs) were serving 432,701 learners, while an estimated 337,721 children remain underserved.

The Education Cluster identified 546 IDP sites outside the 300-meter catchment area of existing TLSs, highlighting significant gaps in access to safe and inclusive learning opportunities.

WeWorld continues to operate across multiple governorates in the Gaza Strip, delivering integrated WASH and education emergency interventions, prioritizing populations with limited or no access to basic services, especially children, women, and persons with disabilities, while working to restore essential services, strengthen resilience, and reduce protection and public health risks.

title: DSWD DROMIC Report #92 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 17 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan.

The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan Protection Monitoring 2nd Quarter 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

Afghanistan’s complex protection context is characterized by continued large-scale returns mainly from Pakistan and Iran, ongoing displacement, economic hardship, and sustained protection risks, especially for women and girls and other vulnerable groups. Community-Based Protection Monitoring (CBPM) plays a central role in informing protection analysis and response. CBPM enables UNHCR and partners to systematically collect community-reported information on protection risks, vulnerabilities, and coping mechanisms affecting returnees, internally displaced persons, and host communities. By generating regular, area-specific evidence, CBPM supports the identification of priority protection concerns, facilitates the monitoring of protection trends over time, and informs UNHCR programming, coordination, and advocacy efforts. The analysis presented in this report is based on data collected through UNHCR’s CBPM tools in the second quarter of 2026, including household-level surveys, key informant interviews (KIIs), and focus group discussions (FGDs). During the reporting period, revised CBPM tools and methodologies were rolled out to improve the collection, analysis, and reporting of community-based protection information. These tools are designed to generate evidence-based information on the protection needs and risks faced by returnee, displaced, and host communities, and to inform UNHCR programming, strategic decision-making, and advocacy, while also feeding into the analysis and information products of the Afghanistan Protection Cluster. Survey locations are selected based on the concentration of returnees and displaced populations. The CBPM covers UNHCR population groups of concern, including returnees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), IDP returnees, refugees and asylum seekers, as well as members of host communities.

title: UNICEF West and Central Africa Region Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1, 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

Cholera resurged in the Republic of Congo, mpox spread across several countries, and the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo triggered heightened preparedness, surveillance and cross-border coordination.

title: UNHCR Regional Bureau for Europe: Mixed Movements Arrival Trends - 2026 Q2
content:
AT A GLANCE

Overall trend: Seasonal rise, but movements remain well below 2025. In the first half of 2026, more than 43,000 arrivals were recorded, 37 per cent fewer than in the same period in 2025. Arrivals increased from around 19,000 in Q1 to nearly 25,000 in Q2, reflecting the typical seasonal rise, especially on the Central and Eastern Mediterranean routes. Despite this increase, Q2 arrivals remained 35 per cent lower than in Q2 2025, when nearly 38,000 arrivals were recorded. Western Africa Atlantic routes: arrivals increase, but remain below 2025 levels. In the first half of 2026, around 3,700 arrivals were recorded, including just over 2,000 in Q2. While Q2 arrivals were 9 per cent higher than in Q2 2025, they remained 53 per cent below the 2025 quarterly average. Arrivals from Mali continued to decline, while Senegal returned as the leading nationality. Western Mediterranean: Increasingly Algerian and only route running above the 2025 mid-year levels. By mid-year 2026, around 8,500 arrivals were recorded on the Western Mediterranean route, 25 per cent more than in the same period in 2025. Algerian nationals accounted for more than half of Q2 arrivals, up from around one third in Q1, and were the only major nationality to increase in absolute terms. Central and Eastern Mediterranean: becomes the highestvolume route. By Q2 2026, the Eastern Mediterranean became the highest-volume route, with nearly 17,000 arrivals, compared with around 14,500 on the Central Mediterranean. This mainly reflects lower arrivals on the Central Mediterranean, where arrivals in the first half of 2026 were less than half the level recorded in the same period in 2025, rather than a major increase on the Eastern Mediterranean. By mid-year, no single nationality clearly dominated the Eastern Mediterranean route, with Bangladeshis, Afghans and Sudanese each accounting for around 22 per cent of arrivals. South-Eastern Europe: Arrivals remain close to 2025 levels. Around 2,800 arrivals were recorded in Q2 2026, 24 per cent more than in the previous quarter. However, the around 5,000 arrivals recorded in the first half of 2026 remained broadly in line with the same period last year. Arrivals were recorded through Albania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia as part of mixed refugee and migrant movements.¹ Unaccompanied and separated children: represented 12 per cent of arrivals in Q2 2026 (excluding Spain), slightly below Q1. This reflects a higher share of adult men among Q2 arrivals, at 78 per cent, compared with an average of around 70 per cent over the past five years. More than 1,600 people lost their life or went missing2 on Mediterranean and West Africa Atlantic routes in the first half of 2026, compared to more than 3400 in H1 2025. While this represents a decrease of more than 50 per cent in absolute terms, it largely tracks the significant decline in overall movement, particularly the Central Mediterranean.

title: Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) Situation - Regional External Update #41 - August 2026
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Rwanda
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Despite progress in ongoing mediation efforts to end the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), violence continued to drive displacement and protection risks, with around 1.3 million Congolese refugees and asylum-seekers still hosted in neighbouring countries by end-August. UNHCR continued to call for sustained protection, humanitarian access and support to host communities.

• The Ebola outbreak added urgency to the response: transmission in the DRC exceeded 7,200 confirmed cases and nearly 3,500 deaths1 across seven provinces since the outbreak was declared in May 2026. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control declared Uganda Ebola-free after 42 days without a new confirmed case. Continued surveillance, preparedness and community engagement remained essential to protect displaced people and host communities.

• Despite the challenges, voluntary returns to the DRC continued, with more than 70,000 Congolese refugees returning from Burundi in 2026 and tripartite frameworks with Tanzania and Zambia supporting principled, phased approaches. UNHCR and its partners continued working to ensure all returns remain voluntary, informed, safe and dignified, backed by reintegration support.

title: WFP Haiti Country Brief, September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Major attack in Kenscoff (14km from UN country offices) shows evolution of armed groups’ tactics such as large-scale hostage-taking to prevent retaliation/force concessions by security forces.
  • 2026 SMART survey results confirm the deterioration of the nutrition situation, with the Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) prevalence increasing to 7.4%, up from 5.1% in 2023, with urban areas among the most impacted.
  • Slow rate of voter registration imperils targeted turnout for December elections, putting the electoral calendar at risk.
  • Approximately 1.1M people are living in the areas most likely to be impacted by El Nino, with an expected assistance gap affecting 435,000 of the most exposed vulnerable people.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• As Haiti faces significant humanitarian and security challenges, WFP has provided large-scale relief throughout 2026, assisting more than 2.3 million people by distributing USD 53 million through cash transfers and 16,800 MT of food through emergency food assistance, nutrition, school feeding, social protection and resilience activities, while operating UNHAS and logistics activities for the entire humanitarian community.

• The attack in Kenscoff marked a significant turning point in armed groups’ adaptation to a new security environment including the progressive deployment of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF). The attack in an area overlooking the affluent Petionville neighborhood killed at least 47 people, displaced as many as 2,650 people, but also resulted in the kidnapping of over 50 hostages. Such tactics are geared to prevent GSF and police retaliation, with indications they could be replicated in order to exact concessions from authorities.

• Forced returns to Haiti also intensified following the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) in the United States. More than 200 people were repatriated on two U.S. deportation flights within one week, while 116 Haitian nationals were returned from the Bahamas, increasing pressure on already vulnerable communities.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes - Emergency Update #5, 11 August - 15 September 2026
content: As Venezuela moves from emergency relief to recovery, thousands of earthquake-affected families still need documentation, protection services and safe accommodation to rebuild their lives. Through UNHCR-supported protection activities, 7,200 people were reached with critical assistance and services. Across the response, more than 10,038 protection and support services were delivered, including legal assistance, counselling, psychosocial support, case management and referrals for individuals with specific protection needs. To help families meet their most urgent needs, 3,356 people received household and relief items. In addition, 1,456 referrals and 320 case management interventions were completed, ensuring that individuals requiring specialized support could access appropriate services and protection pathways. Efforts to improve safety and living conditions also continued. A total of 1,170 solar lamps and reflectors were distributed and installed in temporary accommodation sites and community spaces.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #9 (September 16, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela less than one minute apart, impacting at least seven states—including the capital Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have confirmed 6,509 fatalities, 6,462 people rescued and 226,696 people who have received hospital care following the quakes.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 8,933 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team Type 1 Fixed facility that has so far provided 7,186 consultations.
  • Our teams have delivered more than 1.2 million liters of safe water across displacement sites, have deployed and maintain 32 mobile toilets and have reached more than 400 people through hygiene promotion sessions.
  • Our teams have provided 1,367 MHPSS consultations.

title: IOM Nepal Flood Response - Situation Report #5 | 15 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

The 26 August flash floods in central Nepal have caused significant loss of life, displacement and widespread damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services. Government-led search and rescue operations are on their twelfth day, while access constraints and ongoing verification of displacement and housing impacts remain key challenges.

As of 14 September, the Government of Nepal reports 1,395 bodies recovered, 5,130 people missing and 13,737 people rescued following the 26 August floods, with figures expected to change as access improves. Preliminary humanitarian analysis estimates 84,270 people affected across 17 municipalities in six districts.

The Government-led Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) indicates approximately 7,570 houses affected, impacting around 32,963 people, alongside damage to roads, bridges, agricultural land and critical infrastructure. Priority needs include shelter and essential household items, WASH, food, health and MHPSS services, protection and access to affected communities. Longer-term support requirements include private housing and settlement, economic activities and livelihood rebuilding, repair and replacement of damaged household energy systems, telecommunications, debris and sediment management, and disaster and climate risk management as the damage to infrastructure continues to constrain humanitarian access and delivery. A Rapid Damage Needs Assessment (RDNA) has also been published by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), which further elaborates on the post-disaster needs. 73% of sites reported inadequate sanitation facilities 46% of sites have inadequate water-storage capacity 51% reported no child protection services or referral pathways 54% reported no safe and private spaces for women and girls

IOM is supporting the Government-led response through site assessments, coordination, health, protection, non-food items (NFI), recovery and Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).
