title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • World Humanitarian Day 2026: Remembering those lost and supporting those who serve
  • One year after the earthquake, OCHA head of office highlights ongoing challenges as survivors and returnees face uncertainty
  • Education and health care remain out of reach for many families in Daykundi
  • OCHA on the ground: Coordination, consultation and community engagement in Bamiyan

WORLD HUMANITARIAN DAY 2026: REMEMBERING THOSE LOST AND SUPPORTING THOSE WHO SERVE

The stories of humanitarian crises are often told through numbers. In Afghanistan, nearly half of the population is expected to need humanitarian assistance this year. Millions face food insecurity, displacement, climate shocks and economic hardship. Behind every statistic are people trying to meet their basic needs, and behind every humanitarian response are individuals who choose, every day, to help others despite immense challenges.

Globally, humanitarian workers are operating in an increasingly complex and dangerous environment, facing conflict, insecurity, funding shortfalls and a sharp rise in attacks against aid personnel. Speaking on World Humanitarian Day from Ukraine, the United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher warned that violence against humanitarians is becoming dangerously normalized. Nearly 1,000 aid workers were killed, injured or kidnapped worldwide over the past year alone. Calling for greater accountability and renewed respect for international humanitarian law, he stressed that, "Behind those grim numbers are names. They are colleagues, they are our friends, they are families, and they are the best of us."

In UN offices around the world, including in Afghanistan, the United Nations flag flew at half-mast on World Humanitarian Day to honour humanitarian workers who lost their lives while serving communities in need. It was a moment not only to remember those who never returned home, but also to recognize those who continue to deliver life-saving assistance, often in some of the most challenging conditions.

For humanitarian workers in Afghanistan, the message resonates deeply. They operate in one of the world's most complex environments, navigating access constraints, limited resources and operational challenges to reach people in need. Their work often requires travelling across rugged terrain, to reach communities cut off by distance or disaster, and support families affected by conflict, displacement, poverty and climate shocks. For Afghan women humanitarian workers, who continue to face severe barriers, the challenges can be even greater, yet their role remains indispensable in ensuring that women and girls can access assistance safely, appropriately and with dignity. Despite these obstacles, aid workers across Afghanistan continue to serve with dedication, resilience and commitment.

Among those remembered this year were Anzira, a psychosocial support counsellor and mother of three, who was killed alongside her young son in the crossfire during armed clashes along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, and Anayatullah Anayat, a 24-year-old humanitarian worker who died in a flash flood during a field mission in Nuristan.

Their dedication reflects the commitment of humanitarian workers across Afghanistan, who continue to reach people in need despite insecurity, natural disasters and operational challenges.

In his World Humanitarian Day message, Bruno Lemarquis, the United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Afghanistan, paid tribute to aid workers serving across the country, particularly Afghan women humanitarians, whose expertise, resilience and commitment remain essential to ensuring that assistance reaches women and girls safely and with dignity. "Humanitarian assistance cannot effectively reach women and girls without Afghan women humanitarian workers," he said.

Echoing the call for solidarity, OCHA Head of Office Amy Martin reaffirmed the humanitarian community's commitment to the people of Afghanistan. She noted, "As needs grow and funding falls short, now is the time for solidarity and action."

The work continues because communities continue to need support. Every food package delivered, every patient treated, every protection case managed and every village reached reflects the efforts of humanitarian workers who keep showing up, often at great risk to their lives.

World Humanitarian Day is ultimately about people. It reminds us that humanitarian workers and those they serve are not anonymous figures in reports. They are mothers and fathers, sons and daughters, colleagues, neighbours and friends. Their commitment to humanity deserves not only recognition, but protection.

As the humanitarian community marks another World Humanitarian Day, the message is both simple and urgent: honour the lives that have been lost, support those who continue to serve and ensure that humanitarian workers everywhere can carry out their mission safely and without impediment. Marking the day, Fletcher added: "An attack on any one of us in our humanitarian movement is an attack on all of us".

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 6, 31 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Humanitarian needs remained acute in July as conflict, displacement, food insecurity, climate shocks and continued arrivals from Sudan affected vulnerable populations. Between January and July, 444,556 people were newly displaced, while more than 13,400 refugees and returnees arrived during the month.
  • ฉholera remained the largest public health emergency, despite a significant decline in transmission. By the end of July, 109,908 cumulative cases and 1,720 deaths had been reported. Mpox, measles and cVDPV1 outbreaks continued to strain health services.
  • Acute malnutrition and access constraints remained major concerns, with critical malnutrition levels in parts of Jonglei, Upper Nile and Unity, including 22.3 per cent GAM in Akobo West. Humanitarian access incidents were 51 per cent higher than during the same period in 2025.
  • Funding shortfalls continued to constrain the response, with the 2026 HAC appeal only 44 percent funded. WASH and education remained the most underfunded sectors, leaving critical gaps in service delivery.

title: WFP Pakistan Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Pakistan, the world’s fifth most populous country, holds significant economic and human capital potential, but continues to face overlapping humanitarian and development challenges that strain the food and nutrition landscape. High stunting (40 percent) and 25 million out-of-school children underscore the vulnerabilities that require continued systemlevel support. These vulnerabilities are compounded by recurring shocks. Monsoon flooding and drought risks continue to affect vulnerable communities. Headline inflation rose to 11.2 percent year-on-year in August 2026.

• The latest Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) analysis indicates that 9.2 million people (17 percent of the analysed rural population) across 51 rural districts are projected to experience acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) during April–September 2026, while over 2.7 million children across 45 rural districts face acute malnutrition, including 706,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM).

• WFP implements its Country Strategic Plan in Pakistan, which supports national development priorities. Alongside the provision of critical relief and nutrition support to vulnerable population groups, WFP’s systems enhancement and technical assistance complements the Government efforts to enhance the food and nutrition security of the people of Pakistan.

title: WFP Bolivia Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Prolonged social unrest and road blockades during the second quarter of 2026 affected approximately one-third of the national territory, disrupting access to food, fuel, and essential services. The situation had a particularly significant impact on the cities of La Paz and El Alto, contributing to food price speculation and increased costs of basic commodities.

• In August, adverse weather conditions affected numerous municipalities and communities across the country, resulting in livestock losses, particularly camelid herds, increasing humanitarian assistance needs.

• Rural and Indigenous communities, smallholder farmers, women, children, and populations whose livelihoods depend on climate-sensitive production systems remain among the most vulnerable groups. These populations face heightened risks of food insecurity, income loss, and limited access to health and social protection services.

• The economic context remains challenging, with projected inflation reaching 9.22 percent, according to the Central Bank of Bolivia (BCB). Economic activity continues to be affected by disruptions to trade, fuel supply constraints, and mobility restrictions.

title: Sudan: GBV Safety Audit Report - North Darfur state / Tawilla (June 2026)
content:
The Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Safety Audit for Tawila locality, North Darfur, was conducted in June 2026 under the technical guidance of UNFPA and in collaboration with GBV Area of Responsibility (AoR) partners. The assessment aimed to identify GBV and protection risks affecting displaced populations, particularly women, adolescent girls, female-headed households, children and persons with disabilities, and to inform safer and more gender-responsive humanitarian programming.

The audit identified significant protection concerns, including inadequate night lighting, overcrowded and unsafe shelters, risks during humanitarian distributions, insufficient and unsafe WASH facilities, limited access to health services, lack of safe spaces, and gaps in confidential GBV and PSEA reporting mechanisms. These challenges continue to affect the safety, dignity and access to essential services of women and girls in Tawila.

The report calls for coordinated, gender-responsive and multi-sectoral action across GBV, Protection, WASH, Health, Shelter/NFI and other relevant sectors. Key recommendations include strengthening confidential reporting and referral mechanisms, expanding women- and child-friendly spaces, improving lighting and shelter conditions, ensuring safer and gender-sensitive distributions, improving access to health and WASH services, and strengthening the meaningful participation of women and girls in humanitarian planning and decision-making.

The Safety Audit provides an evidence base to support coordinated follow-up, protection mainstreaming and implementation of GBV risk-mitigation measures across the humanitarian response in Tawila, North Darfur.

title: Monthly Protection Update - July 2026
content: This monthly protection update for Afghanistan provides a comprehensive overview of UNHCR’s different protection programs, aiming to prevent, mitigate and respond to protection risks faced by vulnerable populations in the context of the current humanitarian crisis and in the absence of durable solutions. The data and insights presented are derived from an extensive protection analysis, collected through a variety of robust tools and systems. The activities include protection monitoring, household assessments, voluntary repatriation, returns monitoring, specialized support for persons with specific needs, community engagement, complaints and feedback systems, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), child protection, women protection, and civil documentation. This update aims to highlight key achievements, ongoing challenges, and the critical needs of the affected communities, ensuring a transparent and effective protection response.

title: Situation Report: Information Update on the Situation in Cuba (August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

● The summer months concluded with record power cuts, which included days with 74% of the island turned off, and at least four episodes of disconnection of the National Electric System. As of May 2026, 2,667,000 tons of fuel had stopped entering the country, compared to what was planned.

● Organizations warn of an "alarming stage" of humanitarian impacts, which already cover all sectors of the population and not just vulnerable groups. UN experts urged the international community to act quickly to prevent Cuba from becoming a "silent Gaza."

● More than 3,500,000 people are affected by the water supply, mostly due to the lack of pumping caused by power cuts. Supply cycles through pipes exceed 60 days in some localities, aggravating the risk of disease outbreaks.

● Infant mortality has skyrocketed particularly in territories such as Havana (14.2, in contrast to the indicator of 5.3 in 2020). Neonatological services exhibit a cascading deterioration, with deficient functioning of pulmonary ventilators, incubators and other equipment requiring a stable electricity supply.

● Sanctions have been increased in the logistics, mining, energy and medical services sectors. Although the channels of dialogue between the governments of Cuba and the United States are maintained, Cuban authorities assured that negotiations are stalled.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 310: Week 1 - September 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained broadly stable during the first week of September, although price movements varied across food commodities, vegetables, fuel, and agricultural inputs. Most staple food prices recorded only modest changes during the week. At the same time, diesel and fertilizer prices remained elevated, sustaining pressure on transportation and agricultural production costs. Overall, market conditions remained relatively stable, although elevated prices of key food commodities and agricultural inputs continued to affect household purchasing power and production costs.

Food Categories:

National food prices remained relatively stable during the first week of September, with most staple commodities recording only modest weekly changes. However, several commodities remained substantially above last year's levels, particularly rice, sugar, wheat, cooking oil and potato.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and flour prices experienced negligible week-on-week changes. While compared with last year, wheat grain and low-price wheat flour remained 13% and 12% higher, respectively, while high-price wheat flour was 7% higher.

• Rice: Minor weekly movements were recorded during the week in Palawi and Sholae rice varieties. However, both varieties remained substantially above last year's levels, at 22% and 35% higher, respectively, and were 22% above their three-year averages.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil, pulses and sugar prices increased by 1.3%, 0.9% and 0.6%, respectively, while bread and salt prices remained unchanged. Year-on-year trends remained mixed, with cooking oil and sugar prices 14% and 11% higher, respectively, while pulses and bread were 12% and 3% lower than last year.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices showed mix movements during the week. Onion prices increased by 4.7%, while potato and tomato prices declined by 1.4% and 0.7%, respectively. Despite the decline, potato prices stand 43% higher than last year and 35% above the three-year average, while tomato prices were 30% lower year-on-year.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): The ToT, which reflects purchasing power, continues to remain under significant pressure for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists due to low demand and higher food prices.

• Casual Labour ToT: Nominal casual labour ToT declined by 1.5% week-on-week to 10.2 kg of low-price wheat flour, remaining 14% below last year and 10% below the three-year average. The decline reflects continued pressure from lower labour wages and limited availability of work.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, which is 13% below last year, 17% below the three-year average. Meanwhile, the average wage rates remain unchanged.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist is able to trade a one-year-old female sheep with purchasing 263 kg of wheat flour, which is 14% below last year and 7% below the three-year average, indicating continued weakness in the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and Agricultural Inputs: Fertilizer prices showed minor weekly movements. However, prices remained considerably above last year's levels, with DAP and urea 13% and 28% higher, respectively. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices were 7% and 5% below last year, respectively.

title: CARE International Emergency Situation Report # 1 - Pacific & Timor-Leste El Niño Drought 2026
content:
1. Executive Summary

As the 2026-27 El Niño event intensifies, drier and drought conditions have impacted much of the Pacific region. More than 6-million people across the Pacific and Timor-Leste are now affected by drought. CARE is currently developing response strategies across the region to target growing needs in areas of WASH, Protection, and Food Security, Nutrition and Livelihoods. The current regional funding target is USD2.44million for an initial 9-month response targeting 62,000 people.

2. Situation Overview

Across the Pacific and Timor-Leste more than 6 million people have been affected by El Niño-induced drought conditions. Worsening food insecurity, water insecurity, and protection risks are leading to a deepening of poverty, increased health and hygiene risks, and heightened gender-based violence (GBV) exposure.

The 2026-27 El Niño event is projected to be the strongest ever recorded. The latest relative Niño3.4 index value for the week ending 30 August 2026 is +2.45 °C, well above the El Niño threshold (+0.80 °C) and warmed by around 0.5 °C over the prior fortnight. The strength of this El Niño, in addition to the typical life cycle of an El Niño, suggests this El Niño may persist into the southern hemisphere autumn 2027. The Australian Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) notes the rate of ocean warming observed in the six months to September 2026 is unprecedented in the historical record, with peak SST anomalies potentially exceeding +3.0°C.1 The European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) has characterised the 2026 event as "potentially historic" and has emphasised that El Niño's high predictability creates a clear obligation for timely anticipatory action.

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is currently neutral. As of 30 August 2026, the weekly IOD index is +0.22 °C. After three-weeks above the positive IOD threshold (+0.4 °C), the index has returned to neutral. Risks of a positive IOD to develop during the southern hemisphere spring.

title: Quarterly Protection & Solutions Report | Q2 2026 (April - June)
content:
PROTECTION ENVIRONMENT SNAPSHOT

The protection environment remained challenging across all 33 camps and on Bhasan Char. The Protection Sector’s Q2 Joint Protection Monitoring Report — which combines protection monitoring inputs from seven partners, including UNHCR — found rising insecurity including: abductions and kidnappings, continued activity by armed groups, and tensions driven by competition over scarce resources and services. Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence SubSector data found an increase in both child protection and gender-based violence cases, predominated by intimate partner violence. See the Q2 Joint Protection Monitoring Report for detailed incident-level data. Protection needs increased amid funding constraints and overstretched services. The border between Bangladesh and Myanmar remains officially closed, but individuals continued to seek safety and protection in Bangladesh. In Q2, UNHCR biometrically identified 6,651 newly arrived Rohingya through a joint exercise with the Government of Bangladesh. Restrictions affecting new arrivals — including the absence of formal shelter allocation — contributed to overcrowding, secondary displacement and heightened protection risks. In May, the hyper-prioritized 2026 Joint Response Plan (JRP) update was launched, with protection programming costs reduced 23% compared to 2025 — reflecting the bare minimum required to sustain life-saving protection needs. UNHCR continued to advance transformation initiatives and business efficiencies to reduce costs, streamline operations and promote localization. Efforts included: rationalization of protection partners now implementing efficient integrated case management; integration of child protection, gender-based violence and community-based protection facilities and services; fewer border monitoring missions; and staff reductions or hybrid staffing arrangements, such as protection focal points comprising both UNHCR and partner staff, reducing costs while promoting localization. However, these intensive efforts could not offset funding gaps at current levels. Without fresh funding, pipeline breaks are anticipated in registration, community-based protection, protection case management, child protection case management and outreach activities, and specialized gender-based violence services. Findings by protection partners continued to highlight the link between funding reductions, deteriorating camp conditions, and increasing protection risks. Community feedback and protection monitoring highlighted growing reliance on negative coping mechanisms, including gambling, child labour, child marriage and human trafficking. Trafficking trends continued to worsen, reflecting ongoing economic hardship, limited opportunities and heightened vulnerabilities within the refugee population. Meanwhile, the quarter also saw the emergence of Rohingya youth groups advocating for stronger community protection mechanisms.

title: Yemen SLSC Situation Update – Aden, Taiz & West Coast - 13 September 2026
content:

Hostilities escalating on 3 September across Taiz, the West Coast, Aden Hubs including Hays, Al Khukha, Al Mukha, Mawza, Alwazyah, Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, Almaafer and Almadharibah, triggering one of the sharpest spikes in new and secondary displacement there and placeing additional pressure on receiving sites. title: Yemen: Situation Update #2: Escalation of hostilities and displacement across Yemen (As of 9 September 2026)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Some 11,442 households have been newly displaced countrywide since hostilities escalated on 3 September: 10,310 households across 15 districts in the Ta’iz hub (8,628 in Ta’iz and 1,682 in southern Al Hodeidah), 1,037 in the Aden hub (Lahj 462, Aden 299, Abyan 180 and Ad Dale’ 96) and 95 in Al Bayda, Marib and Sana’a. figures are preliminary and may include some double counting. Fighting continues along the western Ta’iz frontlines (Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi and Mawza’) and in southern Al Hodeidah, while airstrikes and military activity have also been reported along the Marib–Al Jawf axis and in Al Bayda.
  • Displacement remained highly fluid on 8–9 September, with new arrivals reported in Jabal Habashi, Al Ma’afir, Ash Shamayytayn, Al Mudhaffar, Al Misrakh, Al Makha and Al Khukhah. The latest movements indicate a particularly rapid increase in displacement towards Hays and Al Makha, which have emerged as key reception areas for families fleeing the expanding hostilities along the west coast. Continued fighting and shifting frontlines are likely to trigger further displacement and secondary movements.
  • Several existing IDP sites are overwhelmed. At least 908 households are families who were already displaced and have fled IDP sites.
  • West coast access deteriorated on 9 September. Movement was temporarily suspended between Al Makha, Al Khukhah and Hays, and between Aden and Al Makha. Movement within the affected towns was highly restricted, no movement permits were issued and partner staff worked from home.
  • Displacement has also extended southwards into the Aden hub, with more than 1,000 households reported arriving in Lahj, Aden, Abyan and Ad Dale’, with Lahj receiving the largest share. Many newly displaced families are staying with host communities or in self-settled locations outside routine site monitoring, which may limit the completeness of available figures.
  • Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) partners have verified 4,116 households and assisted 2,723 since 2 September; 2,127 verified households are awaiting assistance.
  • Response coverage remains low. Food Security and Agriculture Cluster (FSAC) partners have reached 1,554 of 6,144 households identified for emergency food assistance, leaving 4,390 households without confirmed response coverage, after accounting for planned assistance.; Cash and Markets Working Group (CMWG) partners have reached 1,381 households with emergency multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA); and Shelter partners have reached 147 households against a planning caseload of 11,000 households. No WASH deliveries have yet been verified.
  • Civilian casualties: Between 1 and 9 September, OHCHR verified 14 civilian casualties across eight incidents in Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah, including two children killed, with women and children among those injured. Four additional incidents in Ta’iz, Lahj, Marib and Al Jawf remain under verification and are not included in the verified figures.

title: Yemen: Situation Update #1: Escalation of hostilities and displacement in Ta'iz and southern Al Hodeidah (As of 7 September 2026)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 5,688 households have been reported displaced across Ta'iz and southern Al Hodeidah between 3 and 7 September, following the escalation along the Maqbanah–Jabal Habashi frontlines and their extension to the west coast. Figures remain preliminary and subject to verification and overlap checks.
  • Fighting continues across frontlines. The most volatile areas remain Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, Hays, Mawza' and Al Wazi'iyah, with frontlines continuing to shift in Ta'iz. Displacement is fluid, secondary movements are already being observed and further displacement remains likely while hostilities persist.
  • OHCHR verified data indicates that civilian harm increased markedly in August, documenting 11 incidents that resulted in 54 civilian casualties, including 12 deaths and 42 injuries; since the escalation of hostilities in early September, OHCHR has verified a further 11 civilian casualties across five incidents in Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah — two children killed and nine civilians injured — while four additional incidents in Ta’iz, Lahj, Marib and Al Jawf remain under verification and are not included in these figures.
  • Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) partners have assisted 2,340 households as of 6 September: 1,887 in Ta'iz, 269 on the west coast, 9 in Marib, and 175 households displaced from Marib to Abyan, while 2,636 households have been verified and registered for response in the Ta'iz hub.
  • Around three in four newly displaced households lack adequate shelter, and families are sheltering in open and informal sites without site management coverage.
  • Humanitarian access remains a major operational constraint. Maqbanah is inaccessible, due to road conditions. Distributions in Mawza', Al Wazi'iyah and Hays were suspended between 5 and 7 September.
  • Stocks need replenishment to support an urgent scale-up. Shelter/non-food items (NFIs) partners report a combined funding gap of some US$3.0 million with no contingency stock, the RRM requires US$7.07 million to bridge urgent gaps, and 1,087 households — around 23 per cent of the identified emergency food caseload — have no confirmed response.
  • Al Makha seaport has sustained significant damage and activities are suspended, with implications for markets and supply that have yet to be assessed.

title: IOM Haiti - Situation Report (August 2026)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

As Haiti’s displacement crisis remained at unprecedented levels in August 2026, humanitarian needs were driven by persistent insecurity, repeated population movement, and mounting pressure on host communities and essentials services. Displaced households across affected areas continued to face significant shelter, WASH, health and protection needs. Against this backdrop, localized incidents of armed violence triggered new displacement and humanitarian needs in several affected areas. A major incident in Kenscoff, West Department, southeast of Port-au-Prince, resulted in civilian casualties, destruction of homes, and the displacement of more than 4,200 people according to IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). The incident followed similar violence in July 2026 that had already displaced nearly 6,000 people in the municipality, underscoring the continued deterioration of the security situation and its humanitarian consequences. Despite these challenges, IOM and partners continued to deliver life-saving assistance, including shelter, WASH, health, protection and site management support, while advancing recovery and stabilization efforts.

title: IOM Colombia Earthquake Situation Report #9, 10 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

On August 10, 2026, Colombia was affected by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake, with its epicenter in San José del Palmar, Chocó. In view of the scale of the event, the National Government declared a national disaster and subsequently declared a State of Economic, Social and Ecological Emergency, enabling the activation of mechanisms for response, recovery and reconstruction efforts.
The departments of Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda and Caldas remain the priority departments due to the level of impact. The response is led by the National Government through the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD). In coordination with territorial authorities. The international humanitarian community complements these efforts through the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) and Local Coordination Teams (LCTs), in line with the needs and priorities identified in the affected areas.
Over the past month, needs arising from the earthquake have evolved from immediate assistance to affected populations toward recovery and rehabilitation requirements. During the initial phase, key needs included assistance to injured and affected people, search and rescue, food, temporary shelter, safe drinking water, and continuity of essential services, alongside access and communication challenges that limited the delivery of assistance to some areas.
Subsequently, priorities have focused on ensuring adequate living conditions, protection, and psychosocial support in temporary shelters; expanding housing alternatives and cash assistance; and ensuring the continuity of health and education services. Critical information gaps persist, particularly in rural areas and small and non-capital municipalities, hindering the adequate identification of needs. In addition, adverse weather conditions, which in departments such as Chocó have caused flooding and landslides, are exacerbating existing needs..
At the same time, priorities are shifting toward the recovery of damaged housing and infrastructure, including structural safety assessments and the rehabilitation of educational and road infrastructure.

Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 17 (31 August to 6 September 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

30,560,048 Health screenings supported at PoEs/PoCs 230 PoEs/PoCs supported across affected and at-risk countries 26,500,916 Individuals reached through RCCE activities According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), over 6,200 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) had been reported as of 1 September and more than 3,000 confirmed deaths. The outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of a longstanding triple crisis in eastern DRC, where conflict, displacement and health risks converge, leaving internally displaced persons (IDPs) and mobile populations at heightened risk. Over 50 IOM-managed IDP sites in eastern DRC, located in the areas of Ituri and North Kivu, are impacted by the outbreak. Inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health and shelter services accelerate risks of disease transmission and compound vulnerabilities, impacting the safety and protection of displaced, mobile and host communities. Over 10 per cent of the journeys originating in affected areas of Ituri Province led to a zone without new cases, as per latest data from IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). Nearly 4 per cent of travellers leave Ituri for other locations across DRC, including Kinshasa, as well as to other countries, including Uganda and Tanzania. At the same time, data indicates a total of 171 fatalities intercepted at points of control (PoCs) – highlighting the continued importance of expanding health operations across DRC to effectively detect, prevent and respond to potential new cases. Given ongoing transmission in Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé Provinces in DRC, bordering the prefectures of Haut-Mbomou and Mbomou in CAR, there remains a high risk of cross-border spread. Porous borders, informal crossings and frequent cross-border population movements linked to trade, family ties, health-care-seeking behaviours, livelihoods, displacement and insecurity may facilitate transmission and compound existing humanitarian vulnerabilities. Investments in preparedness, including strengthening screening, community and event-based surveillance, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, alongside strengthening data systems and pre-positioning of essential supplies at priority border locations, are therefore urgently required to support early detection and mitigate cross-border spread. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, particularly at points of entry (PoEs), PoCs and in displacement sites, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries. IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of cross-border transmission. Preparedness interventions are also implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, the Central African Republic (CAR), Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

title: Ukraine Health Cluster Bulletin #7 (July 2026)
content:
• Ukraine recorded its deadliest month for civilians since May 2022, and most severe overall since March 2022. According to UN HRMMU, 437 people were killed and 2,610 injured, up 30 per cent from June and 70 per cent compared to the same period in 2025. Long-range missiles and drones remained the leading cause of civilian casualties.
  • Kyiv was among the hardest-hit cities, including a 2 July attack with 74 missiles and nearly 500 drones that killed 30 people, and a further strike on 6 July, killed 19 and injured 60. On 19 July, 41 ballistic and hypersonic missiles were launched at Kyiv, marking the largest single wave to date, according to ACLED. Other urban centers, like Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Kherson, were also heavily affected. Health partners continue to provide support to first responders, reaching 1,067 people and prepositioning to health facilities for the treatment of 2,495 people, as of 31 July.
  • Attacks affecting warehouses, medical supplies, and health logistics have become an increased concern, with incidents intensifying through July into the publication period. Between January and July 2026, UN OCHA recorded 20 humanitarian warehouses damaged or destroyed, while WHO SSA verified 9 attacks on health care impacting warehouses, both humanitarian ones and those used by regional health authorities. This damage, combined with disruptions to partner operations, is having a considerable impact on health service delivery in frontline areas.
  • Increased use of glide bombs in areas closer to the frontline, combined with short-range drones, is intensifying risks for civilians and for the delivery of health services; UN OCHA recorded 210 humanitarian access incidents in 2026. Shelling, attacks, and disruptions to essential services such as water and gas continue to drive displacement. Across transit centers where health partners operate, 21,482 people were registered in July; a 35 per cent more than in June. For the first time, Dnipropetrovska oblast was the leading area of origin with more than 8,000 evacuees, followed closely by Donetska oblast. Health partners provided 4,471 health consultations in July 2026.
  • Health Cluster participated to the inter-sectoral preparedness plans to protect water supply to health facilities across Odesa, following attacks on Chornomorsk’s pipeline that cut water access for over 100,000 people. The Health Cluster also monitored the public health consequences of damaged water supply affecting health facilities and communities in Kharkivska and Dnipropetrovska oblast.

title: COI Query - Cuba: Situation of people living with HIV/AIDS
content:
Situation of people living with HIV/AIDS

1. Legislation and implementation Information on legislation and implementation related to HIV/AIDS was scarce among the sources consulted by EUAA within the time constraints of this query response. However, the following information may be relevant.

Article 42 of Chapter 5: Rights, Duties and Guarantees, of the Constitution of Cuba (2019) states that:

‘All people are equal before the law, receive the same protection and treatment from the authorities, and enjoy the same rights, liberties, and opportunities, without any discrimination for reasons of sex, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, ethnic origin, skin color, religious belief, disability, national or territorial origin, or any other personal condition or circumstance that implies a distinction injurious to human dignity’.1

A 2023 Spanish-language article by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) on gender and human rights barriers in the HIV response, stated that Cuba has updated its regulatory framework in recent years, further promoting the reduction of gender inequalities, respect for human rights, and efforts to combat HIV-related stigma and discrimination, as well as discrimination based on other personal characteristics. More specifically, according to the article, the Constitution of the Republic of Cuba (2019), the National Program for the Advancement of Women (PAM) (2021), the Comprehensive Strategy for the Prevention and Attention to Gender Violence and in the Family Setting (2021), and the Family Code (2022) were among the regulations with the greatest impact in this regard. These instruments allowed for a more comprehensive approach to discrimination by incorporating considerations relating to gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity, which were identified as fundamental aspects in addressing structural obstacles to equality, inclusion, and sustainable development.2 Corroborating information could not be found.

A 2023 Spanish-language UNDP report on rights and legal literacy in the national response to STIs, HIV and hepatitis indicated that Cuba does not have a special criminal law for people living with HIV that criminalizes HIV transmission or exposure.3 However, Article 232 of the 2022 Penal Code, ‘Propagation of Epidemics’, criminalises anyone who maliciously spreads or facilitates the spread of a disease, with a penalty of three to eight years’ imprisonment.4

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 19 - 31 August 2026
content:
Armed drone strikes affecting health care occurred in multiple contexts, including direct attacks on hospitals, as part of wider assaults on towns and during multiple strike attacks targeting health workers conducting search and rescue operations. In total, these drone strikes damaged or destroyed health care facilities on 246 occasions and killed 37 health workers while injuring 124 others. The strikes disrupted service delivery through program closures, reduced access and staff shortages, as well as the psychological impact on the health work force.

The use of drone-delivered explosives impacting health care surged by 43% in 2025, with 410 incidents recorded, compared to 286 in 2024. These incidents accounted for 34% of all incidents where explosive weapons affected health care in 2025, up from 16% in 2024. Incidents were reported in 12 countries in 2025 – one more than in 2024 – with new incidents of drone use impacting health care documented in the DRC, Iran, and Yemen.

SHCC Attacks on Health Care
This section aligns with the definition of attacks on health care used by the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC).

Africa
Democratic Republic of the Congo
19 August 2026: In Birambizo locality, Rutshuru territory, North Kivu province, Birambizo General Referral Hospital was looted by unidentified armed perpetrators, who stole medicines, medical equipment and office supplies. The looting occurred on the same day that the hospital resumed activities following nearly four days of suspension, disrupting the provision of healthcare and access to care. Source: All Africa

Publicly reported incidents affecting Ebola response measures in the DRC
17 August 2026: In Kandoyi village, Aru territory, Ituri province, Kandoyi Health Centre was vandalised, and health workers were threatened by community members amid tensions related to the Ebola response, forcing almost all patients to leave the facility, including recently operated patients and pregnant women. Only a few health workers returned to provide minimal emergency services, while the medical director returned to the facility on 22 August under protection from the Congolese National Police (PNC). Source: Radio Okapi

18 August 2026: In Malikuti village, Rungu health zone, Haut-Uélé province, two Red Cross volunteers conducting an Ebola burial were attacked and injured by local community members and later were evacuated to Isiro for medical care. Sources: All Africa, Health Policy Watch and International Committee of the Red Cross

19 August 2026: In Beni city, North Kivu province, three Red Cross volunteers participating in Ebola response activities were attacked and injured by a group of individuals, disrupting the provision of emergency health and humanitarian services. Equipment used in the intervention was also destroyed. Sources: All Africa, Health Policy Watch and International Committee of the Red Cross

19 August 2026: In Kasanga Tuha village, Bunji health zone, North Kivu province, an Ebola safe and dignified burial team was attacked by unidentified perpetrators, killing and injuring an unspecified number of people. Source: Actualite

19 August 2026: In Mungamba village, Komanda health zone, Irumu territory, Ituri province, a vehicle used by an Ebola safe and dignified burial team was stoned and damaged by unidentified perpetrators while the team was conducting response activities. The team was subsequently escorted by the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC). Source: Actualite

27 August 2026: In Vuromo-Kakuva locality, Mukuna area, Katwa Health zone, Beni territory, North Kivu province, Bethesda Dispensary was set on fire by unidentified perpetrators at around 0100hrs amid rumours linked to the Ebola virus disease. Source: Actualite

Data by Insecurity Insight shows that since the outbreak on 21 May and 31 August 2026, 47 attacks on Ebola response measures have been reported in the DRC. Ebola treatment centres have been attacked and damaged 14 times, including nine cases of facilities being deliberately set on fire. In addition,16 response workers were injured and seven others kidnapped. Data is collected daily, with continuous backdating as new sources and incidents are identified or additional information becomes available. Therefore, the data may differ from the version retrieved on 04 September following subsequent updates.

title: occupied Palestinian territory (oPt) Situation Analysis: [24/8/2026] - [30/8/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 110 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 5 Sep 2026
content:
In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Colombia Emergency Response, Situation Report #2 (18 August – 10 September 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

466,709 People affected 101,416 Uninhabitable homes Colombia continues to face a large-scale humanitarian emergency following the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck San José del Palmar, Chocó, on 10 August. As of 9 September, at least 466,709 people had been recorded as affected across 15 departments and 496 municipalities. The earthquake has also caused widespread disruption to essential infrastructure, affecting 400 health facilities and 141 water supply systems, alongside thousands of educational and community facilities.ii

The impact is particularly severe in Chocó and Valle del Cauca. In Chocó, the earthquake is compounding pre-existing vulnerabilities linked to armed conflict, displacement, geographic isolation and limited access to basic services. Humanitarian access remains especially difficult in rural areas, including Litoral del San Juan and San José del Palmar.

Affected communities face significant and overlapping humanitarian needs, from access to food, safe water and adequate shelter to protection and psychosocial support. Mental health and psychosocial impacts have emerged as one of the major consequences of the disaster, with anxiety, acute stress, hypervigilance, insomnia and persistent fear of further aftershocks continuing three weeks on.iii CESVI’s field consultations also point to other emerging protection risks: in Buenaventura, informants reported looting of damaged or abandoned homes and individuals posing as humanitarian staff to gain access to houses.iv

Further, consultations conducted by CESVI with the Buenaventura Mayor’s Office and Secretaría de la Mujer, together with women community leaders from the San Francisco neighbourhood, highlighted the disproportionate impact of the earthquake on women heads of household, caregivers and small entrepreneurs, whose livelihoods and care responsibilities are closely interlinked.

These findings form part of CESVI’s expanded Rapid Needs Assessment, building on the initial assessment presented in SitRep#1, covering the period 10 - 17 August. Between 12 and 27 August, CESVI carried out 776 household surveys and 35 key informant interviews with community leaders and referents across Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), Quibdó, and other municipalities of Chocó. A rapid WASH assessment of 5 collective shelters in Quibdó was also conducted on 24 August. The findings confirm persistent, and in some cases worsening, needs across housing, livelihoods, protection and psychosocial wellbeing, as outlined below.

title: BIH: Fire - 10-2026 - #2 (2026-09-10)
content:
Description

During 9 and 10 September 2026, Bosnia and Herzegovina experienced multiple simultaneous forest and vegetation fires, with the most critical situation reported in the Konjic area. High temperatures, dry vegetation and intermittent strong winds complicated firefighting efforts across several locations, while some roads were temporarily closed due to heavy smoke and the immediate fire threat.

The most significant wildfire occurred in the Repovica area near Konjic, where the fire line advanced towards the settlements of Galjevo and Ovčari. Fire suppression operations involved the Konjic Professional Fire Brigade, Jablanica firefighters, the Neretvica Volunteer Fire Brigade, Prenj Forestry Service, Civil Protection teams, the Federal Civil Protection Air Tractor aircraft and local residents. Due to the seriousness of the situation, helicopter support from the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina was also requested. According to the Konjic Civil Protection and Fire Service, the Repovica fire has been contained; however, all response teams remain deployed due to continuous flare-ups. At the same time, active fires remain in the Dabića Poljana, Ratkamen, Ćesim and Ljubuča areas, while the fires in Bitovinja and Čuhovići–Delića Polje have been contained and are being monitored by local residents.

Between Konjic and Mostar, the wildfire affecting the Rujište–Borke section resulted in the temporary closure of the main road due to dense smoke and the risk of further fire spread. Firefighters from Konjic and Mostar continued protecting the road corridor and surrounding terrain. At Rujište, the fire remains under control, although response teams continue monitoring the area because of the risk of reactivation caused by strong winds.

In the Prozor-Rama municipality, fires remain active at several locations, including Dašnjik, Kozo, Markešići, Ljubuša and Proslap, where strong winds have repeatedly reignited flames and complicated suppression efforts.

In Jasenica near Mostar, the wildfire affected forested areas and low vegetation, destroying several electricity poles and increasing the risk of power supply disruptions. The fire has been brought under control, while emergency services continue monitoring the affected area. At the same time, a separate vegetation fire broke out in Zagrebačka Street in Mostar near the Rondo area, affecting grass and low vegetation on private land before being quickly contained.

In the Tomislavgrad municipality, one of the country's largest fire fronts extended over more than 20 kilometres at its peak, threatening forests, pastureland and agricultural areas. In Tuzla Canton, the wildfire near Živinice required approval for the deployment of Armed Forces helicopters, reflecting the complexity of the incident and the need for additional aerial firefighting capacity. An active wildfire was also reported on Mount Treskavica, where inaccessible terrain and intermittent strong winds continue to hinder suppression operations.

According to the operational assessment of the Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina, approximately 2,350 to 6,200 people are located in areas potentially exposed to the direct or indirect impacts of these wildfires, including smoke exposure, possible evacuation needs, electricity disruptions and transportation restrictions. The highest risk remains in the Konjic area, while rural communities in Prozor-Rama, Tomislavgrad, Mostar, Živinice and the Treskavica mountain area also remain affected.

NS Requests International Assistance: No

No

General

Other

Monitoring the situation on the ground, while maintaining communication and coordination with representatives of the Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCSBH).

Actions taken by RCRC

General

Other

Summary

No need for now

Actions taken by National Society

General

Water & Sanitation

Other

Summary

Red Cross Mostar staff are actively participating in the work of the Crisis Headquarters and continue to monitor the situation on the ground. The Red Cross Živinice deployed teams to the affected area and distributed water to the protection and rescue services involved in the firefighting operations.

Actions taken by others

Government authorities and Civil Protection services have mobilised available firefighting and emergency response capacities to contain the active wildfires. The Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina have been authorised to provide helicopter support for firefighting operations, while the Federal Civil Protection Administration has deployed aerial firefighting capacity, including an Air Tractor. Local Civil Protection services, professional and volunteer fire brigades, forestry services and local communities continue to participate in firefighting and monitoring activities. Traffic has been temporarily restricted on some road sections affected by fire and smoke.

title: DSWD DROMIC Report #80 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 11 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan.

The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.
