title: Chad: Project Highlights
content:
Improving food security and nutrition and women’s empowerment in communities of eastern Chad province of Wadi Fira affected by the Sudan crisis

Objective

To protect and strengthen agricultural and pastoral livelihoods, improve the food security and nutrition of vulnerable households, promote the empowerment of women and contribute to social cohesion among refugee, returnee and host communities in the department of Dar-Tama, province of Wadi Fira.

Activities implemented

• Distributed a total of 20 125 kg of rainfed seeds, including 4 375 kg of millet, 1 750 kg of cowpea and 14 000 kg of groundnut to 350 farming households (12.5 kg of millet, 5 kg of cowpea and 40 kg of groundnut per household).

• Distributed an additional 1 050 vegetable seed packages (52.5 kg in total) to the 350 households, including 350 tomato, 350 okra and 350 onion seed packages (one 50-g package of each seed type per household) and tools (one shovel, one daba hoe, one local hoe, one watering can, one rake and one pickaxe).

• Trained 20 household representatives on gender, nutrition and agricultural techniques, including food groups and hygiene, technical guidelines for vegetable crops, soil fertilization techniques and integrated pest management.

• Distributed 49 tonnes of cotton seed cake and 40 tonnes of nutritional blocks (140 kg of cotton seed cake and five 20-kg cartons of licking blocks per household) to 350 pastoral households.

• Organized a livestock vaccination campaign, vaccinating 97 880 animals and deworming an additional 4 763.

• Rehabilitated three pastoral wells in the canton of Koursigué.

title: South Sudan: Project Highlights
content:
Support to the vulnerable livelihoods of agropastoralists in South Sudan

Objective

To safeguard the livestock assets of agropastoral and pastoral households affected by floods.

Activities implemented

• Trained 62 community animal health workers (CAHWs) in disease surveillance and equipped them with animal health kits comprised of essential supplies (antibiotics, vaccines and dewormers).

• Built one multipurpose solar-powered borehole in Tonj South.

• Distributed vegetable seeds and tools to 25 people (women and youth) and provided training on good vegetable production practices.

• Constructed a milk bar in Juba County and trained 30 people, including 28 women, in milk production, processing and marketing and financial management.

Results

• Enhanced CAHWs’ capacities to actively carry out livestock interventions, accurately recognize and identify diseases, report animal health issues and administer vaccines effectively, leading to a reduction in disease incidents and livestock mortality.

• Protected livestock assets of 17 661 households through the treatment of over 605 000 animals by trained CAHWs.

title: IOM Colombia Earthquake Situation Report #8 03 September 2026
content:
On 10 August 2026, Colombia was struck by a magnitude 7.4 earthquake, with its epicenter in San José del Palmar, Chocó. Given the scale of the emergency, the National Government declared a national disaster situation and an Economic, Social and Ecological Emergency. Since then, Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, and Caldas have remained priority departments due to the extent of the impact.

In Colombia, the emergency response is led by the National Government, within the framework of the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD) and under the coordination of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD). At the territorial level, departmental and municipal authorities, and local UNGRD personnel guide the identification of needs and response priorities.

The international humanitarian community complements the National Government- led response by aligning its capacities with the priorities identified by the authorities. At the national level, this coordination takes place through the Humanitarian Country Team (EHP) and, at the departmental level, through Local Coordination Teams (ELCs), in coordination with territorial authorities.

title: Brazil, Rio Grande do Sul | Floods - Final Report (MDRBR011)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Between 29 April and 4 May, heavy rainfalls devastated Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, causing floods, landslides, and mudslides. This catastrophic event, the worst climate disaster in the state's history, affected 478 out of 496 municipalities. Over 1,000 millimetres of rain fell during this period, leading to significant destruction1. By 20 August, the Brazilian Civil Defense reported that 2,398,255 people were affected, with 806 injuries and 182 deaths. The disaster forced 422,753 people from their homes, with 78,165 seeking refuge in official shelters at the height of the crisis3. During the first month of the crisis, water levels decreased in most areas, allowing some displaced families to return home and begin cleaning up their houses.

However, on 16 June, heavy rains hit the state, with an average of 200mm of rainfall in 24 hours. Further floods affected 19 municipalities along the Caí, Cadeia, and Sinos rivers, prompting evacuation messages. In some municipalities, such as Porto Alegre, the percentage of people in shelters rose again to 20% of its citizens nearly 2 months after the crisis. Besides basic needs such as clothing, food, hygiene and cleaning items, the prolonged period in shelters adds a heavy psychological toll on the affected population.

Based on figures from the Rio Grande do Sul state’s Government, the number of people displaced in shelters decreased by 64% from the previous reporting period4, reflecting a gradual return to normalcy for some families5. However, as of 16 December 2024, approximately 1,233 individuals remain in temporary shelters, highlighting the ongoing need for humanitarian assistance.

Because of the receding waters, there was an increased risk of waterborne diseases due to contact with sewage and contaminated water. As of 15 August, the Ministry of Health reported 26 deaths from leptospirosis, 788 confirmed cases and 7,129 suspected cases as of the latest update. Additionally, official reports of acute diarrhoea9 were registered in the region since the beginning of the crisis.

The economic damages were estimated at R$ 88.9 billion10 (around 1.3% of the state's GDP), primarily affecting the productive sectors (69%) and social areas11 (21%), with significant losses in infrastructure and environmental damages as well. The floods led to a decrease in the state's economic output by an expected 1.3% and the potential loss of up to 432,000 jobs, representing a 7.3% reduction in the workforce. Many have lost their means of livelihood, including crops and livestock, adding to the socio-economic toll of the disaster. Inflation rates impacted food prices up to 250% increase for the first weeks after the disaster, stabilizing in the next months. Twelve months after the floods, there are still challenges remaining to tackle. Some families, displaced to temporary shelters, have no place to return, as their homes were either destroyed or located in high-risk areas. The rehabilitation and reconstruction of their homes are required to ensure their return. Additionally, the loss of income-generating activities continues to pose a challenge, with significant difficulties in their reactivation. Among the long-term challenges are the lack of contingency plans at the local level and the absence of community disaster risk preparedness systems.

The agricultural recovery, especially in livestock sectors like dairy, beef, and poultry, will take time, and food security remains a major concern. Local authorities and organizations continue to provide emergency relief, but the overall rebuilding process is expected to be long and difficult. Significant needs persist in the humanitarian response. Mental health support, access to cleaning and hygiene materials, and water quality remain critical concerns. Evaluations in newly affected municipalities have identified more remote communities requiring basic items, while WASH assessments have highlighted poor water quality in many areas.

With the onset of the rainy season in May, the absence of community-based early warning systems remains a concern. In response, operational efforts over the past months have focused on strengthening the capacities of Brazilian Red Cross staff and volunteers to contribute to the design of municipal contingency plans that actively engage local stakeholders in each territory, while also ensuring the allocation of dedicated emergency funds to support both response and recovery efforts.

title: Nepal Flash Floods: UN Women Gender Alert #2 (07 September 2026)
content:
The Alert identifies significant protection and inclusion concerns in holding centres and temporary shelters, including overcrowding, lack of privacy and safe spaces, GBV and exploitation risks, inadequate WASH facilities, caste-based discrimination and barriers for persons with disabilities. It also highlights gaps in maternal and reproductive health services, food and nutrition, livelihoods and the growing burden of unpaid care work on women.

A central message is the critical role of women’s rights organizations (WROs) as frontline humanitarian actors. The Alert calls for WROs and organizations representing marginalized groups to be meaningfully involved in assessments, decision-making, targeting, monitoring and recovery, with direct and flexible funding to sustain their response capacity.

Key recommendations include ensuring safe and accessible shelters and WASH facilities, strengthening GBV and MHPSS services and referral pathways, maintaining maternal and newborn care, ensuring women’s equitable access to food, cash and livelihoods, systematically collecting sex-, age- and disability-disaggregated data, and establishing accessible feedback and complaints mechanisms.

UN Women is supporting the Government-led response through humanitarian coordination, advocacy and partnerships with WROs, organizations of persons with disabilities, youth-led and other community organizations. It is also mobilizing resources for its women-led Community Kitchen initiative, which provides emergency food assistance while supporting women’s leadership, livelihoods and longer-term recovery.

title: Situation Report 7 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (Date: 5th September 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview (Bihar & Uttar Pradesh) - 2nd to 5th Sept 2026

Severe monsoon flooding affected large parts of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, driven by rising water levels in the Ganga and its major tributaries. In Bihar, official bulletins recorded 10.26 lakh people affected across 11 districts, while wider inter-agency and media assessments indicated up to ~28 lakh people impacted across 13 districts and 270 panchayats, with key rivers—including the Ganga, Punpun, Gandak, Kosi, Burhi Gandak and Ghaghra—flowing above danger marks at multiple stations. In Uttar Pradesh, flooding linked to the swelling Ganga, Varuna and Ghaghra inundated 35 districts, 79 tehsils and 658 revenue villages, affecting 3.46 lakh people, with thousands evacuated and shelters activated as “residents used boats to travel through waterlogged streets in flood-affected residential areas along the swollen Varuna river in Varanasi.” Together, the two states experienced widespread displacement, infrastructure disruption, crop losses and escalating humanitarian needs as river levels continued to rise.

1. Bihar Floods

Impact on Humans

Flooding has affected 7.8 to 10.26 lakh people across 11 districts, with wider estimates reaching 28 lakh across 13 districts. Relief operations include shelters for 1,553 people, 36 community kitchens serving over 1.14 lakh meals, 693–912 boats deployed, and distribution of plastic sheets, dry ration and food packets in key affected areas. Three flood-related deaths were confirmed by 5 September (one 12-year-old girl in Punpun block on 3 Sept, and two adult drowning cases on 4 Sept in Danapur Diyara and Maner).

Animal husbandry losses

Flood reports from Bihar Inter-Agency Group and state animal husbandry data indicate around 70,000 livestock affected across multiple districts, with grazing lands and fodder supplies submerged. Fodder distribution has begun in districts like Chapra, Purnea and Bhagalpur, with several thousand quintals supplied to protect cattle and small ruminants from starvation.

Structural and Property Damages

Flooding and riverbank erosion have led to collapse of at least 18 houses into the Gandak in West Champaran (Siswa Kuti, Yogapatti block), with hundreds of acres of cropland lost along Yogapatti and Madhubani blocks. In Bhagalpur’s Raghopur area, a serious breach of the Raghopur–Kazikoraiya marginal embankment (250–400 m) has allowed floodwaters to approach the railway line and inundate diara villages, affecting around 5,000 residents. Urban flooding has entered parts of Patna, Bhagalpur and Munger, submerging low-lying neighbourhoods, university campuses, hostels and religious sites (e.g., Ajgaibinath temple complex in Sultanganj).

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 19 - 31 August 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified at least 14 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care linked to the SAF in 2025. These included four instances between February and August in Nyala city in which SAF aircraft and drone strikes damaged health facilities. SAF armed drone strikes also damaged a hospital in North Darfur and were used close to another facility in North Kordofan, endangering patients’ access to the facility.

In other hospital attacks, the SAF occupied three hospitals in Khartoum in late March: the Ear, Nose and Throat Hospital; Khartoum Teaching Hospital; and Zaytouna Hospital. Between January and August 2025, the SAF reportedly arrested six health workers in four incidents, often accusing staff of links to opposing conflict parties. In one reported arrest, the SAF tortured and interrogated a doctor detained in Gezira on accusations of being an RSF fighter. The fates of all six arrested health workers were not recorded.

title: Nepal Flood Emergency Situation Report | Reporting Period: 4 to 6 September 2026
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

Heavy monsoon flooding across Dhading District, Bagmati Province, has severely damaged critical public health, educational, and transportation infrastructure in Galchhi Rural Municipality.

Thick silt and mud deposits, averaging up to 60cm deep, blocked primary access roads and disabled essential utility systems, disrupting healthcare delivery and isolating local student populations.

Buddhist Tzu Chi Foundation is coordinating with local administrators, hospital directors, military and police personnel, and community volunteer networks to mobilize emergency cleanup operations, restore public utilities, and prepare necessary relief distributions.

OPERATIONAL RESPONSE

Bhagawati Secondary School Emergency Cleanup

Bhagawati Secondary School in Dhading District was heavily impacted by mud and water deposits, rendering the school campus unsafe for classes. A massive emergency sanitation operation mobilised over 200 personnel, including parents, teachers, students, local villagers, and military personnel, to clear mud and sanitise the premises.

To restore water supply, the cleanup team inspected the school's 168-meter-deep well and installed large-capacity water-storage tanks to secure sanitary water for campus cleaning and long-term student needs.

A critical bottleneck remains: the collapse of a key connecting bridge has severely disrupted student commutes. Students who previously took a short 20-minute walk must now take a hazardous 1-hour detour. Tzu Chi and local authorities are currently evaluating safe alternative pedestrian routes

title: Congo Flood 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRCG026)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
19-11-2025
What happened, where and when?

Exceptionally heavy rainfall during November 2025 triggered flash floods and severe flooding across the departments of Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire in the Republic of the Congo, causing significant humanitarian consequences and widespread material destruction. According to the Congolese Red Cross (CRC), approximately 50,000 people were affected, 22,842 people were displaced or evacuated, and at least 55 people were injured.

The floods particularly affected low-lying and densely populated neighbourhoods in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, where water levels rose rapidly following torrential rains and the overflow of rivers and drainage systems. Several neighbourhoods were submerged after the Tsiémé River in Brazzaville and the Nzoko River in Pointe-Noire exceeded normal levels. Meteorological services reported rainfall levels nearly twice the seasonal average, accompanied by a significant rise in the water level of the Congo River and its tributaries, reaching approximately 5.62 metres above normal levels.

The floods caused extensive damage to homes, community infrastructure and livelihoods. Thousands of houses were partially or completely destroyed, roads and drainage systems were damaged, and more than 1,750 hectares of agricultural land were flooded across the two targeted departments. Many affected families lost household belongings, productive assets and sources of income. Most displaced households sought shelter with relatives, neighbours or host families, often in overcrowded and precarious living conditions.

The disaster also generated significant public health and WASH concerns. Floodwaters damaged water points, sanitation facilities and household latrines, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases, including cholera, diarrhoea and typhoid. In several affected communities, access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation was severely disrupted, while stagnant water increased exposure to malaria and other vector-borne diseases.

In response to the emergency and following the Government’s appeal for humanitarian assistance, the Congolese Red Cross rapidly deployed 60 volunteers (30 in Brazzaville and 30 in Pointe-Noire) to support search and rescue activities, rapid assessments, first aid and community sensitization. With the support of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) through the DREF operation MDRCG026, the National Society implemented a four-month emergency response targeting 2,500 vulnerable households (approximately 12,500 people) through multipurpose assistance delivered via voucher-based support, alongside health, WASH, PGI and community engagement activities.

The operation also mobilized 150 trained volunteers and community actors who supported epidemic prevention activities, hygiene promotion, psychosocial support, community-based surveillance and accountability mechanisms throughout the intervention. Lessons learned and Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) findings later confirmed that the operation contributed positively to meeting urgent household needs and restoring dignity among affected populations, despite persistent humanitarian needs and operational challenges in some areas, particularly in Brazzaville.

title: Yemen Flood 2025 | DREF Final Report (MDRYE016)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
21-08-2025
What happened, where and when?

Between August and September 2025, widespread torrential rainfall and flash floods affected large parts of Yemen. As of September 2025, an estimated 73,218 households approximately 512,526 people were affected across 20 governorates of Yemen.

The floods damaged or destroyed homes, IDP shelters, roads and other essential infrastructure, while also causing losses of livestock and household assets. Floodwater contaminated water sources and increased the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases, including cholera and malaria. Access to some affected communities was constrained by damaged or blocked roads, further complicating assessment and response activities.

Internally displaced communities were among the most severely affected. Of the total caseload, at least 37,865 households, approximately 265,055 people were internally displaced, representing nearly 52% of all affected households. Many of these families experienced secondary or tertiary displacement, further compounding their existing vulnerabilities and increasing their immediate shelter, NFI, WASH and protection need.

The most affected governorates were Hajjah, Aden, Marib, Taiz and Al-Hodeidah, which together accounted for approximately 71% of the
total affected caseload.

title: Kenya Complex Emergency 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRKE068)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
22-10-2025
What happened, where and when?

Kenya experienced a prolonged and severe drought emergency driven by consecutive below-average rainfall seasons, prolonged dry spells, and the cumulative impacts of climate variability across the country’s Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs). The drought resulted in widespread depletion of water sources, reduced pasture and browse availability, declining livestock productivity, increased livestock losses, reduced household food availability, and worsening livelihood insecurity among pastoral and agro-pastoral communities. The crisis affected vulnerable households that rely heavily on rain-fed agriculture and livestock-based livelihoods. As the drought persisted, communities increasingly adopted negative coping strategies, including reducing food consumption, selling productive assets, migrating in search of water and pasture, and increasing reliance on humanitarian assistance.

By the end of the operation in May 2026, drought impacts continued to affect vulnerable populations despite localized improvements following the March–May 2026 rains. The humanitarian situation remained fragile, with several ASAL counties experiencing Crisis food insecurity conditions (IPC Phase 3) and some vulnerable populations facing heightened risks of acute malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and loss of livelihoods. The drought emergency was compounded by reduced humanitarian funding, limiting the ability of partners to sustain assistance at the required scale. Additionally, emerging climate-related shocks, including flooding in some parts of the country during the MAM 2026 rainy season, placed further pressure on already vulnerable communities and humanitarian resources.

The drought primarily affected Kenya’s Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs), particularly pastoral and agro-pastoral counties in northern and eastern Kenya. The DREF-supported response targeted some of the most drought-affected areas, including:

_ North Eastern Region (Mandera, Wajir and Garissa) – including vulnerable pastoral communities experiencing severe water shortages, reduced livestock productivity, and food insecurity.

_ South Rift Refion (Baringo County and Narok County) – particularly drought-affected communities dependent on pastoralism and mixed livelihoods.
_ North Rift Region– Counties affected by prolonged drought conditions, limited water availability, and declining livestock-based livelihoods.
_ Coast Region– where pastoral households faced reduced access to water, pasture, and essential services.
_ Lower Eastern and Upper Eastern Regions – where drought impacts affected pastoral livelihoods, food security, and access to basic services.

The broader national drought response covered multiple ASAL counties, with KRCS supporting interventions including emergency food assistance, cash voucher assistance, water trucking, rehabilitation of community water systems, nutrition support, and livestock interventions across affected pastoral areas.

The drought emergency developed over several consecutive seasons following below-average rainfall and failed or poor-performing rainy seasons in Kenya’s ASAL regions. The humanitarian situation intensified during the 2024–2025 period, with the impacts continuing into 2026 due to prolonged livelihood depletion and slow recovery among affected communities.

At the time of the DREF implementation period, the crisis had reached a critical stage, with the 2025 lean season showing a significant increase in acute food insecurity compared to previous years. Humanitarian needs remained elevated into May 2026, despite some temporary improvements associated with the March–May 2026 rainfall season.
The DREF operation was therefore implemented during a period of heightened vulnerability to provide timely humanitarian assistance, protect lives and livelihoods, and address urgent needs related to food security, nutrition, water access, health, and livelihood support among drought-affected communities.

title: Nepal: Flash Floods - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #1 (Reporting period: 26 August – 04 September 2026)

title: IDN: Volcanic Eruption - 09-2026 - Situation Report: Escalation of Volcanic Activity at Mt. Krakatau, Sunda Strait (2026-09-06)
content:
Description

Situation Overview: Mt. Krakatau Volcanic Activity

Background and Alert Status
Mt. Krakatau, located in the Sunda Strait, has shown a significant escalation in volcanic activity since early July 2026. Following a prolonged period of dormancy, activity intensified, prompting the Geological Agency to raise the alert status from Level II (Waspada/Caution) to Level III (Siaga/Alert) on July 2, 2026.

Eruption Timeline
Based on monitoring by the Geological Agency, the eruption commenced on Friday (04/09) at 23:07 WIB and continued until Sunday (06/09) at 00:04 WIB. Audible rumbling sounds were reported from the Pasauran volcanic observation post in Banten.

Regional Impacts

  • South Lampung Regency: The eruption has resulted in volcanic ashfall across the region. Local authorities have heightened emergency preparedness and temporarily suspended all tourism activities to Sebesi Island and the Mt. Krakatau area. As of the latest update, there are no reports of casualties or structural damage. Residents have been advised to wear masks.
  • Pandeglang Regency: Impacted areas have experienced felt tremors and volcanic ashfall. No casualties or damage have been reported to date. The public is urged to wear masks, minimize outdoor activities, and strictly maintain a 3 km exclusion zone from the center of volcanic activity.
  • Tanggamus Regency: Significant ashfall has affected several sub-districts, including Pematang Sawa, Kelumbayan, Cukuh Balak, and the Kota Agung area. The ash has impacted residential settlements and daily community activities. Residents are advised to wear masks and limit outdoor mobility.

Aviation and Infrastructure Disruption
The eruption has severely impacted aviation operations due to the dispersion of volcanic ash in the surrounding airspace. This has led to the temporary closure of several key airports, including Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, Halim Perdanakusuma, Radin Inten II, and Budiarto. Mitigation measures, such as flight delays, cancellations, and rerouting, have been implemented to ensure aviation safety.

Current Response
Data collection and continuous monitoring of the impacts of Mt. Krakatau’s eruption are currently ongoing.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by Federation

General

Other

Summary

IFRC CCD is monitoring and coordinating closely with PMI NHQ for further update from the field and for further support if required

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary

RCRC Movement actors maintain active communication with PMI NHQ, following updates from the field and evaluating potential support requirements.

Actions taken by National Society

General

Damage/Needs assessment

First Aid

Relief/Supply distribution

Other

Human remains management and identification

Summary

PMI Response Actions PMI NHQ has mobilized additional logistical assets to augment the local response capacity in Banten and Lampung. The support package consists of 100,000 masks, 100 pairs of protective goggles, and 3 oxygen concentrator units. These items are being prioritized for distribution to areas with the highest concentration of volcanic ashfall to prevent Acute Respiratory Infections (ARI). In response to the situation, the Indonesian Red Cross (PMI) has undertaken the following activities: 1. Assessment: Conducting rapid field assessments to determine the immediate needs of the affected population. 2. Personnel Mobilization: Mobilized 23 personnel (including volunteers and Satgana/Disaster Response Team) to the affected areas. 3. Disaster Preparedness Socialization: Providing safety and disaster preparedness awareness to the community, particularly regarding volcanic hazard mitigation. 4. Health Services: Deployed one (1) ambulance unit for emergency standby and community support. 5. Mask Distribution: Distributed 1,500 masks to residents in Lebak Regency. PMI Cilegon City has provided 15,500 masks to support PMI Lampung's response efforts. 6. Coordination: Maintaining continuous coordination with local governments, BPBD, and other relevant agencies to ensure an integrated response.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Indonesia through BNPB, BPBD, relevant Ministries, and Local Governments has implemented the following strategic measures: 1. Deployment of Tactical & Rapid Assessment Teams BNPB has deployed advance tactical teams to Banten and Lampung provinces to conduct direct on-site monitoring. These teams are responsible for performing Rapid Needs Assessments (RNA) regarding physical damage and identifying urgent humanitarian requirements in the field. 2. Logistics and Health Mitigation Authorities are distributing essential relief supplies and medical-grade masks to communities in ashfall-affected areas. This measure is a priority to mitigate the risk of Acute Respiratory Infections (ARI/ISPA) among the vulnerable population. 3. Weather Modification Operations (WMO) A Weather Modification Operation (locally known as OMC) has been launched from Pondok Cabe Airport. The mission aims to stimulate artificial rainfall to suppress and clear volcanic ash dispersion from the atmosphere over Banten, Lampung, and DKI Jakarta. 4. Aviation and Maritime Safety Management The Ministry of Transportation, in coordination with InJourney Airports, has enforced the temporary closure of several impacted airports, including Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and Radin Inten II, to ensure flight safety. Additionally, maritime authorities have issued safety advisories for all vessels navigating the Sunda Strait to remain on high alert.

title: BIH: Fire - 09-2026 (2026-09-07)
content:
Description

Wildfires have been affecting large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina since early August 2026, with the situation particularly severe in Herzegovina, where NASA fire-detection systems recorded 1,292 hotspots in just the first 13 days of August — three times more than in the same period last year. The 2026 fire season has been driven by prolonged drought, high temperatures and strong, shifting winds, resulting in numerous simultaneous wildfires across both entities.

Currently active fires (as of 6 September 2026) are affecting multiple regions: Bihać, Kalesija, Mrkonjić Grad, Kupres / Tomislavgrad, Bosanski Petrovac, Drvar and Prozor-Rama, where helicopters of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina were deployed following approval from the BiH Presidency, with around 30 troops also engaged on the ground in Bihać. Between Drvar and Glamoč, fire has affected the villages of Savići, Poljice and Crni Vrh, with several houses destroyed overnight after strong winds re-ignited the blaze. In the Poljice area (Kajtezi hamlet), the fire reached residential structures directly, prompting an urgent air-support request from the Municipality of Drvar.

Fires are also active around Sarajevo: a large fire broke out in the upper Bijela river canyon and surrounding plateau in the Trnovo municipality, on the slopes of Mount Bjelašnica, with smoke reaching Sarajevo and causing measurably increased air pollution at monitoring stations in the western part of the city. Firefighters and forestry workers from KJP "Sarajevo-šume" have been battling a fire line roughly 26 kilometres long above Ostojići, an operation further complicated by landmine contamination in parts of the affected terrain. A separate fire on Mount Trebević, near East Sarajevo, broke out in late August and was extinguished after multi-day firefighting efforts involving over 100 personnel and a helicopter from the RS Police Air Unit; the area remains subject to preventive monitoring due to smouldering material in the karst terrain.

Elsewhere, fires around Trebinje, Nevesinje, Konjic and Neum have been active for several weeks, with the Konjic fire on Džepska planina burning for over seven days. In Nevesinje, fire has reached close to the village of Humčani, with local firefighters and residents defending homes, while a second fire front is active at Zalom. In the Bileća area (Kazanci), two houses have burned over the past ten days. Trebinje — the fire near the city landfill at Obodina has been stabilized, with more than 100 people engaged;

Affected population and impact: No fire-related deaths or injuries have been confirmed in BiH in available reporting. Impact has primarily manifested as property damage (partial destruction of homes in Drvar, Prozor-Rama and Bileća municipalities) and disruption to daily life in affected rural communities, several of which have mobilised residents alongside firefighters to defend homes. Air quality in Sarajevo has fluctuated between "Good" and "Moderate" (AQI (US) 38–75) over recent days, with localised readings reaching "Unhealthy" levels for PM10, posing a heightened risk to residents with pre-existing respiratory or cardiac conditions across the broader Sarajevo Canton population (413,593 per the 2013 census). Municipalities directly affected by active fires or immediate fire threat have a combined population in the tens of thousands (see population breakdown provided separately), though the number of people within the immediate fire-risk zone (specific villages/hamlets) is considerably smaller than total municipal populations.

Response operations involve the Armed Forces of BiH (helicopters and ground personnel), professional and volunteer firefighting units, forestry management companies (Sarajevo-šume, Prenj, Borja, Lisina), Mountain Rescue Service teams, police aviation units (RS MUP), and — for the most severe fires near the Croatian border — regional aerial support including a Croatian Canadair CL-415 aircraft.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: Yes

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary

No need for now.

Actions taken by National Society

Summary

For the time being, there has been no need for operational activities by Red Cross staff in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We continue to closely monitor the situation and will respond in a timely manner if needed, particularly considering the involvement of firefighting units and the reported destruction of residential houses. During the previous period, the Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCSBiH) published a social media awareness campaign to inform the public about how to stay safe and what actions to take if they find themselves in a wildfire-affected area. In addition, RCSBiH reached out to Šume BiH to initiate a meeting aimed at discussing future cooperation on reforestation activities in areas where this is feasible and needed. One of the main concerns remains the inaccessibility of affected areas in forested locations, where landmines are still present, significantly complicating firefighting and response efforts.

Actions taken by Federation

General

Other

Summary

The Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCSBiH) remains in close communication with IFRC colleagues, and we continue to monitor the situation and developments on the ground.

Actions taken by others

The Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina have deployed military helicopters to support wildfire suppression operations. In Herzegovina, Croatia has been requested to provide aerial firefighting assistance with its available capacities. Similarly, in the Bihać area, additional support has been sought due to the scale of the wildfire affecting extensive forested areas.

title: DSWD DROMIC Report #71 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 06 September 2026, 6PM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan. The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "Pilandok" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM, Tropical Storm "Pilandok" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

title: South Sudan Humanitarian Flash Update (Restoring Life-Saving Services: UNICEF Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) – Wiechjol and Waat), August 2026
content:
Overview:

UNICEF and partners completed Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) missions to Wiechjol in Akobo County and Waat in Nyirol County, Jonglei State, restoring immediate access to life-saving health, nutrition and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services for conflict-affected, displaced and returnee communities. After months of disrupted humanitarian access, the missions delivered approximately 8.3 metric tons of critical supplies and provided nutrition screening, primary healthcare, household water-treatment support, hygiene promotion and referrals for children and pregnant and lactating women requiring further care. The intervention provided a critical humanitarian lifeline for communities that had been largely cut off from assistance following months of conflict, population displacement, and disrupted service delivery. Through an integrated package of health, nutrition and WASH interventions, UNICEF and partners delivered immediate life-saving support to conflict-affected, displaced and returnee populations. The missions screened 1,666 children for acute malnutrition, provided 1,241 primary health care consultations, reached 2,075 people with hygiene-promotion messages, and distributed essential hygiene supplies, including soap to 3,250 households and buckets to 948 households. Teams also identified and referred vulnerable children and women requiring additional care, including 146 children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 58 pregnant and lactating women at nutritional risk. As the first humanitarian assistance delivered in several months to these locations, the missions also generated critical information on humanitarian needs and service gaps, helping inform follow-up actions and the gradual restoration of essential services in hard-to-reach areas of northern Jonglei.

title: Desert Locust Bulletin 575 (5 September 2026)
content:
SOLITARIOUS POPULATIONS IN THE WESTERN REGION

In August, the grouping locust populations declined compared to the previous months in the Western Region. However, a few groups, and mainly isolated adults and hoppers, were present. A few adult groups were seen in southeastern Algeria and southwestern Libya, where transiens hoppers were detected and isolated adults were present. In Mauritania, increasing solitarious adult populations continued to be seen, and isolated hoppers were observed. Solitarious adults were seen at some sites in northern Niger and at many locations in Chad. No locusts were seen in Morocco since mid-July, and no more locusts were reported elsewhere. In the Central Region, there was an unconfirmed report of adult groups in the interior of Yemen, and no locusts were seen in Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia and Oman. In the Eastern Region, no locusts were seen in Iran, Pakistan and India. During the forecast period, increasing populations will appear in the southern part of the Western Region, where summer breeding is expected to increase in Mauritania, southern Algeria, northern Mali, Niger, Chad and southwestern Libya. Hopper and adult groups may form by the end of the forecast period. Surveys should continue at high intensity in the summer breeding areas of these countries, where preventive control operations may be required. In the Central Region, small-scale summer breeding is expected to occur in the summer breeding areas of Sudan, western Eritrea, and the interior of Yemen, and winter breeding may commence on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal plains, but no significant developments are expected. In the Eastern Region, summer breeding may occur along the Indo-Pakistan border; however, no significant developments are expected.

title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2, 4 September 2026
content:
Highlights

• Nepal flash flood has affected an estimated 84,270 people, including 32,021 children and 1,854 persons with disabilities across 17 municipalities in six districts.
• Essential services for children and families are severely disrupted. Fifty water supply systems and 20 schools have been damaged, while four health facilities have been destroyed and two partially damaged.
• UNICEF is delivering lifesaving support across WASH, child protection, health, nutrition, education and risk communication, working closely with the Government of Nepal and humanitarian partners to reach the most affected communities.
• Around 48,000 people have been reached with essential WASH supplies, while damaged water supply systems were restored in five priority districts.
• 2,700 cartons of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) have been provided for the treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition.
• Psychological first aid (PFA) and community-based psychosocial support has been provided to 1,029 flood-affected people, including 462 children, while specialized mental health and psychosocial support has reached 1,714 people, including 574 children and adolescents.

• Learning materials have been dispatched to support continuity of education, including 2,694 student kits, 148 teacher kits and 43 early childhood development kits.
• US$17.2 million is required to meet the immediate needs of children and families affected by the flash floods, with additional resources needed to support recovery and rehabilitation efforts.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Flash Update No. 1 - Anak Krakatau Eruption, Volcanic Ashfall and Concurrent Forest Fire & Haze Situation (6 September 2026)
content:
1. Situation Overview

Anak Krakatau remains at Level III (SIAGA/Alert). PVMBG/Badan Geologi reports that the volcano has remained at Level III since 2 July 2026. A series of Strombolian eruptions continued through 5 September, producing incandescent ejecta, volcanic ash and sustained lava-fountain activity. PVMBG recommends that communities, visitors and tourists do not approach or conduct activities within a 3 km radius of the active crater.

Volcanic ash has reached populated areas beyond the immediate vicinity of the volcano. Ashfall has been officially reported in coastal Banten and volcanic ash was detected at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport. In addition, IHCP has received field-confirmed observations of volcanic ash in Jakarta, Depok and Bogor on the morning of 6 September. At the time of this update, IHCP has not identified an official BMKG/PVMBG publication defining the complete ground-level ashfall footprint across these three cities; the geographic extent, concentration and duration of ashfall therefore require continued official verification.

No tsunami threat has been identified under the current eruption scenario. In 2018, a tsunami occurred due to the activity of the volcano. However, BNPB, citing PVMBG's assessment, reported that the post-2018 Anak Krakatau edifice remains relatively small and is not considered capable of a collapse of sufficient scale to generate a tsunami under current conditions. Monitoring continues and coastal communities should continue to follow official instructions.

title: Nepal: deadly flash floods - September 4, 2026, no. 2
content:
Key figures

● 4,521 people in shelters across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading

● 5,053 people missing

● 1,259 deaths recorded

● 12,038 people rescued

Highlights

● Corus teams are on the ground in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, assessing needs and coordinating with local authorities.

● Distribution of 500 hygiene kits and 1,500 sets of clothing is now underway for people affected by the flooding.

● Corus is procuring two 5,000-liter water tanks to help address urgent water storage and distribution needs identified through the WASH cluster in Nuwakot.

Situation Overview

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche in the upper Bhote Koshi watershed near the ChinaNepal border triggered a massive debris flow and flash flood that swept down the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system. The disaster caused extensive loss of life and widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other critical infrastructure. Rasuwa and Nuwakot are the two most severely affected districts. Local education authorities estimate that approximately 600 students remain unaccounted for across the two districts, although verification is ongoing.

Search, rescue and relief operations continue. Some communities remain isolated because roads and bridges have been damaged or washed away. An alternate road route to Rasuwa has opened, but conditions remain rough and slippery, particularly with continued rainfall. Air transport remains important for reaching communities that cannot be accessed by road and delivering relief supplies.

Authorities continue to monitor upstream water accumulations and debris blockages. Further flooding, landslides and debris movement remain possible.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 2 (4 September 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

Our humanitarian response

Plan International Nepal is responding to the flash floods and landslides in the most affected areas, prioritising children and adolescents, girls, young women, pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities and other marginalised groups.

Food Security, Non-Food Items and Livelihoods

Response and achievements

● 229 families, approximately 1,000 people, in Nuwakot received food packs through Plan International and partners.

● 125 families at a holding centre in Uttargaya, Rasuwa, received food and NFI packs through coordination with the local government.

● 26 displaced families (104 people) staying at a holding centre in Belkotgadi, Nuwakot, received food packs and 35 blankets.

● 78 food packs were handed over to the local government in Bidur, Nuwakot, to support affected families.

● 300 shelter kits and 300 kitchen kits were distributed in Belkotgadi and Ward 7 of Nuwakot, reaching approximately 2,700 internally displaced people (IDPs).

● Three generator sets and power supplies were provided through the Ministry of Home Affairs to support holding centres and help restore essential communications in Rasuwa.

● Procurement is underway for 1,500 additional food packs through Plan International’s partner DEPROSC Nepal, coordinated with WFP to address identified food gaps and minimise duplication.

title: Syrian Arab Republic Drought 2025 - DREF Operational Update (MDRSY017)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
08-08-2025
What happened, where and when?

Since the launch of this DREF operation in August 2025, the humanitarian situation in Syria has remained highly complex, with the impacts of severe drought continuing to interact with economic decline, deteriorating public infrastructure, prolonged pressure on basic services, and increasing climate-related hazards. Although parts of the country experienced localized improvements in rainfall during the 2025/2026 rainy season and severe flooding affected sections of the Euphrates Basin between May and June 2026, these events were insufficient to reverse the cumulative impacts of consecutive years of below-average rainfall, depleted groundwater reserves, and years of underinvestment in water infrastructure. Consequently, water insecurity remains a critical humanitarian concern across many governorates.

Throughout the implementation period, water and sanitation services continued to face significant operational challenges. Ageing infrastructure, persistent electricity shortages, limited financial and institutional capacity, rising operational costs, and shortages of essential equipment and spare parts have constrained the ability of water establishments to adequately operate and maintain critical water systems. These factors continue to reduce service reliability and place additional pressure on already fragile water supply networks.

Despite localized rainfall and flood events, the underlying structural drivers of water insecurity remain largely unchanged. Groundwater resources continue to experience increasing pressure due to unsustainable abstraction and unregulated well drilling in some areas, while high levels of non-revenue water resulting from ageing distribution networks and inefficient irrigation practices continue to increase demand on already stressed water resources. These pressures have further reduced the resilience of local water systems and, in some communities, have contributed to increased competition over limited water resources, affecting access to safe and reliable water supplies for vulnerable populations.

Between May and June 2026, flooding along the Euphrates River affected Ar-Raqqa and Deir-ez-Zor governorates, damaging water stations, irrigation infrastructure, and transport routes. While the floods temporarily increased surface water availability in some locations, they also disrupted water services and caused additional damage to critical WASH infrastructure. The simultaneous occurrence of prolonged drought impacts in many parts of the country and flood-related damage in others illustrates the growing variability of climate-related hazards and the increasing vulnerability of Syria's water resources and water service infrastructure.

These evolving conditions demonstrate that improving water security requires not only responding to climate-related emergencies but also strengthening the resilience of essential water systems. These evolving conditions demonstrate that improving water security requires strengthening the resilience of essential water systems through more efficient water resource management, reduced water losses, and sustainable management of available water resources, supported by community participation. Such measures are essential to sustain safe drinking water services, reduce humanitarian risks, and enhance the resilience of vulnerable communities to future climate related shocks.

Communities across Syria remain highly vulnerable to both slow-onset hazards, such as drought, and sudden climate-related events. These overlapping risks continue to undermine reliable access to safe drinking water and sanitation services, reinforcing the need for sustained humanitarian interventions that strengthen essential WASH infrastructure and improve the resilience of affected communities.

title: Nepal, Asia-Pacific | Flash Flood - Emergency Appeal Operational Strategy (MDRNP022)
content:
TIMELINE

26 August 2026: A massive surge of water enters the Bhote Koshi River bordering China. Floodwaters rapidly impact Timure, Rasuwaghadi, and Syafrubeshi towns in Rasuwa District and other towns further downstream in Nuwakot and Dhading Districts. The Government of Nepal issues evacuation orders and mobilises security forces. The Prime Minister’s Office convenes a high-level emergency meeting to assess the evolving situation and coordinate response measures. Additionally, the government holds a second emergency meeting and declares three districts and 15 municipalities as crisis-affected areas for three months while expediting relief and rescue operations.

26 August 2026: The NRCS activates its EOC on 26 August 2026. The NRCS is supporting the response through the mobilisation of staff and volunteers, search and rescue support, first aid and health assistance, emergency relief distributions, shelter and household items, WASH support, and dead body management, including the recovery, safe handling, identification, and dignified management of deceased persons. Other humanitarian partners are supporting complementary food, shelter, health, WASH, and protection activities, while international assistance and funding continue to be mobilised.

26 August 2026: The IFRC allocates CHF 999,934 from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) to support the immediate response, targeting 20,000 of the most affected people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading. A CHF 100,000 Emergency Advance Payment request is signed enabling immediate access to funding.

28 August 2026: The IFRC launches a Federation-wide Emergency Appeal of CHF 25 million (CHF 18 million secretariat) to provide early recovery and recovery support to approximately 28,000 people in three districts.

28 August 2026: Multiple IFRC surge role alerts are issued, and the Regional Operational Coordinator, Communications Coordinator, and WASH Coordinator arrive in Nepal to provide technical support.

DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

On 26 August 2026, a major ice–rock avalanche occurred in the upper Bhote Koshi watershed near the China–Nepal border. An estimated 1km2 of ice and rock detached from a slope, picking up loose proglacial sediments downstream and transforming into a highly mobile sediment- and water-laden debris flow. Initial assessments suggest that the resulting outburst flood in the upper watershed was an order of magnitude or more greater than normal seasonal flooding.

A powerful debris flow of sediment moved rapidly downstream, causing widespread destruction across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. Reports indicate that water levels in the Trishuli River rose up to nine metres above normal levels, inundating settlements and damaging critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, schools, police stations, markets, health facilities, telecommunication towers, electricity poles, financial institutions, vehicles, hydrometeorological stations, customs infrastructure, and multiple hydropower projects. Timure border market was among the hardest-hit areas. The disaster has disrupted transportation along several key highways and roads, while authorities have restricted accessto river corridors due to ongoing risks. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) issued a red alert for downstream districts, while the Government of Nepal convened an Emergency Disaster Council meeting chaired by the Prime Minister to coordinate search and rescue operations, damage assessments, and humanitarian response. Relief supplies have been mobilised from the Kathmandu Humanitarian Staging Area, with health response coordination led through national emergency mechanisms and partners. The scale of the physical damage, service disruption, and impacts on communities along the river corridor has created significant humanitarian needs requiring immediate relief and early recovery support.

title: DSWD DROMIC Report #70 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 06 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan. The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

title: Bosnia & Herzegovina — Migrant Mobility Situation Report (July 2026)
content: This report provides insights into the profiles, experiences, needs, routes travelled and intentions of migrants transiting through Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH).1 Data were collected from 1 to 31 July 2026. IOM carried out a route observation exercise in the Republika Srpska, Sarajevo Canton, Posavina Canton, Tuzla Canton, Bosnian-Podrinje Canton and Una Sana Canton to monitor trends in entries and exits as well as transit modalities within BiH. IOM also surveyed 66 migrants in active transit locations such as bus stops or at key entry and exit locations throughout the country as well as 369 migrants in two transit reception centres (TRCs) in BiH (Blažuj, and Lipa).

title: Nepal Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 6
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

More than a week after the 26 August flood, search and rescue has largely given way to relief operations. NDRRMA reports 1,259 deaths, 5,083 people out of contact and 12,038 rescued. Access remains the principal constraint, with damaged roads and bridges slowing the movement of relief supplies into upper Rasuwa, and several locations reachable only on foot.

Alongside the Government of Nepal, the Humanitarian Country Team launched a Flash Appeal in support of the Government-led response. The appeal seeks US$49.6 million to provide life-saving assistance to 84,270 people (19,284 households) in 17 municipalities across six districts: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha and Tanahu. All identified affected people are targeted, of whom nearly 40 per cent are children.

Requirements cover ten sectors through the end of 2026, with roughly three quarters concentrated in five: food security (US$7.94 million), WASH (US$7.9 million), health (US$7.6 million), logistics and emergency telecommunications (US$7.33 million) and shelter (US$7.1 million). The appeal complements the Government's Official Disaster Relief Appeal of 27 August and the NDRRMA-led operation. It is a time-bound humanitarian response, not a recovery plan; recovery and reconstruction needs will be addressed through the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment.

To sustain the immediate response ahead of the appeal, the CERF allocation has been recalibrated to US$2.5 million, prioritizing life-saving assistance in the worst-affected districts.

The Logistics Cluster has been activated to support partners with logistics coordination, information management and common services, working with the Ministry of Home Affairs to identify and address transport bottlenecks. With WFP's support, a coordination base for the UN and partners is being established in Bidur, Nuwakot, providing shared operational and office space for agencies and cluster coordinators working closer to affected communities.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Food and non-food items are in sufficient supply in the market areas in Bidur - Nuwakot. Relief supplies continue to build up in Nuwakot, as access challenges hinder the delivery of assistance to many of the most severely affected communities in Rasuwa.

Protection remains a key concern, as women, men, and children continue to share common spaces in displacement centres, raising potential protection risks and limiting privacy for vulnerable groups. Psychological counselling and social and behaviour change (SBC) interventions on personal and menstrual hygiene are needed.
Additional priorities include addressing WASH needs, improving displacement site management and tracking, establishing safe spaces for children, and providing specialized nutritious food to pregnant and breastfeeding mothers and children under five.
