title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.10: Measles in the Region of the Americas (1 September 2026)
content:
Summary of the Situation

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 33 of 2026 (which ended on August 22, 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 51,027 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.6-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (32,566), Mexico (12,607), the United States (2,777), and Canada (1,117) account for the vast majority (96%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 55 deaths have been reported, including 36 in Guatemala, 18 in Mexico, and one in Bolivia (1).

During EW 31 and 32 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 1,162 new confirmed cases of measles in seven countries and territories, representing a 28.1% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 29–30; 1616 new cases, of which 921 were retrospectively accounted for since the last situation report was published) (Figure 1). Of the 1,162 new confirmed cases reported during EW 31–32, Guatemala accounted for 611, followed by the United States with 239, Peru with 211, and Mexico with 96 while Bolivia reported three cases and Canada and Honduras one each.

title: Honduras - Operational update - July 2026
content:
Context

July was marked by continued violence, extortion, forced displacement risks and legal developments affecting the protection environment in Honduras.

Reports during the month highlighted persistent organized criminal activity, violence against women, risks affecting children and youth, and concerns around housing, land and property rights.

Violence and extortion continued to affect community safety, mobility and access to services. The Violence Observatory of the National Autonomous University of Honduras reported an average of six killings per day and more than 1,000 homicides so far in 2026. Transport representatives warned that extortion continued to affect public transport operations, while education sector actors reported that criminal groups continued to target schools and teachers in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula.

Women, children and adolescents remained exposed to heightened protection risks. The National Commissioner for Human Rights in Honduras (CONADEH) reported that one woman was killed every 25 to 30 hours and raised concern over high levels of impunity. Child protection actors also reported persistent violence affecting children and adolescents, including violent deaths, sexual violence and recruitment by criminal groups.

Housing, land and property issues continued to generate protection concerns. Civil society, Garifuna, Indigenous, Afro-descendant and rural community representatives expressed concern that recent land-related legislation and eviction processes could increase risks of displacement, criminalization and pressure on communities involved in long-standing land disputes. In southern Honduras, civil society organizations also raised concerns over the social and environmental impacts of renewable energy projects, including alleged effects on land rights, access to water and livelihoods.

Climate-related displacement risks also remained relevant in southern Honduras. In Cedeño, local and national authorities, humanitarian organizations and community leaders coordinated around planned interventions to address the risk of climate-related displacement. In Choluteca, efforts to strengthen the multi-hazard early warning system for the Choluteca River highlighted the importance of integrating protection considerations into disaster preparedness and municipal risk management.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #52 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 31 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Continued insecurity and protection concerns in southern Lebanon: Military activity, including airstrikes, shelling, demolitions, and incursions, continued across South and Nabatieh governorates, affecting civilian safety, humanitarian access, and recovery efforts.
  • Returns continue, but humanitarian needs remain acute: Displacement levels continued to decline gradually, with more than 823,000 people recorded as returned to their areas of origin. However, insecurity, damaged housing, disrupted services, explosive hazards, and limited livelihood opportunities continue to hinder sustainable return and prolong humanitarian needs among returnees, displaced populations, and host communities.
  • Humanitarian response scales support amid funding and access challenges: Ongoing access constraints, infrastructure damage, and persistent funding shortfalls continue to challenge response operations and the restoration of essential services in conflict-affected areas.
  • Humanitarian funding remains limited: As of 31 August, Flash Appeal received US$332.4 million (52 per cent) received against US$639.9 million. Humanitarian organizations warn that limited financial resources could undermine the continuity of critical assistance, including food support, healthcare, protection services, shelter assistance, coordination activities and recovery interventions.
  • 2026 Flash Appeal concludes on 31 August 2026: From September to December the 2026 Lebanon Response Plan (LRP) Addendum will provide the framework for addressing additional humanitarian and stabilization needs arising from the escalation through the end of 2026.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Humanitarian conditions in Lebanon remain fragile amid continued military activity, insecurity, displacement, and impediments to return. During the reporting period, Israeli military operations continued across South and Nabatieh governorates, including airstrikes, artillery fire, demolitions, incursions, and land-clearing activities affecting communities in Nabatieh, Marjaayoun, Bint Jbeil and Tyre districts. Airstrikes were reported in Mansouri and Tayr Harfa (Tyre District), while shelling affected Ainata and Beit Lif (Bint Jbeil District). Additional military activity and demolitions were reported in Mansouri, Majdal Zoun, Haddatha, Bani Hayyan, Houla, Baraachit, Khiam and surrounding areas, further affecting civilian safety, humanitarian access and recovery efforts.

Civilians and emergency responders continue to face significant protection risks. On 26 August, Israeli forces reportedly opened fire on a Lebanese Civil Defence team from Qlayaa (Marjaayoun District, Nabatieh Governorate) while it was responding to a fire near Deir Mimas after receiving authorization to access the area. Although no injuries were reported, the team was forced to withdraw. The incident followed a similar episode the previous evening, when shells reportedly landed near the same crew during follow-up firefighting activities. These incidents underscore the operational risks faced by first responders in conflict-affected areas. Reports during the period also pointed to extensive destruction of civilian infrastructure across southern Lebanon, including residential buildings, businesses, schools, hospitals, roads, electricity networks and water systems. On 24 August, a temporary school complex established by the municipality in Mais al-Jabal (Marjaayoun District, Nabatieh Governorate) was reportedly destroyed during demolition and bulldozing operations.

Security situation remained particularly unstable in parts of Nabatieh Governorate. Repeated strikes were reported around the Ali al-Taher heights, while military activity also affected Nabatieh, Kfar Rumman, Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Arab Salim, Rashaf, Haris, Haddatha, Khiam and Mays al-Jabal. On 24 August, the Ministry of Public Health announced the recovery of the bodies of two men in the Doha-Kfar Rumman area who had previously been reported missing. On 27 August, an airstrike in Arab Salim reportedly killed one woman and injured six others, including a child and two older persons.

Explosive ordnance contamination continues to pose a serious threat to civilians. During the reporting period, a war-remnant explosion in Tayr Debba (Tyre District, South Governorate) reportedly injured one person. On 31 August, a child was reportedly killed and another injured after a suspected cluster-munition remnant detonated in Haboush (Nabatieh District). Such incidents highlight the ongoing danger posed by unexploded ordnance and explosive remnants of war in residential areas, agricultural land and public spaces. The presence of explosive hazards continues to limit mobility, impede access to livelihoods, and delay reconstruction and recovery activities.

As of 26 August, 334,353 people remained displaced across Lebanon, while 823,337 people had returned to their areas of origin. Although displacement continues to decline gradually, insecurity, damaged housing, degraded infrastructure, limited services, explosive contamination and livelihood constraints remain major obstacles to sustainable return. Humanitarian needs remain substantial among displaced populations, returnees and host communities, while humanitarian operations continue to face access constraints linked to insecurity, damaged infrastructure, telecommunications disruptions and explosive hazards.

Funding shortfalls continue to affect response capacity, with the 2026 Flash Appeal receiving US$332.4 million (52 per cent) of the US$639.9 million requested as of 31 August.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 011 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - September 2, 2026
content:
• The earthquake has triggered a large-scale humanitarian emergency. More than 466,600 people have been affected, including 331 fatalities, thousands of people injured or missing, and more than 36,000 homes destroyed. The emergency continues to affect entire communities, with severe damage to basic infrastructure, education facilities and access to essential services.
  • Urgent needs persist, alongside risks of compounded impacts. In addition to the damage caused by the earthquake, many communities are facing compounded impacts from other emergencies and risks associated with armed conflict. The Government response is prioritizing health, water, temporary shelter and humanitarian assistance; however, humanitarian needs remain significant.
  • Humanitarian action and international support remain essential. At least 29 humanitarian organizations have provided assistance to nearly 123,000 people across 49 municipalities, complementing the response led by national and local authorities. The international community has mobilized more than US$40 million, while the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum continues to seek funding to address the needs of affected populations through the end of the year.
  • Coordination among authorities, humanitarian organizations, the private sector and international partners remains critical to saving lives, restoring essential services and supporting the recovery of affected communities.

This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia, based on inputs from humanitarian partners and official reports. Information as of 2 September 2026, 17:00 hrs.

title: Pakistan Rain Monitor - Issue Number 10 (01- 07 September 2026)
content:
Using remote sensing techniques, the seven-day forecast of total rainfall for the country is analyzed against the long-term average rainfall to highlight the areas which are expected to receive above normal, normal and below normal rainfall. The satellite data for a period of thirty years from 1993-2023 is extracted from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data) and analyzed to estimate deviation from normal rainfall. For the forecast of total precipitation for next seven days, the data is sourced from global model of ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).

Satellite-based rainfall forecast analysis for 1-7 September indicates above normal rainfall across central and northern Pakistan, while below normal rainfall is expected in Sindh, southern Punjab and Balochistan. Additional rainfall over already affected northern and central areas may exacerbate the risk of flooding, GLOF and landslides, particularly in vulnerable locations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu & Kashmir, and northeastern Punjab.

title: Protection Risk Monitoring System Concept Note January 2026 [EN/UK]
content:
Background and Rationale

Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion by Russian Federation on Ukraine, protection risks faced by affected populations have evolved in scale, severity, and complexity. Ensuring a coherent, evidence-based, and community-centered understanding of these risks is essential for effective protection response, advocacy, and strategic decision-making.
In 2022, the Global Protection Cluster (GPC) developed the Protection Analytical Framework (PAF) as a qualitative, risk-focused analytical approach to strengthen protection analysis across humanitarian contexts. Building on this, in 2023 the GPC, together with Protection Clusters globally, initiated the consolidation of Protection Monitoring Tools (PMT) and PAF into a unified Protection Risk Monitoring System (PRMS). This system is currently implemented in several operations (including Syria, oPt, Sudan, South Sudan, Haiti, and West Africa) and is now being introduced in Ukraine.
The PRMS transformation responds to the need to:
▪ Align protection monitoring with the 15 GPC Protection Risks, while ensuring alignment with Ukrainian context and focus on priority protection risks identified by partners.
▪ Harmonize protection analysis across protection actors including Child Protection and GBV areas of specialization, partners, and data providers.
▪ Strengthen the translation of protection risks into People in Need (PiN) and Severity estimates.
▪ Ensure more inclusive and consultative protection information collection and analysis, enabling participating organizations meaningful contributions, visibility and application of collected data as per established protocols
▪ Ensure that protection analysis systematically informs humanitarian planning, advocacy, and programming – both at operational and strategic level, including the HNRP and Protection Analysis Updates (PAUs), and linking up with humanitarian coordination system and wider information landscape in Ukraine, namely the HCT, ICCG, IMWG HOCGs, ABCs, national and sub-national clusters and partners, Data Coordination Group. This includes complementarity with UNHCR’s Protection Survey.
▪ Build in flexibility to provide protection analysis on specific thematic issues or for specific locations where protection risks are seen to become more acute.
▪ Enhance skill-building among protection partners in Ukraine to collect and analyze protection information for improved protection outcomes for IDPs and other war-affected populations.

title: ACTED South Sudan Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) - Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) Report, Majoknythiou Reception Centre & Host Communities, Northern Bahr el Ghazal State 2026
content:
Contextual Background

Majoknythiou Reception Centre, located in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State, is one of the principal entry points for South Sudanese returnees and refugees fleeing the ongoing conflict in Sudan. Since 1 June 2025, the reception centre has received approximately 6,727 households (20,344 individuals), resulting in sustained humanitarian needs and placing considerable pressure on reception facilities, essential services, and the resilience of surrounding host communities. In response, ACTED implemented Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) targeting vulnerable returnee and refugee households residing at Majoknythiou Reception Centre and the surrounding communities of Rum-Mawel, Dhony-Dhony, Machar Akoon, Warayen, Mabokdakloc, Yiththiou, Majokyith, and Tomkieu.

These communities continue to experience increased demand for basic services and livelihood opportunities due to the continuous influx and settlement of displaced populations, while existing infrastructure and service delivery remain limited. Through its sustained operational presence, ACTED has supported beneficiary reception and registration, vulnerability assessments, community engagement, and the delivery of MPCA. To date, the programme has assisted 1,040 vulnerable returnee and refugee households (approximately 6,240 individuals), enabling families to address their most urgent needs with dignity, flexibility, and autonomy in prioritizing household expenditures. The intervention has been implemented in close coordination with humanitarian partners and local authorities, supported by robust beneficiary targeting and verification processes, accessible Complaints and Feedback Mechanisms (CFM), and comprehensive PostDistribution Monitoring (PDM), thereby strengthening programme quality, accountability to affected populations, and evidence-based decision-making.

This report presents findings from a Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) survey conducted among 362 randomly selected beneficiary households to assess the effectiveness, relevance, and accountability of the MPCA intervention. The assessment evaluates how beneficiaries utilized the cash assistance, the extent to which priority needs were met, beneficiary satisfaction with the assistance received, access to complaints and feedback mechanisms, and the overall effectiveness of cash assistance in improving household wellbeing. The findings demonstrate that MPCA enabled households to meet critical immediate needs, particularly food, shelter, healthcare, transportation, debt repayment, and other essential household expenditures. Beneficiaries generally reported high levels of satisfaction with the assistance and valued the flexibility provided through unconditional cash transfers.

However, the assessment also highlights that cash assistance alone cannot fully address the longer-term challenges affecting displaced households. Continued population movements, limited livelihood opportunities, rising market prices, and increasing pressure on host community resources continue to constrain recovery and resilience. The findings reinforce the importance of predictable, timely, and accountable cash assistance delivered alongside complementary investments in livelihoods, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, and shelter to support sustainable recovery and strengthen household self-reliance. Building on its established field presence, experienced programme and MEAL teams, and strong community engagement and accountability systems, ACTED remains well positioned to support the priorities of the Cash Working Group by delivering high-quality, evidence-based, and accountable cash programming while contributing to coordinated humanitarian responses across Majoknythiou Reception Centre and the surrounding host communities.

The FSLC 2026-2027 Winter Response combines life-saving food assistance with emergency livelihoods support to address immediate food needs while protecting critical productive assets during the winter period.

title: Gender Alert #1: Critical Protection Needs of Women and Girls Following the Flores Earthquake Indonesia
content:
The Gender Alert highlights critical protection and gender-specific needs following the 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck Flores Island, East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia, on 15 August 2026. As of 30 August, the earthquake had caused 111 deaths, injured 1,629 people and displaced 188,161 people across eight districts. Women, pregnant and lactating women, children, adolescents, older people and persons with disabilities account for a significant proportion of those affected.
The alert identifies heightened protection risks for women and girls in displacement settings, including gender-based violence, limited access to maternal and reproductive health services, and gaps in safe and inclusive evacuation facilities. Damage to nine hospitals and 68 community health centres has further disrupted access to essential services.
It calls for gender-responsive humanitarian assistance, improved collection of sex-, age- and disability-disaggregated data, strengthened GBV coordination and survivor-centred services, and gender- and disability-inclusive WASH, shelter and evacuation facilities. The alert also emphasizes the importance of safe spaces, dignity supplies, psychosocial support and meaningful engagement of women’s organizations and persons with disabilities in the response.
This is jointly developed by the Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and Child Protection, Republic of Indonesia; Indonesia Humanitarian Coordination Platform (IHCP); UNFPA; and UN Women.

title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Flash Update #5 (As of 1 September 2026)

HIGHLIGHTS

  • The Rasuwa floods have claimed 1,003 lives, with 3,916 people still out of contact and 11,814 rescued (NDRRMA, 1 September, 13:00). Six days on, urgent needs include dignified management of the dead, family tracing, and psychosocial support.
  • 3,458 displaced people are living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools. Key gaps remain in who is displaced, where they are, and their needs, making displacement tracking and multi-sector assessments urgent.

title: UNICEF Somalia Humanitarian Situation Report No. No. 2 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Somalia’s humanitarian situation deteriorated sharply during the first half of 2026. The humanitarian caseload expanded from the 4.8 million people initially identified in the HNRP to approximately 6 million by June, driven by drought and other climate shocks, disease outbreaks, conflict, insecurity, displacement and contracting resources. An estimated 1.9 million children required acute malnutrition treatment, including 493,000 with severe acute malnutrition.
  • Despite limited funding, UNICEF maintained lifesaving assistance, treating approximately 200,000 children with severe acute malnutrition; providing 235,000 people with critical WASH supplies; enabling 309,000 people to access primary health care; and supporting 62,000 children with emergency education.
  • UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children appeal was only 24 per cent funded at mid-year. Education and Child Protection are unfunded at over 90 percent. Severe underfunding constrained service coverage, supplies and partner capacity as risks for children intensified, leaving critical gaps among most vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities in Somalia.

title: Nepal Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRNP022)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event 26-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

A major flash flood struck Nepal's Rasuwa district on 26 August 2026, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The flood breached riverbanks and travelled downstream through the Bhote Koshi into the Trishuli River, with extensive impacts into Nuwakot and Dhading Districts. (ICIMOD, 26 August 2026). The flooding was so massive that there are reports that the water level at the Trishuli River rose to 9 meters above the normal level, engulfing towns, bridges, schools, hydropower, etc. on the way downstream. (ICIMOD, 26 August 2026)

The disaster caused severe damage to settlements, markets, police stations, roads, and hydropower facilities, with Timure border market heavily impacted and villages along riverbanks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading reporting destruction. Authorities have reported severe damage in Timure market, customs office, multiple hydropower projects, etc. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has issued a red alert for downstream districts including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan, while the Government convenes an Emergency Disaster Council meeting chaired by the Prime Minister to coordinate search and rescue, preliminary damage assessment, and humanitarian standby operations, with relief dispatches mobilised from the Kathmandu Humanitarian Staging Area and health logistics coordinated through Health Emergency Operation Center, Ministry of Health and Food Safety, and WHO.

Travel has been discouraged on Prithvi Highway, the Galchi-Nuwakot-Rasuwa-Syabrubesi road, Muglin-Narayangadh road. Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police has reportedly halted vehicles heading toward Rasuwa and other affected districts. People working, fishing, or conducting activities near the Trisuli River have been restricted from going into the river corridor.

A DREF of approximately CHF 1 million was launched on 26 August to kickstart the response and CHF 100,000 Emergency Advance Payment was provided as immediate support to the Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) to start lifesaving activities. On 27 August, the IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal with a Federation-wide funding requirement of CHF 25 million (18 million IFRC Secretariat) as part of the support to NRCS for conducting response and recovery activities in the affected districts.

title: Iraq Imminent Population Movement 2026: Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRIQ020)
content:
Event development

Events impact

The escalation of regional hostilities during February 2026 had significant humanitarian repercussions across Iraq. A series of airstrikes, missile incidents, and drone attacks occurred within Iraqi territory, including strikes in Jurf Al-Sakhar south of Baghdad and repeated attacks targeting strategic locations in the Kurdistan Region. These incidents heightened insecurity among civilians and increased concerns over the potential expansion of hostilities into populated areas.

The impact on communities extended beyond the immediate effects of the attacks. Fear of further escalation, coupled with uncertainty regarding the security situation, prompted precautionary movements among families residing near locations perceived to be at risk.

Households in Baghdad, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Diyala, Wasit, Maysan, and Basra reported concerns over personal safety, disruptions to transportation routes, and potential interruptions to essential services. Many families temporarily relocated to stay with relatives or within host communities, while others restricted their movements and adopted precautionary measures to reduce exposure to potential risks.

According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), at least 90 households had been identified as displaced in relation to the crisis by the end of March 2026. In addition, increased cross-border mobility was observed as the conflict affected movement patterns throughout the region. By the end of March, IOM recorded 843 arrivals from Iran, 551 departures to Iran by Iraqi citizens, and 181 returnees from Iran.

The humanitarian consequences extended beyond displacement. Airspace restrictions, security measures, and concerns over the safety of critical infrastructure disrupted livelihoods, access to services, and freedom of movement. Vulnerable groups, including women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, and those already displaced by previous crises, faced heightened protection concerns and increased barriers to accessing essential services. The escalation also placed additional pressure on host communities and local service providers, particularly in areas already supporting internally displaced persons, returnees, and refugee populations.

While the scale of displacement remained localized compared to previous crises in Iraq, the events demonstrated the vulnerability of communities to regional instability and underscored the importance of preparedness, protection, and humanitarian assistance for populations affected by sudden security shocks.

title: Comoros | Cholera - Simplified Early Action Protocol Activation (sEAP №: MDRKM015 | sEAP2023KM02)
content:
RISK ANALYSIS

Prioritized hazard and its historical impact.

Cholera is the prioritized hazard for this Early Action Protocol (EAP) in Comoros, where it remains a significant public health threat. Comoros, though not cholera-endemic, is highly connected, by sea and air, to East and Central African countries with recurrent cholera outbreaks, notably Tanzania, Mozambique, Kenya, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Rwanda, Burundi, and Ethiopia. Between December 2024 and January 20261, these seven countries reported a combined 101,351 cases and 2,452 deaths – except for Kenya and Rwanda, whose outbreaks ended in December and November 2025 respectively – all reportedly had ongoing active cases through January 2026.

The country’s cholera risk is heightened by structural vulnerabilities2, notably its exposure to multiple hazards whose impacts are amplified by climate change3. The principal climate risks facing the Comoros include sea level rise, storm surges, coastal flooding, rising temperatures, and more frequent and intense extreme weather events, alongside the degradation of critical marine ecosystems. Over time, these hazards have evolved from episodic extreme events into a chronic and intensifying multi-hazard regime, characterized by growing variability and the compounding of risks. This transition is evident in both historical trends and future projections of climate variables (see Climate Risk Timeline in Comoros, Annex 1), which indicate a continued escalation in the frequency and severity of extreme events. As a result, climate-related shocks increasingly act as drivers of public health crises, exacerbating vulnerabilities to waterborne diseases such as cholera and other climate-sensitive health risks.

In addition, precarious living conditions affecting parts of the population, together with limited access to essential services (health care, safe water, hygiene, and sanitation), increase the likelihood of deteriorating sanitary and environmental conditions. Taken together, these factors can create environments conducive to the survival, circulation, and transmission of Vibrio cholerae, particularly during periods of water stress, heavy rainfall, flooding, or disruptions to basic services.

Cholera manifests as acute, profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, and leg cramps, progressing to severe dehydration and death within hours without treatment. Key risk drivers in Comoros include case importation from neighboring countries, seasonal peaks during the rainy season (November–May), and mass gatherings like "Grand Weddings," featuring large crowds and shared meals.

Cholera has been a recurrent threat in Comoros since 1975, with seven major epidemics documented over nearly five decades, underscoring both the severity and the cyclical nature of outbreaks. Critically, Comoros is not cholera-endemic: the majority of documented epidemics has been traced to an imported source, typically introduced via maritime travel, fishing vessels, or population movement from cholera-affected countries in East Africa and the wider Indian Ocean region, before spreading through local transmission once introduced. This importation pattern reflects Comoros' geographic position as a maritime crossroads with high population mobility (commercial shipping, fishing, diaspora travel, and migration to/from Mayotte) rather than the persistence of endemic Vibrio cholerae reservoirs within the country.

Since 1975, the cumulative burden exceeds 29,000 cases and 672 deaths, with an average case fatality rate (CFR) of 3.16%, markedly above the WHO emergency benchmark of 1%. The most recent outbreak, which occurred in 2024, was similarly linked to an imported case – documented as originating from a boat arriving from Tanzania – and coincided with a rainy season marked by severe flooding and significant damage. The floods led to the destruction of essential infrastructure and the contamination of water sources, thereby increasing the risk of spreading cholera and other waterborne diseases. This outbreak was the largest ever recorded in the country, with 11,171 cases and 153 deaths4. Vulnerable groups were disproportionately affected, with children under 15 accounting for over 35% of reported cases and 67% of deaths. Beyond the immediate health impacts, cholera outbreaks cause major socioeconomic disruptions, including the closure of markets and businesses, a sharp decline in tourism, and the interruption or deterioration of education services.

title: Burundi BVD Ebola preparedness - DREF Operational Update (MDRBI026)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

21-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 15 May 2026, the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially declared an outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease (BVD) caused by the Bundibugyo strain in Ituri Province, in the northeastern part of the country. On the same day, the Republic of Uganda also declared an outbreak of the same Ebola strain, with the epicenter located in Ituri. In response to the evolving situation and the cross-border implications of the outbreak, the World Health Organization (WHO) subsequently recognized the event as a major public health concern due to its spread in border areas and the high risk of regional transmission.

The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccine, increasing concerns among health authorities and humanitarian partners. Ebola Virus Disease is a severe and often fatal illness transmitted through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, contaminated materials, or infected animals. The disease can cause large outbreaks with significant mortality if not rapidly contained.

As of the date the emergency plan of action was written (May 2026), the epidemiological situation was showing more than 1,000 suspected cases and 220 deaths had been reported across the affected provinces of Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu in the DRC, including cases linked to Uganda. As of 3 August 2026, more than 3300 confirmed cases had been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), compared with 20 confirmed cases in Uganda. In addition, more than 1,400 confirmed deaths had been recorded in the DRC, while Uganda had reported two confirmed deaths.

Although Uganda declared the end of the outbreak on 28 July 2026, the epidemiological situation in the DRC remained highly concerning. The outbreak had not yet reached its peak, with transmission continuing to expand and new health zones being affected. Given the close cross-border population movements between the DRC and neighbouring countries, including Burundi, the continued spread of the disease in the DRC posed a significant risk of cross-border transmission and underscored the need to maintain heightened surveillance, preparedness, and response capacities.
The situation continues to evolve, creating heightened concern for neighboring countries due to intense cross-border population movements and trade.

Burundi is considered a high-risk country due to its geographical proximity to the affected areas and its strong social and economic links with both the DRC and Uganda. Particular concern exists along major travel and trade corridors connecting Burundi to affected areas, including the Bujumbura–Goma, Bujumbura–Kivu, and Bujumbura–Entebbe routes, through both land and air transport. The provinces bordering the DRC, as well as major entry points and urban centers receiving travelers, are considered areas at heightened risk of disease importation.

Recognizing the threat posed by the outbreak, the Government of Burundi, in collaboration with health partners including the Burundi Red Cross Society and the IFRC, finalized and validated a National Ebola Preparedness and Response Plan on 22 May 2026. Preparedness efforts remain ongoing as the outbreak continues to evolve in neighboring countries and the risk of importation into Burundi remains high.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Protection Update #11 - Q2 2026
content:
UNHCR’s Protection Response

▪ The protection response by UNHCR and our partners provides tailored support to those most in need, aims to strengthen inclusive national systems and services, and encourages the participation of internally displaced people (IDPs) and returnees in decisions that affect them.

▪ Our protection response complements, reinforces and strengthens the capacity of national protection services to serve the growing population in need, in line with the Memoranda of Understanding with relevant Ministries and Oblast authorities.

▪ In implementing our protection response, we work directly with communities, including our network of supported community-based organizations and IDP Councils, and predominantly local NGO partners. In 2026, 13 out of 14 UNHCR funded partners are Ukrainian NGOs.

title: WFP Republic of Congo Country Brief August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP assisted 176,288 people across the Republic of Congo in June–July 2026, delivering 929.4 mt of food and USD 788,192 in cash assistance to vulnerable populations.
  • Through food voucher distributions in Bouenza, 733 schoolchildren benefited from nutritious meals while strengthening market access for local farmers and supporting local food systems.
  • WFP and the National Institute of Statistics launched the Comprehensive Analysis of Food Security and Vulnerability on 29 July. Data collection begins in August across all 15 departments, with findings set to inform the Government's 2027–2031 National Development Plan and WFP's 2027–2031 Country Strategic Plan.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Republic of Congo (RoC), home to a population of 6.1 million, continues to face structural vulnerabilities despite its abundant natural resources. The economy remains heavily dependent on oil while economic stagnation, rising global food prices and high public debt at 97 percent of GDP-continue to exacerbate poverty and unemployment. More than half of the population lives below the poverty line, while youth unemployment remains, particularly high, at 42 percent.

• Domestic agricultural production meets only 30 percent of national food requirements, leaving approximately one-third of the population food insecure and highly vulnerable to external shocks. Women, children, refugees and indigenous peoples are disproportionately affected due to limited access to resources, weak food systems and recurrent climate-related shocks, including flooding in high -risk departments.

• WFP is present in 14 of the country’s 15 departments, supporting food security and nutrition among vulnerable population through emergency response, school feeding, resilience building, and support to national systems.

title: WFP Nepal Situation Report on the Rasuwa Flood Response, 01 September 2026

title: WFP Iran Country Brief, August 2026 (Reporting period: July 2026)
content:
IN NUMBERS

35,611 people assisted in August (51% female)

487.2 mt food distributed in June

USD 372,987 cash transferred in June

USD 24 required in the next six months (August 2026 – January 2027)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Despite the escalation in the region, WFP remains steadfast in its commitment to the people it serves. The operation in Iran continues without disruption, with teams on the ground ensuring uninterrupted delivery of food and cash assistance to the most vulnerable refugees residing in settlements. WFP is also in close consultation with the Government to explore opportunities to scale up its operations.
  • As part of the ongoing inclusion of 7,000 newly referred refugees, almost 3,000 beneficiaries have been added to the settlements since March 2026, with additional eligible individuals expected to be incorporated progressively in WFP assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The Islamic Republic of Iran, an upper-middle income country of over 91 million people, is among the world’s largest refugee-hosting nations, sheltering around 1.7 million refugees of various documentation statuses according to UNHCR. According to the Government of Iran, upwards of 6.1 million reside in the country, including unregistered individuals, mainly from Afghanistan and Iraq, living in urban areas. With no viable return options, sustained assistance remains critical, particularly for over 35,000 highly vulnerable refugees living in 20 settlements nationwide.

Recently, an additional 7,000 refugees were referred by settlement managers, by the Government of Iran, for WFP assistance. Further referrals from CAFIA are expected.

WFP Iran’s Interim Country Strategic Plan (ICSP 20232027) supports over 35,000 food-insecure refugees through cash and in-kind food assistance, a refugee girls’ education cash incentive, and a school feeding initiative consisting of nutritious school snacks. Moreover, WFP continues to equip refugees with complementary livelihood skills aimed at supporting their resilience and preparedness for voluntary, sustainable repatriation to their country of origin once the situation is conducive.

WFP has been operating in Iran since 1962, initially for its first emergency earthquake response until 1978, and subsequently reinitiating operations to address the refugee crisis from 1987 onwards.

In light of the recent escalation in the region, WFP continues to monitor the situation and activated its emergency preparedness capacities to support the most vulnerable individuals with their emerging needs.

title: Nepal Landslides & Flash Floods: Situation Report #2 (August 31, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is in Nepal, mobilizing mobile medical teams that will provide urgently needed care to communities devastated by the flash floods and landslides caused by last week’s massive glacier avalanche.

Situational Context

Entire villages, roads, bridges, electricity systems, and health facilities were wiped out after a glacier avalanche near the Nepal-China border triggered massive floods, apocalyptic landslides, and registered a force equal to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake.

Casualty figures are likely to rise as search-and-recovery efforts continue, with current reporting showing 939 people dead and 4,247 missing in Nepal. Chinese authorities have also reported 16 fatalities and 546 missing. These numbers include tourists from dozens of countries and local community members that were caught by floodwaters as children headed to school and people started their workdays. The affected area is a popular tourist area where people go on pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and other religious groups.

Nepal’s government has been forced to begin mass burials in some areas after the amount of bodies washing ashore began to significantly exceed morgue capacity.

This disaster left a roughly 40-mile path of destruction, but the flow of debris traveled as far as 62 miles and there are reports of bodies washing ashore up to 250 miles downstream in Nepal and 100 miles downstream in neighboring India.

As access improves along the Trishuli River, the scale of humanitarian need is becoming clear. Affected communities will need support to meet nearly every basic need across the health; water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH); mental health and psychosocial (MHPSS); food; essential non-food (NFI) item; and other sectors.

Monsoon season and the threat of secondary disasters are making recovery efforts more difficult as conditions remain dangerous. Heavy rains over the last few days have swelled the Trishuli River and increased threats to already affected communities. Nepali authorities are also encouraging communities and first responders to remain on high alert as the Bhotekoshi River has continued to rise.

title: NRC Somalia: Monthly Programme Update (July 2026)
content:

  • Deyr brings both recovery potential and risk. A 90% chance of enhanced rainfall, with some areas potentially receiving 400+ mm, could improve water, pasture and livelihoods but also increase flooding, disease and displacement risks, with El Niño likely to persist.

  • Political, security and funding pressures are narrowing humanitarian space, non-state armed actors, clan conflicts and federal– state tensions continue to drive violence and access constraints, while nearly 40% cuts in multilateral funding and reduced AUSSOM financing are weakening response and security capacity.

title: Sierra Leone Floods 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRSL019)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
05-09-2025
What happened, where and when?

In the early hours of 31 August 2025, Sierra Leone experienced intense and prolonged torrential rainfall that triggered widespread flooding across several parts of the country. The volume and duration of the rainfall exceeded the capacity of drainage systems and natural waterways, resulting in rapid water accumulation, river overflows, and extensive flooding in affected communities.

The floods affected 17 communities across seven districts: Bonthe, Kenema, Bo, Moyamba, Kono, Falaba, and Koinadugu. The disaster caused significant humanitarian impacts, with homes damaged or destroyed, schools and health facilities affected, and essential services disrupted. More than 11,080 people (2,216 households) were affected, including over 4,000 people who were temporarily displaced and sought refuge in schools, public buildings, or with host families.

The flooding also had a significant impact on livelihoods and food security. More than 2,500 hectares of farmland were inundated, resulting in crop losses and disruption to agricultural activities, the primary source of income and sustenance for many households. Communities that relied on farming and natural resources experienced reduced access to productive assets, loss of income, and increased vulnerability to food insecurity.

Affected populations faced urgent humanitarian needs, including access to safe drinking water, food assistance, emergency shelter, household and hygiene items, healthcare services, and protection support. Vulnerable groups, including children, older persons, persons with disabilities, pregnant and lactating women, and displaced households, faced heightened risks due to displacement, reduced access to essential services, and exposure to unsafe living conditions.

In response, the Sierra Leone Red Cross Society (SLRCS), with support from Movement partners, rapidly mobilized emergency response interventions to address immediate humanitarian needs and support early recovery. Assistance provided through the operation enabled affected households to meet their basic needs, reduce health and protection risks, and restore a sense of safety and dignity during a period of significant disruption.

By the end of the intervention period, floodwaters had receded across the affected districts and communities had largely transitioned from the emergency phase to early recovery. Through the DREF-funded shelter intervention, 241 houses had been reconstructed, while the remaining nine houses were at the final stages of completion. In addition, 1,000 households received two rounds of multipurpose cash assistance, enabling them to meet their immediate food and nutritional needs and replace essential household items lost or damaged during the floods, including bed sheets, drinking buckets, laundry bowls, cooking utensils, cups, sleeping mats, and blankets.

The assistance also supported priority recovery needs such as hygiene supplies, water treatment and storage materials, healthcare costs, transportation, communication, and other household expenditures identified by affected families. Access to basic services gradually improved, markets resumed normal operations, and affected households were increasingly able to restore their daily activities and livelihoods.

The operation contributed significantly to reducing immediate humanitarian needs, restoring minimum living conditions, and supporting the dignity and well-being of flood-affected households. It also strengthened community resilience and enhanced the preparedness and response capacity of SLRCS to respond to future climate-related emergencies. However, residual needs remained at the close of the operation, particularly among households affected by the loss of crops, agricultural inputs, and other livelihood assets. Many families continued to face challenges restoring their income sources and recovering from the economic impacts of the floods. Additional support is required to strengthen livelihood recovery, restore agricultural production, enhance household resilience, and support longer-term recovery efforts for vulnerable communities in flood-prone areas.

This condition has had an impact on delays in health treatment, even causing cases of death among self-settled IDPss. In West Manggarai, all IDPs are still independent, while the distribution of logistics has only reached the sub-district level and has not been supported by a clear call center or complaint mechanism. Although the logistics stock is actually sufficient, the distribution is not optimal due to limited human resources, access constraints, and a lack of a strong information connection with the post. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen coordination and mapping the role and scope of partner support through the 5W mechanism to ensure that interventions are directed, do not overlap, and reach all areas in need.

o Displacement and Protection Clusters: although coordination has begun and involves many organizations, the compilation of 5W data is still in process, so the available information has not been fully consolidated into one integrated system. In addition, the harmonization of response planning and implementation across sectors and regions still needs to be strengthened to prevent overlap or service gaps. Multi-hazard risk analysis is still in the development stage, so a comprehensive risk picture is not yet available to support anticipatory steps. On the other hand, the ongoing implementation of the Joint Needs Assessment (JNA) and Joint Market Assessment (JMA) means that the information base on the needs of affected communities and market conditions is not fully available as a reference for decision-making and the prioritization of interventions.

o Sub-cluster for the Protection of the Elderly, Disability, and Other Vulnerable Groups (LDR): complete disaggregated data on vulnerable groups is not available, thus hindering the identification of needs and the targeted distribution of assistance. In addition, limited access to clean water, especially for people with disabilities who are internally displaced, is still a major challenge in meeting basic needs. This condition is exacerbated by the still high demand for hygiene kits and clothing and limited access for people with disabilities to humanitarian services and assistance, thereby increasing the vulnerability of this group to health, protection, and welfare risks. In addition, limited access to assistance and accessibility of evacuation posts is also a problem.

o Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Sub-cluster: there is a risk of health problems due to water quality that has not been monitored evenly, as shown by the increase in diarrhea cases in Nagekeo Regency and the lack of optimal water quality checks in all affected areas. At the same time, the need for emergency sanitation facilities remains high, as reflected in the mobilization of portable latrines across regions and the lack of comprehensive SOPs for fecal sludge management (which will be discussed at the AMPL Sub-cluster coordination meeting on Saturday). The fulfillment of AMPL needs also still depends on cross-regional support and coordination with various partners, so it has the potential to create service gaps if coordination is ineffective. Post-disaster conditions also increase the risk of environmentbased diseases related to water, sanitation, waste, and disease vectors, requiring sustainable interventions such as water quality monitoring, waste management, and vector control.

o Child Protection Sub-cluster: there is still a need to strengthen the child protection system in the affected areas, both in terms of service capacity and coordination between related agencies. The mechanism for reporting and referral cases of violence against children is also still inadequate, so it needs to be strengthened so that each case can be identified, reported, and handled quickly and appropriately. In addition, the IDPs and post-disaster situation increase the vulnerability of children to various protection risks, including violence, exploitation, neglect, and other forms of violations of children's rights. Although various partners have provided psychosocial support services, the needs of affected children are still high and require wider and sustainable coverage of services. On the other hand, the availability and quality of child protection services are not even in all affected areas, so it is necessary to expand and standardize services, including strengthening the SAPA Post and coordination mechanisms in each district.

o Health Cluster: maintaining the continuity of health services in the midst of limited service capacity (which is prioritized for pregnant women, maternal mothers, newborns, the elderly, women with disabilities), continued handling of trauma cases, especially orthopedic injuries that have the potential to not be reported optimally due to weak surveillance systems, as well as the increased risk of ISPA due to the dry season and evacuation conditions. In addition, there is still a need for hygiene kits and waste management to prevent environmental health problems, special attention to the health of pregnant women as a vulnerable group, and limited availability of drugs in several health centers. Other challenges include coordination between district and provincial HEOCs, the extent of the affected areas, and the low utilization of formal health services because some people prefer traditional medicine; mobile health services that reach evacuation points are needed. All of these efforts are also constrained by limited operational support, particularly transportation facilities for mobilizing health workers, logistics, and field services.

There was a shift in the disease pattern in disaster-affected areas, from acute trauma cases to infectious cases, accompanied by an increase in dog-bite cases. Although trauma cases had decreased in the second week, the cases were found again. The most commonly reported diseases at evacuation points include ISPA, gastrointestinal disorders, skin diseases, non-communicable diseases such as hypertension and diabetes, maternal and child health problems, and reproductive health, including the tendency of pregnant women to be reluctant to access health center services. In addition, psychosocial impacts are also experienced by survivors and health workers. The latest surveillance data shows a significant increase in diarrhea cases, although some of them are accumulated reports since day one. Meanwhile, a report from the Reok Health Post, Manggarai shows that many children and toddlers are dehydrated and have Acute Respiratory Infection (ISPA), while the most common complaints in adults are headaches and fever.

o Reproductive Health Sub-cluster: disruption of puskesmas operations and high demand for emergency reproductive health service facilities, which threaten access to services for pregnant women, mothers, newborns, and other vulnerable groups. The main priorities are increasing the capacity of health tents, restoring the function of health facilities, and ensuring the sustainability of reproductive health services during the emergency response period and recovery transition.

o Nutrition Sub-cluster: There are still high cases of underweight, and several cases of malnutrition have been found, although there are no toddlers with severe malnutrition. The most vulnerable groups include infants, toddlers, pregnant women, and adolescent girls who require continuous monitoring and nutrition interventions. The implementation of nutrition services also faces obstacles because not all targets are concentrated at the posts, so some vulnerable groups may be unreachable for screening, supplementary feeding (PMT), and supplementation activities. In addition, the limited number of nutrition workers due to the impact of disasters reduces the capacity to conduct monitoring, education, and case follow-up in the field. In terms of assistance, the donation of formula milk requires strict supervision because suboptimal water quality and hygiene can increase health risks for infants and children. On the other hand, although services through PMBA kitchens and various nutrition interventions have been running, the coverage is still limited to some areas so it is necessary to expand and strengthen services to reach more vulnerable groups in the affected areas.

title: Lebanon Health Sector Emergency Situation Report Issue #22 - August 31, 2026
content:
Situation Update

Lebanon's health system continues to operate under significant pressure as insecurity, population movements, access restrictions, damaged infrastructure, and resource limitations disrupt the availability and continuity of essential services.

No attacks on healthcare were reported during the period. Since 2 March, 214 attacks on healthcare, including 124 attacks on ambulances, have been documented, resulting in 135 deaths and 410 injuries. These incidents continue to disrupt health services and highlight the need to uphold International Humanitarian Law and protect healthcare workers, facilities, ambulances, and patients.

Of the supported facilities in conflict-affected areas, 21 Primary Health Care Centers (PHCCs) and 3 hospitals remain closed, while the majority continue to operate. Service continuity has been maintained or restored in several locations through emergency repairs, temporary service arrangements, outreach activities, prefabricated structures, and adjusted staffing modalities. The Ministry of Public Health, through the National Tuberculosis and AIDS Programme, has reopened its center in Tyre following conflict-related disruptions, restoring essential TB screening, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, awareness-raising, and community outreach for communities in Tyre and surrounding areas. Tebnin Governmental Hospital has also resumed maternity services; however, two hospitals in Bint Jbeil District remain unable to resume vital maternity services, while additional support is needed as partner budgets are insufficient to meet demand for the remainder of 2026.

Partners continue to provide PHCCs and hospitals with essential medicines, medical supplies, and support for emergency care. Across affected areas, PHCCs and Primary Health Care Satellite Units (PSUs) continue to deliver essential primary care, including immunization, chronic disease management, maternal and child health, nutrition, referrals, and community outreach. PSUs remain active across South and Nabatieh, covering most villages, while functional PHCCs continue to provide essential services. Vaccination delivery improved during the second quarter of 2026, with a 19 per cent increase in children vaccinated and a 22 per cent increase in doses administered compared with the first quarter; however, coverage for the main antigens remains below national targets. Support to emergency rooms in selected governmental hospitals continues to facilitate urgent care for Lebanese and non-Lebanese patients and ease pressure on referral and hospitalization services. Persistent gaps in ANC utilization and midwifery availability continue to affect maternal and newborn health outcomes

In North Lebanon, an increase in hepatitis A cases has prompted community awareness activities on transmission risks, preventive measures, early recognition of symptoms, and timely care-seeking. The situation reinforces the need for sustained surveillance, risk communication and community engagement, and coordination with WASH actors. Persistent Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) gaps also continue to be reported across regions, including limitations in service availability, hospitalization and referral pathways, funding, access to psychotropic medicines, and specialized support for children and adolescents.

Under the 2026 LRP Addendum, sector efforts through December remain focused on preserving access to critical services and advancing emergency preparedness, stabilization, and restoration of essential health system functions.

title: Nepal: Flood Response Situation Report #2 | 31 August 2026
content:
Situation Overview

  • On the morning of 26 August 2026, sudden and severe flash floods swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems in central Nepal, affecting communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, including the Rasuwagadhi border crossing area. The floods have caused significant loss of life, displacement, and widespread damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services along the affected river corridor.
  • As of 31 August 2026, 903 bodies have been recovered across Chitwan (272), Nawalparasi East (207), Nawalparasi West (151), Nuwakot (95), Gorkha (62), Dhading (55), Tanahun (37) and Rasuwa (24). Authorities report that 4,347 people remain missing, while 267 people have been injured. 1 A total of 10,451 people have been rescued, including 261 foreign nationals. More than 20,800 security personnel have been mobilized to support search and rescue, relief and security operations. Air operations remain critical to reaching inaccessible locations.
  • The scale and location of displacement remain largely unverified, with no consolidated national figures available and existing displacement data concentrated in a limited number of sites. Preliminary humanitarian analysis estimates that approximately 84,270 people have been affected across 17 municipalities in six districts: Rasuwa, Dhading, Nuwakot, Gorkha, Chitwan and Tanahu.
  • Displacement and housing impacts continue to be verified. In Nuwakot, preliminary assessments indicate that 1,897 households have been displaced, with 1,267 houses completely damaged and a further 1,253 partially damaged. Physical access remains severely constrained by damaged roads and bridges, unstable riverbanks, and disrupted telecommunications and electricity infrastructure. The 42 km Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi road has sustained extensive damage, significantly restricting surface access to upper Rasuwa and the border area. The Prithvi Highway, a critical route linking Kathmandu Valley with western Nepal, remains blocked along the Mugling–Malekhu section due to major road erosion and slope instability at Krishnabhir and Pareva Bhir in Dhading District.
  • Several hard-to-reach communities remain dependent on air operations or alternative foot access, limiting assessments and the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Damage to critical infrastructure is extensive, affecting homes, health facilities, schools, water-supply systems, roads, bridges, electricity infrastructure and telecommunications. Assessments are ongoing, particularly in hard-to-reach areas, and the full extent of displacement, humanitarian needs and infrastructure damage has not yet been confirmed.

title: Health Sector Bulletin, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Hospital reconstruction accelerating: Syria signed an agreement with InterHealth Canada to rehabilitate and modernize 14 major public hospitals nationwide. The program covers buildings, medical equipment and hospital operating systems and is planned over approximately two years.

• Eastern Syria receiving new investment: More than $10 million was allocated to health services in Raqqa, including rehabilitation of Raqqa National Hospital. In Deir-ez-Zoir a new cardiac catheterization, prosthetics, emergency, pediatric and neonatal services opened, while construction of a specialized oncology hospital was launched.

• Additional facilities reopened or expanded across several governorates. Five health facilities opened in rural Idlib, including two dialysis centers; Homs opened a pediatric cardiology unit and upgraded dialysis services; Tadmor National Hospital received a $1 million grant and opened dialysis capacity; Douma National Hospital also reopened following rehabilitation supported by Japan and WHO.

• Measles, polio, Hepatitis A and other communicable diseases (AWD, cutaneous leishmaniasis, scabies, etc.) remain active public-health concerns, especially where vaccination, safe water and routine health services are suboptimal.

• Nutrition has become a stronger national priority. The MoH and UNICEF are moving nutrition programming from fragmented humanitarian projects toward a nationally led system. The Ministry says nutrition services operate through 929 primary health centers, and a new national nutrition survey and updated strategy are being prepared. UNICEF's August assessment estimates 587,000 children need treatment for wasting, including around 96,000 with severe wasting. New international funding targets child health and malnutrition. On 24 August, South Korea and the UN launched a $18.95 million humanitarian/early-recovery package. UNICEF's $7.95 million component will support health, nutrition and education for at least 400,000 vulnerable children and women, while WFP plans treatment for moderate acute malnutrition for 28,000 children under five and pregnant or breastfeeding women and girls.

• MoH is expanding specialist campaigns and diaspora participation. Syrian expatriate physicians have now reportedly carried out around 2,000 operations through more than 20 specialist medical campaigns, alongside local staff training. The MoH Telegram channel also announced “Recovery Bridges – SAMS 15” for September with SAMS and Global Medical Foundation Australia, covering multiple medical and surgical specialties across eastern, central, Damascus-area and Aleppo facilities.

• Syrian diaspora doctors expanding specialist care: Syrian authorities reported that expatriate medical teams have conducted roughly 2,000 surgeries through more than 20 specialized campaigns, while also training local health workers and introducing newer medical technologies.

• World Bank $75 million health project moves into implementation - the official World Bank procurement plan on 10 August.

• Health financing reform is moving forward. Authorities want a redesigned public-sector health insurance system completed before the end of 2026, including a larger provider network, digital administration and stronger oversight. This is important because out-of-pocket spending remains one of the main barriers to care.

• The Health Minister met Norwegian Foreign Minister on 24 August (health-sector priorities, potential new projects, health investment and expanding successful experience with digital automation).

• The Health Minister met Germany's chargé d'affaires in Damascus to discuss cooperation, coordination and future health-sector partnership.

• The Health Minister met Norwegian Foreign Minister to discuss health-sector priorities, possible new projects, investment and the expansion of digital health-service automation.

• The World Humanitarian Day, the Global Health Cluster, joins all humanitarians in honouring health workers who continue to provide life-saving care in the most dangerous conditions and the families who live with these risks and losses alongside them. The statement reflects on what is lost when health workers are attacked: lives, expertise, trust, relationships and vital care that communities depend on. It also calls for stronger protection of health workers and health care, respect for International Humanitarian Law, and accountability when those protections are violated. The full statement: https://healthcluster.who.int/newsroom/news/item/19-08-2026someone-is-waiting-for-them-to-come-home.
