title: Vanuatu Volcanic Eruption 2026 - Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRVU013)
content:
Event development
Update regarding the event’s development

The anticipated event did not fully materialise into a major volcanic eruption. Ambae Volcano remained at Alert Level 3, indicating a minor eruption.

Monitoring through July 2026 confirmed that the volcano continued to emit smoke, gas and ash, with volcanic glow visible at the summit. However, the activity remained within the designated three-kilometre danger zone around the active vents, and the likelihood of escalation to a moderate eruption was assessed as low. Risks from ashfall, volcanic gases, acid rain and contaminated water sources remain, particularly for nearby and downwind communities.

These hazards may continue to affect water supplies, subsistence gardens, health and livelihoods. Residents have been advised to remain outside the designated danger zone, avoid streams during heavy rainfall and continue following official Vanuatu Meteorology & Geohazards Department (VMGD) advisories.

title: Panama Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRPA022)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
16-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since the beginning of August 2026, Central America has experienced a sequence of tropical waves that have generated prolonged conditions of atmospheric instability, characterized by intense rains, thunderstorms, and gusty winds.

In Panama, Tropical Wave No. 32, which entered the national territory on August 12, caused damage mainly in Bocas del Toro, the Ngäbe- Buglé region and Guna Yala, including falling trees, road interruptions and difficulties in accessing communities and sectors of Changuinola. (1)

On August 16, 2026, the Panamanian Red Cross began operational activation and coordination of its response in Bocas del Toro. At 6:00 p.m., SINAPROC issued a green alert for Bocas del Toro, the Ngäbe-Buglé Region, and the Naso Tjër Di region due to the forecast of heavy rains, thunderstorms, strong winds, possible rapid flooding of rivers and streams, flooding, and landslides. In response, the National Society activated monitoring and coordination with its committees in Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí, and Veraguas; prepared to mobilize assessment teams; and maintained an operational presence at the Bocas del Toro Provincial Emergency Operations Center. The Changuinola Committee also supported preventive evacuation efforts in Puente Blanco. These actions marked the operational start of the National Society's response.

On August 17, the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA) issued a watch warning for rains and storms, warning of accumulated precipitation and soil saturation levels above 65%, with the possibility of river overflows and landslides, mainly in Bocas del Toro, the Ngäbe-Buglé region, mountainous areas of Chiriquí, north and south of Veraguas, south of Los Santos, east of Panama, Guna Yala, Emberá Wounaan, Darién and North and Central Panama. (5)

The intense rains caused flooding with significant impacts particularly in Changuinola, Almirante and Chiriquí Grande. Given the persistence of meteorological and hydrological conditions, a risk scenario associated with new intense rains, sudden flooding of rivers and streams, floods, landslides and damage to communication routes is maintained. (1) (2) (3) According to the latest report from the Bocas del Toro Provincial Emergency Operations Center, approximately 2,853 families are reported affected, equivalent to about 14,265 people, distributed in more than 20 communities. Assessments are still ongoing to determine more precisely the magnitude of the damage and the needs of the population. (6)

The floods have caused damage to homes, water, sanitation and hygiene, health, livelihoods and essential household goods. Post-event conditions also increase the risks associated with vector-borne diseases, diarrhoeal diseases and other conditions linked to exposure to contaminated water and soil. (1) (6)

Although some families have progressively begun to return from shelters to their communities and homes, humanitarian needs and limitations persist in recovering minimum conditions of habitability, sanitation and security. (1) (6)

title: Global Price Watch July 2026 Prices (August 31, 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • In West Africa, Sahel staple prices were mixed and seasonally higher in July. Prices were generally lower than last year in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, below the five-year averages outside conflict-affected and refugee-hosting areas. Prices were mixed in Nigeria, stable in Togo, and firming seasonally in Benin and northern Côte d’Ivoire. Refugee demand in eastern Chad, fuel, shipping, and transport costs in Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, and CAR kept prices locally elevated (Page 3).
  • In East Africa, staple food prices remained elevated and stable in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Djibouti, and declined in Burundi, Uganda, Somalia, Tanzania, and parts of South Sudan, mainly due to improved availability from harvests, stable fuel prices, and enhanced cross-border inflows. Prices increased in Sudan and parts of South Sudan amid increased market demand and dwindling supplies, currency depreciation, high fuel prices, and localized market disruptions due to conflict and poor road conditions (Page 5).
  • In Southern Africa, maize prices were mixed in July. Prices fell from June by 9.9 percent in Zambia and 8 percent in Mozambique due to ample 2025/26 harvest supplies, and held stable in Malawi, Zimbabwe and Lesotho. In South Africa, prices rose 7 percent on average and trended up across markets in Madagascar due to early stock depletion. Prices were below July 2025 in Zambia, Lesotho, and South Africa, where white maize was 28 percent lower, but above last year in Mozambique and Angola (Page 7).
  • In Central America, supply depended on imports during the lean season, with prices stable in Guatemala but rising in Honduras due to tighter domestic supply, sluggish imports, and higher transportation costs. Red and black bean prices were below 2025 levels. In Haiti, local food prices declined following the main harvest. In Venezuela, monthly inflation increased, and food prices increased in USD and VED, driven by currency depreciation and disruptions after the earthquakes. In Colombia, cereal prices remained stable below 2025 levels, and tuber prices increased from 2025 levels driven by higher costs (Page 9).
  • In the Middle East and Europe, staple food price trends remain mixed. In Lebanon, wheat flour, sunflower oil, and lentil prices were stable. In Syria, rice remained stable while wheat flour increased, with pressure from higher fuel prices despite currency appreciation. Wheat flour prices declined in Gaza as inflows increased; in the West Bank, wheat flour and rice prices were stable, though market access is constrained. In Yemen, wheat flour and basmati rice remained stable in Aden, while cooking oil increased amid higher shipping insurance fees and fuel costs. In Ukraine, bread and cereal prices were stable, while potato prices declined sharply (Page 11).
  • In Asia, staple food prices remained mixed. Prices were broadly stable in Sri Lanka, while seasonal tightening, elevated transport costs, and trade- and conflict-related disruptions sustained price pressures in Pakistan, Burma, and parts of Nepal. Wheat flour prices rose unseasonably in Pakistan, remaining nearly 40 percent above the five-year average, while prices remained well above average in Burma. In Nepal, prices were largely stable with sharp localized increases in coarse rice and potato prices in Kathmandu (Page 13).
  • International markets showed mixed trends in July. Maize prices increased 6.8 percent as the first U.S. yield fell below expectations, rice prices decreased 1.2 percent but remain 13.9 percent above July 2025, and wheat rose 10.4 percent as Black Sea exports stalled and heat spells drove reduced EU crops. Brent crude oil averaged 84 USD/bbl, and fertilizer prices fell an average of 4.4 percent, led by urea. Most commodity prices remained above July 2025 levels. Maize and rice stayed below the five-year average, and wheat was near the five-year average (Page 2).

title: Factsheet: Europe responds, solidarity in action - Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid assistance in 2026
content:
Civil Protection

European assistance is coordinated through the ERCC under the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.
National capacities are reinforced by rescEU strategic reserves and Copernicus emergency mapping.

Wildfires across Europe

10 activations in 8 countries since April 2026.

41 aircraft, over 1000 first responders moved across borders to support firefighting operations in addition to 777 firefighters who were already pre-positioned in high-risk areas ahead of the summer across 14 countries.

More than 400 Copernicus satellite maps produced in 2026.

The European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) provides early warning and fire monitoring tools, supported by satellites.

In the longer term, 12 new firefighting planes and 5 helicopters are being procured. They would form the permanent rescEU fleet, with the first helicopter already delivered and stationed in Romania. It is operational for the 2026 wildfire season. Its first deployment was during the operations against the wildfires in Serbia in August 2026. The other firefighting rescEU assets will gradually become available (first airplanes as of 2028, other helicopters next year).

Crisis response around the world

Venezuela: around 750 responders and experts from 18 countries. Over 200 tonnes humanitarian assistance via EU Humanitarian Airbridge and €5 million in emergency humanitarian funding.

Colombia: tents, water filters, kitchen sets, satellite mapping and €2.35 million in emergency humanitarian funding.

Middle East: More than 13,000 people were brought back home to Europe, following the beginning of hostilities in Iran, in March 2026.

Ukraine: Over 5,000 patients evacuated to European hospitals through medevac operations.

title: UNFPA Flash Update: Nepal Floods (29 August 2026)
content:
On 26 August 2026, severe flash floods affected the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, initially impacting Rasuwa and subsequently downstream areas of Nuwakot, Dhading and towards Chitwan. The floods have caused significant loss of life and extensive damage to critical infrastructure. Approximately 10,000 households have been affected, 626 people are currently reported to have died and more than 2,400 people are missing.

Based on available population data, 310,076 people live in the affected areas, including approximately 86,820 women of reproductive age and 4,430 pregnant women. Damage to health facilities, roads, bridges and electricity infrastructure is disrupting access to life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric referrals, as well as complicating the delivery of essential humanitarian assistance.

UNFPA has mobilized 2,000 dignity kits for affected women and girls, with delivery to affected communities facilitated through the Government of Nepal and the Nepal Red Cross Society. The response also includes the deployment of two mobile health units, alongside reproductive health supplies, to help maintain life-saving reproductive and maternal health services in affected areas. Remote psychosocial support services have also been activated to provide immediate remote assistance to affected populations, with a standby roster of trained personnel available for rapid deployment as psychosocial needs emerge.

title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Flash Update #4 (As of 31 August 2026)
content:
This report is produced by the Office of the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Nepal, in collaboration with humanitarian partners and the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). It covers the period from 27 to 31 August 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • According to NDRRMA’s latest bulletin (31 August 2026, 09:00), the death toll has reached 903, with 267 people injured (156 discharged) and 4,247 individuals still reported missing.
  • A total of 10,451 people have been rescued to date, including 252 foreign nationals and 3,344 Nepalis rescued by helicopter.
  • Government-led search and rescue efforts have mobilised 20,819 personnel across affected areas.
  • The Government has allocated emergency financial assistance of NPR 10 million (~65,000 USD) each to Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, and NPR 0.5 million to Dhading.
  • Government relief operations have deployed 34 trucks, 35 jeeps, and 8 helicopters, alongside 5 helicopter deliveries of medical supplies to support affected communities.
  • Joint rescue operations are ongoing at hydropower projects including Trishuli 3A, Haku Besi, Trishuli 3B, and Chilime, involving Nepali, Indian, and Chinese rescue teams.
  • A command post in the Government of Nepal disaster management authority has been activated, and 15 emergency sectoral coordination teams have been deployed to support health, communications, roads, and electricity restoration.
  • Transportation on the Mugling-Malekhu section of the Prithvi Highway remains completely blocked due to toe-cutting at Krishna Bhir and Parewa Bhir.
  • Power supply has been restored in Dhading and Nuwakot; restoration work continues in Rasuwa.

17 15 municipalities declared flood emergency and another 2 impacted

65,000 People need emergency WASH support

22,100 People need protection support

19 Schools damaged

10,451 People rescued

20,819 Search and rescue personnel deployed

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Five days after the flash flood of the Trishuli River swept through Raswuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, the Government of Nepal’s response efforts continue at scale, with more than 10,000 people rescued and over 20,000 personnel mobilised for search and rescue operations, while authorities report 903 fatalities and 4,247 people still missing.

The Government has officially declared a flood emergency in 15 municipalities and designated two additional municipalities as impacted, underscoring the scale of humanitarian needs across the affected areas.

The Government created 15 Task Teams to streamline response actions: Emergency Communication Restoration Team, Electricity Restoration and Backup Power Team, Search, Rescue and Evacuation Team, Emergency Health and Medical Response Team, Dead Body Management Team, International Assistance and Donor Coordination Team, Transport and Road Connectivity Team, Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment Team, Missing Persons and Family Assistance Team, Relief (Food, Water and Essential Supplies), Airport Coordination Team, a team to make public the names of the rescued, disappeared and the dead, Camp Management Team, and Social Media Regulation/Management.

International assistance has been robust and continues to grow, reflecting strong global solidarity and support for the response effort.

title: UNICEF Colombia Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • From January to April, Colombia’s humanitarian crisis worsened, affecting 630,000+ people. UNMAS recorded 121 armed drone incidents through May (up 146%). Ethnic communities comprised 49% of victims, mainly across Chocó, Cauca, Norte de Santander, Nariño and Antioquia. Additionally, 51 child recruitment cases were identified, primarily in Norte de Santander and Cauca.
  • During the same period, disasters affected 538,000 people, primarily through floods (92%). Heavy rains and a cold front have impacted 216,000+ people across 24 Córdoba municipalities since early 2026.
  • Forecasts show the 2026–2027 El Niño could affect 4.3 million people across 508 municipalities, including 2 million at high risk and 2.3 million at extreme risk of water shortages.
  • As of June 30, the 2026 HAC reached 41,913 people (16% of 254,800 targeted), including 33,127 children (18% of 180,240 targeted). By June 30, the country office secured $14.1M of the $27.1M required for the 2026 HAC (52% funded).

title: Myanmar Health Cluster Bulletin August 2026
content:
Highlights

- Simultaneous Cholera/Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD) outbreaks reported from Yangon, Sittwe, Mon, and Ayeyarwady in same townships as 2024 outbreak. At the same time, AWD cases detected in other floodaffected areas in Sagaing (Shwebo), Mandalay and Bago. Early detection triggered immediate response from partners, resulting in a decline in cases so far, while risk of further spread remains high

- Heavy monsoon rains resulting in severe flooding affecting over 470k people in Sagaing (16 townships), Mandalay (4 townships), Magway (4 townships), Ayeyarwady (3 townships), and Mon.

- Floods also resulting in increase in malaria and dengue cases, especially in endemic areas in Karenni, Tanintharyi, Kachin, Chin and Sagaing. Partners are reporting severe shortages in supplies, especially bednets

- Data collected from 49 health partners shows 813,434 people have been reached with life-saving health services in 227 townships in Myanmar during the first half of 2026. Overall, health partners reached 896,871 people in need of humanitarian health services in all 330 townships of Myanmar in this same period

- Between 1 January and 31 August 2026, 101 attacks on health care were reported by Insecurity Insight, as compared to 53 verified incidents by WHO’s Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA).

- Over 200,000 people remain displaced in Magway since May as a result of conflict.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Lebanon Crisis (7 July - 8 August 2026)
content:
Persistent humanitarian and protection challenges continue to affect communities across Lebanon. Displacement and returns remain volatile, particularly following the 5 August escalations and the subsequent evacuation warning issued for al-Mansouri.

As of 6 August 2026, a total of 25,503 people—53 per cent of them women and girls—remain displaced across 242 collective shelters. Displaced people report receiving limited information or inadequate notice about shelter closures and available alternative accommodation. This increases the risk of involuntary or secondary displacement, disrupts access to essential services, and contributes to further psychological distress.

Protection concerns remain acute among people experiencing prolonged displacement and those returning to conflict-affected areas. Women and girls, adolescents, older people and persons with disabilities face heightened risks associated with overcrowding, damaged housing, limited privacy, gender-based violence, financial hardship, and barriers to essential services.

UNFPA estimates that approximately 390,000 women of reproductive age are among the displaced and returnee population, including around 16,000 pregnant women, with an estimated 1,800 expected to give birth each month. Many pregnant women are returning to areas where health infrastructure has sustained significant damage. Three hospitals and 27 primary health centres remain closed, the continued need for life-saving sexual and reproductive health supplies and services, particularly maternal healthcare and emergency obstetric care.

Since the onset of the crisis in the beginning of March, UNFPA has reached 43,445 displaced people with sexual and reproductive health services and 47,126 people with gender-based violence prevention and response activities. This support has been delivered through 55 health facilities, nine mobile medical units, 24 mobile GBV teams and 19 women and girls’ safe spaces, serving people in collective shelters and host communities.

However, access constraints and funding shortfalls continue to limit UNFPA’s ability to reach people in need. UNFPA has been appealing for US$25 million to address the urgent needs of 450,000 people. To date, only 16 per cent of the required funding has been secured, leaving a significant gap in the resources needed to sustain critical humanitarian and protection services.

title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Rasuwa flood), 31 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Nepal flash floods have affected an estimated 65,000 people, including 22,100 children, across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun districts. An estimated 903 people have been reported dead, while approximately 4,247 remain missing. The death toll continues to rise.
  • Many families have been displaced, with most staying with host families, while others are sheltering in Government-run holding centers.
  • Critical infrastructure has been badly affected, including six health facilities and at least 19 schools destroyed or damaged, disrupting children’s access to healthcare, safe water, education and protection services.
  • UNICEF delivers life-saving support across water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, nutrition, child protection, social protection, education and risk communication, while strengthening local and national systems and capacities to sustain service delivery, support recovery and build resilience to future emergencies.
  • Critical UNICEF supplies for about 19,000 people have been provided to Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. These include hygiene kits, buckets, soap, disinfectant, collapsible jerrycans, water purification products and risk communication materials.
  • UNICEF urgently requires US$17.2 million to support immediate humanitarian response for affected children and families. Internal resources have been mobilized to kick-start the response, but additional funding is urgently needed.

title: WFP Timor-Leste Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• Timor-Leste, a least-developed small island state of 1.3 million people, has made notable progress in reconstruction, human rights, and development since independence in 2002, yet it still faces major nutrition and food security challenges, exacerbated by natural hazards.
• Stunting among children under five remains among the world’s highest. The 2024 IPC analysis shows 27 percent of households are acutely food-insecure, while the 2023 cost-of-diet study found that 75 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet, with food prices up 78 percent since 2019. Low agricultural productivity, poor maternal and child nutrition practices, high poverty rates, limited safety nets, and frequent climatic shocks further weaken food systems and household resilience.
• WFP’s country strategic plan (CSP 2026-2030) supports the Government of Timor-Leste's vision for zero hunger and contributes to the National Strategic Development Plan 2011-2030. The overall goal of the CSP is to improve food security and nutrition by strengthening existing social protection programmes (Bolsa da Mãe Kondisionál, Merenda Eskolár), the food value chain, supply chain management, and emergency shock preparedness and response.

title: Islamic Republic of Iran: Humanitarian Update No. 07 | As of 31 July 2026
content:
This Humanitarian Update is produced by OCHA Regional Office for the Middle East and North Africa (ROMENA) on behalf of and in collaboration with UN agencies and humanitarian organisations. It covers the period from 1 to 31 July 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • Strikes resumed for 13 consecutive nights (12-24 July) mainly in southern provinces and coastal regions. Some people temporarily relocated from the most affected areas, including from the islands to the mainland, and received assistance in temporary shelters and schools.
  • The strikes caused renewed damage to civilian infrastructure, including a desalination and water supply facility in Hormozgan disrupting drinking water supply for about 10,000 people. Emergency water supply was provided to affected communities.
  • Iran’s Ministry of Health reported 60 deaths and 670 injuries due to hostilities between 27 June and 24 July, including six women and three children.
  • Country-wide response to people affected by the escalation since February is ongoing.

KEY FIGURES

3.4K+ Civilians killed (figure is for the period 28 February-9June, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #9, 11 June 2026)

33K+ Civilians injured (figure is for the period 28 February-9June, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #9, 11 June 2026)

149K+ Civilian units damaged (figure is for the period since 28 February as reported by the Iranian Red Crescent Society on 7 June 2026)

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Hostilities escalated in July with a significant increase in strikes reported in southern and coastal areas, most notably from 12 to 24 July. Damage has been reported in civilian infrastructure including residential buildings, roads, bridges, tunnels, electricity infrastructure, desalination facilities, mineral water facilities, grain and wheat flour warehouses, airports, maritime traffic control tower, communication and meteorological infrastructure. Most damaged roads were reported to quickly reopen but concerns remain over risks to access to essential commodities and services. Civilian property was damaged, including fishermen’s boats and tourism businesses.

HUMANITARIAN IMPACT AND NEEDS

Health

According to Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education (MoHME), renewed hostilities in July resulted in at least 60 deaths and 670 injuries, and additional damage to health infrastructure. Damage to electricity infrastructure has disrupted power supply to hospitals and cold chain systems for vaccines and medicines. Emergency backup power is needed for cold chain warehouses, hospitals, and health facilities in affected areas. Sustained health workforce support and timely delivery of medical supplies remain also critical.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

Damage to water and power infrastructure continues to limit access to safe drinking water including in areas reliant on chlorinated systems and brackish groundwater. In Hormozgan Province, a desalination and water supply facility was hit on 18 July, reportedly disrupting drinking water supplies for around 20 villages with a population of more than 10,000 people. Earlier on 12 July, Bunji desalination plant in Hormozgan Province and Hendijan drainage pumping station in Khuzestan Province were damaged. A rapid assessment by the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) indicated that over 8,000 people in Minab and Qeshm of Hormozgan Province lost access to safe drinking water due to damage to desalination and water supply infrastructure. Priority needs include water disinfection, restoration of water infrastructure, temporary storage and water trucking, and safe water provision.

Food Security

Food remains available in markets while rising prices undermine affordability. The Statistical Centre of Iran reported household year-on-year inflation reached 87.9%, while food inflation stood at 128.1%. The minimum food basket cost increased by more than 41% between 28 February and 27 July, reaching around IRR 57.3 million (roughly USD $37) per person per month. Lower-income households are experiencing severe pressures, with increased needs for targeted food and cash assistance.

Protection

Strikes in southern areas have disrupted livelihoods and caused temporary relocations in affected areas. Demand for Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services continues to exceed available resources in some locations. Challenges persist in reaching the most vulnerable and geographically dispersed populations. Continued investment in local partner capacity is needed to sustain service quality, coverage, and effective delivery.

Education

As of 22 July, a total of 1,507 educational facilities, including 1,288 schools across the country have been damaged (since February). While most facilities that sustained minor damage have been repaired, at least 40 schools still require rehabilitation

Shelter and Non-Food Items

Several affected households require shelter and non-food items support, particularly in the southern islands where populations have been temporarily relocated. Approximately 500 families moved from Abu Musa, Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb islands, and are currently hosted in temporary centres in Bandar Abbas, Hormozgan Province.

Early Recovery

About 300 fishing vessels were reportedly destroyed, affecting the livelihoods of up to 60,000 fishermen in Hormozgan Province. An initial assessment identified approximately 9,000 fishermen who had lost their assets in need for multi-purpose cash assistance support. As of 31 July, an estimated 10 million tonnes of debris and construction waste have been generated in affected urban areas making debris clearance critical to emergency response and the rehabilitation of essential civilian infrastructure.

Cultural Heritage

Since February 2026, a total of 149 heritage sites, including 54 museums, seven historic areas, and five UNESCO World Heritage sites across 18 provinces, were damaged. Recovery remains constrained by limited funding, specialized expertise, and restoration materials.

RESPONSE

Health

The United Nations Agency for Children (UNICEF) is supporting the restoration and maintenance of access to basic healthcare, while several UN agencies are supporting the health system with equipment to strengthen resilience against power outages. UNICEF delivered three prefabricated health units to Ilam, Kurdistan, and Ahvaz to temporarily replace damaged service delivery points. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is providing generators to hospitals and vaccine storage facilities. The World Health Organization (WHO) procured three power generators and uninterruptible power supply units for hospitals in Abadan, Khorramabad, and Bandar Abbas. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) delivered two refrigerated vaccine trucks to the MoHME to strengthen national vaccine cold chain capacity in southern provinces. The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) is supporting inclusive public health services through financing health personnel costs and procuring essential medicines and medical equipment.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

UNICEF provided 10 prefabricated latrines, 10 water storage tanks and three sludge pumps to the affected provinces of Hormozgan, Khuzestan, and Sistan and Baluchestan. A total of 3,060 household hygiene, baby, and menstrual hygiene kits, 760 incontinence kits, and 6,000 collapsible jerry cans were delivered to these provinces. UNDP is providing emergency chlorination and disinfection units to restore water treatment, rehabilitating priority pumping capacity, while deploying temporary water storage tanks, water tankers, and small-scale reverse osmosis units to sustain safe water supply in affected communities. NRC is preparing the distribution of household hygiene kits and menstrual hygiene kits in Qeshm and Minab in Hormozgan Province.

Food Security

The Government continues its measures to maintain essential commodity supplies and stabilize markets. The World Food Programme (WFP) is providing food and cash assistance to 35,666 refugees, including daily bread through supported bakeries and wheat flour distributions, while school feeding continued via take-home rations for about 9,000 students. NRC is planning to provide multi-purpose cash assistance for about 1,000 relocated families from southern islands to Bandar Abbas and Qeshm.

Protection

UNICEF, in partnership with NRC, implemented a humanitarian cash transfer programme targeting 1,233 vulnerable host-community households in the provinces of Kerman, Bushehr, Yazd, and Sistan and Baluchestan to support access to essential needs. IOM provided multi-purpose cash assistance for protection, health needs, and emergencies to affected host communities and Afghan nationals. UNHCR and local NGOs are delivering MHPSS services, targeting about 8,000 individuals by end of 2026.

Education

UNHCR supported the construction of four schools in Yazd, Qom, Isfahan, and Tehran provinces, for refugee and host-community students in underserved areas, with three additional school construction projects under preparation. UNHCR continues to support refugee access to tertiary education through the DAFI scholarship programme, benefiting 199 refugee students with tuition and living allowances. NRC is planning to rehabilitate schools and WASH facilities and provide equipment to nine schools in Hormozgan, six schools in Tehran and two schools in Alborz provinces.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

UNICEF, through a national NGO partner, delivered 3,000 rapid response packages including first aid kits, essential hygiene and non-food items, and child-friendly items to Chabahar, Qeshm, Sirik, Jask, Bandar Khamir, and Bandar Abbas. IOM distributed 54 wheelchairs for migrants with disabilities and working to provide the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) with shelter kits and hygiene kits. UNHCR provided cash assistance to around 4,700 refugee families between March and July (around 20,000 individuals) to support essential needs, including food, shelter, healthcare, and other critical expenses.

Early Recovery

UNDP delivered machinery components for debris removal operations to Tehran Waste Management Organization and 22 power generators to Tehran Mitigation and Management Organization to support emergency operations and recovery efforts. UNDP is also providing rescue and emergency equipment to IRCS including medical and hospital beds, loaders, excavators, and forklifts, in addition to training.

Cultural Heritage

The restoration of 149 damaged heritage sites is reportedly underway by national authorities. The United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is preparing a technical damage assessment mission to Iran, that will include a rapid assessment of the Golestan Palace World Heritage site.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #211 - 31 August 2026
content:
Highlight

On 27 August, Mr. Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia and Middle East and North Africa, visited the UNHCR’s Community Centre for refugees at Romexpo, in Bucharest, accompanied by UNICEF Representative in Romania, Ms. Anna Riatti. During the visit, the Director was briefed on activities at the centre by Mr. Pablo Zapata, UNHCR Representative in Romania, and discussed with the UNHCR teams and partner NGOs about their activities dedicated to the protection and inclusion of refugees, as well as the support provided by UNICEF to refugees from Ukraine. The visit was also an opportunity to discuss the importance of maintaining such community spaces, which offer not only access to essential services, but also opportunities for connection, learning and integration for people forced to leave their homes.

On 29 August, UNHCR in collaboration with NGO Green Revolution (Roaba de Cultură), and partners of the Refugee Response Plan (RRP), hosted “Together in the Park” - a celebration of multiculturalism, community, and culture. The open-air event - with live music and workshops for children - was the third in a series of community activities aimed at fostering social cohesion, multicultural understanding, and solidarity, bringing together refugees, migrants, and the host community in Bucharest. The event was made possible thanks to the generous support of ARCUB. The fourth “Together in the Park” event supported by UNHCR will take place on 26 September.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territory (oPt) Situation Analysis: [3/8/2026] - [9/8/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: UNICEF Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (BVD Outbreak in DRC: Regional Preparedness and Readiness in Neighboring and At-Risk Countries), July 2026
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
Highlights

  • Regional preparedness efforts continue across at-risk countries as the Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) outbreak remains active in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Uganda officially declared the end of its outbreak on 28 July 2026, and no confirmed cases have been reported in other neighboring countries to date. Nevertheless, sustained population movements, porous borders and humanitarian vulnerabilities continue to present a risk of cross-border transmission, requiring heightened vigilance and preparedness measures.
  • UNICEF is supporting governments in 10 priority at-risk countries to strengthen readiness, early detection and response capacity. Efforts focus on infection prevention and control (IPC), WASH, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), surveillance, emergency coordination and preparedness at key points of entry. Countries continue to conduct simulation exercises, train frontline workers, engage communities and pre-position essential supplies to ensure rapid detection and containment of any imported case.
  • Cross-border preparedness remains a key regional priority. UNICEF is supporting coordination among neighboring countries, including through regular preparedness reviews, information sharing and technical support to strengthen operational readiness and ensure a harmonized regional approach to outbreak prevention and response.
  • Funding gaps continue to constrain preparedness activities across the region. UNICEF requires US$25.4 million to sustain preparedness and readiness efforts in 10 at-risk countries. Timely and predictable financing remains essential to maintain readiness capacities and address vulnerabilities before international spread occurs.

title: WFP Madagascar Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • July marked the sixth and final cycle of the 2025–2026 lean season response in the Grand Sud. WFP has reached 537,635 people.
  • The first national drought monitoring bulletin issued in July introduced projections for a strong El Niño, highlighting heightened risks for the upcoming season and reinforcing the importance of early action.
  • Recurrent shocks are exposing the limits of short‑term emergency response and reinforcing the need for sustained investment in human capital, climate‑resilient food systems, and shock‑responsive social protection. Immediate resource mobilization remains critical to ensure operational readiness for the emergency response to the 2026–2027 lean season and cyclone seasons, with USD 44.1 million required to sustain humanitarian assistance and protect resilience and nutrition gains.

title: Islamic Relief - Rohingya Crisis Humanitarian Advocacy Updates
content:
Highlights

Milestone: The Rohingya crisis entered its tenth year on 25 August, marking nearly a decade of mass displacement with no durable solution in sight.

Displacement: Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, where many continue to face restrictions on education and livelihood opportunities amid declining international funding (see page 2).

Myanmar: Around 500,000 Rohingya remain inside Myanmar, caught in ongoing conflict and facing serious protection risks (see page 2).

Our response: In 2026, Islamic Relief reached more than 150,000 Rohingya refugees with shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), food assistance and other essential services (see page 7).

Earthquake recovery: We supported communities in Myanmar affected by a major 2025 earthquake through shelter repairs, livelihood recovery assistance and Ramadan food distributions (see page 4).

Advocacy: Islamic Relief calls for greater refugee protection, sustainable humanitarian funding, accountability, and ensuring any future return of Rohingya refugees is safe, voluntary and dignified (see page 3).

title: Lebanon Humanitarian Advocacy Update
content:
Conflict and protection: Attacks have continued in Lebanon since the ceasefire in March 2026, causing 16,585 casualties, further displacement, delayed returns, and ongoing violations of international law (see page 2).

Humanitarian funding: Funding shortfalls continue to undermine humanitarian efforts, with only 52% of the 2026 UN Lebanon Flash Appeal funded.

Our response: Despite access constraints and funding cuts, Islamic Relief Lebanon has expanded its emergency response and adapted programmes to reach those most affected as displacement patterns evolved (see page 6).

Advocacy: Islamic Relief advocates for a permanent ceasefire, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, safe and dignified returns, accountability for violations, respect for international humanitarian law, and increased humanitarian assistance (see page 5).

title: Ukraine Situation: Moldova - Operational Update (July 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

As of July 2026, 145,803 refugees from Ukraine are present in the Republic of Moldova, representing an increase of nearly 13,000 people compared to July 2025. Many refugees have achieved greater stability and self-reliance; however, those with acute vulnerabilities still face challenges in meeting basic needs and accessing adequate care and support services. Efforts therefore remain focused on supporting refugees’ inclusion in national systems and services, alongside targeted protection and assistance for those with heightened needs.

The Refugee Accommodation Centre (RAC) network continues to consolidate, while the need for affordable housing persists. The number of centres has decreased from 56 in 2023 to 11 as of 22 July 2026, with two additional centres in the process of closing. Upon completion of the consolidation process, nine RACs are expected to remain operational. As of end-July, the remaining centres accommodated 628 refugees with significant care and support needs, including older people (33 per cent), children (30 per cent), and persons with disabilities (12 per cent). Many require daily assistance with mobility, personal care, medication management, or supervision. Ensuring access for Temporary Protection beneficiaries to national care services will be critical to providing sustainable support for refugees with longer-term care needs.

title: UNHCR Syria Operational Update - July 2026
content:
Syria has entered a new phase marked by large-scale returns and persistent humanitarian vulnerability.

While around 1.7 million refugees and 1.9 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) have returned since December 2024, 15.6 million people still require humanitarian assistance.

As return movements continue, ensuring sustainable reintegration through access to housing, services, documentation, livelihoods and community support is central for Syria’s recovery.

In line with Syria’s National Recovery Priorities and the Government’s “No Tents, No Camps” vision, UNHCR supports this transition while maintaining protection and humanitarian assistance for vulnerable populations.

title: Palestinian Refugees in Lebanon In Their Own Voices: Living in Permanent Survival Mode - Volume 13 | Spring 2026
content:
WAR HAS ACCELERTED DECLINING PROSPECTS

This report captures a critical inflection point for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon, where long-standing structural vulnerabilities have converged with the impact of the 2026 war. The conflict has not created these inequalities, but it has sharply exposed and intensified them, revealing how fragile existing systems had already become.

Even before the latest escalation, years of economic collapse and declining international funding had pushed many families into survival mode, as access to healthcare, education and livelihoods steadily eroded, while humanitarian institutions were forced to scale back services due to sustained funding shortfalls.

Anera conducted the research, data collection and roundtable consultations that inform this report just months before the escalation. While conditions have since deteriorated further, the findings remain highly relevant in documenting the shrinking support systems shaping how communities are experiencing the conflict’s impact. For Palestinian communities, largely excluded from national safety nets, there are no viable alternatives when aid contracts.

In December 2025, Anera brought together 15 community-based and international organizations to examine how funding cuts were reshaping daily life in Palestinian communities. Participants described a humanitarian landscape in which needs were rising as resources declined, with Palestinian refugees among the hardest hit. They warned that reduced support was accelerating deterioration across nearly every aspect of life faster than existing systems could respond. The subsequent escalation of war has only intensified these pressures, adding new emergency demands and underscoring how little margin for shock remains.

Addressing this crisis requires more than data. It requires close attention to frontline perspectives in order to understand both immediate needs and longer-term consequences. Drawing on organizational perspectives and direct testimony, this report shows that essential services have been reduced to a minimum, prevention and development programming has largely collapsed, and women and children are bearing a disproportionate share of the burden. Ultimately, what emerges is a reality that risks being overlooked: a long-standing lack of legal rights combined with the steady erosion of services and future prospects that the war has accelerated but did not begin. By bringing together the views and experiences of refugees and the organizations that serve them, this report offers a clearer understanding of the crisis and a call for renewed coordination and investment in Palestinians in Lebanon.

title: Situation Report II - Nepal Flash Flood
content:
CURRENT SITUATION

  • The flash flood and debris flow that struck Nepal’s Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system on 26 August has evolved into a large-scale humanitarian emergency, with rapidly rising casualties, hundreds of people still unaccounted for, widespread infrastructure damage and a continuing risk of secondary flooding along downstream river corridors.
  • The latest reports indicate a rise in death toll to 553, with 977 still missing. More than 3,700 people have been rescued. The figures remain provisional and continue to change as search, rescue and body recovery operations progress.
  • At least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected and require urgent humanitarian assistance, according to the IFRC.
  • 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges and approximately 40 km of roads have been damaged, severely affecting connectivity and access to affected communities.
  • Electricity, telecommunications, drinking-water and hydropower infrastructure remain disrupted or damaged, while the destruction of roads and bridges is continuing to constrain humanitarian access.
  • Secondary flood risk remains high following the reported breach of a debris-created barrier lake near the Chhochen Khola–Purepu Tsangpo confluence, upstream of the Bhotekoshi. Nepalese authorities have been conducting aerial reconnaissance and monitoring water levels as communities downstream remain at risk of another surge.

title: Nepal Flood Emergency Situation Report | Reporting Period: 28–29 August 2026
content:
Locations: Galchi Rural Municipality, Dhading District; Chitwan District; Kathmandu, Nepal

Situation Overview

Flash floods have affected Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts in northern and central Nepal. Damaged infrastructure and restricted access continue to hamper relief efforts. In Galchi Rural Municipality, Dhading District, flooding destroyed a suspension bridge and damaged local infrastructure.

Operational Response
Medical Outreach and Dignified Management of the Deceased

On 28 August, a team from Tzu Chi Malaysia did an assessment visit to a hospital in Chitwan District that is receiving and managing bodies recovered from upstream flood-affected areas. The hospital reported acute shortages of mortuary capacity, body bags and Personal Protective Equipment (clothing). There was also a lack of protective supplies for security personnel, health workers and other responders handling bodies. Tzu Chi immediately procured 120 sets of Personal Protective Equipment (clothing) together with masks and gloves in Kathmandu. The supplies are being prepared for air transport to the hospital in Chitwan District.

On 29 August, Tzu Chi Singapore prepared 300 body bags for delivery to Singapore Changi Airport. The items are planned for air shipment to Kathmandu to support a dignified management of the deceased, subject to transport arrangements and coordination.

title: Vanuatu Ministry of Health: Watery Diarrhoea Outbreak in Tanna Island, Tafea Province - Situation Update No. 1 - Report Date: 25 August 2026 I Reporting Period: 10-21 August 2026
content:
Overview

  • From 10 August to 25 August 2026, a total of 81 cases of watery diarrhoea were reported through Lenakel Hospital.
  • The weekly number of reported cases exceeded the outbreak alert threshold of 34 cases, resulting in the declaration of a watery diarrhoea outbreak in Tanna Island.
  • Most cases were reported through Lenakel Hospital.
  • Hotspot communities include Lounuloul, Imai, Isla, Lamtavekel, Loueiau, and lmarap.
  • Case definition: Three or more loose or watery stools within a 24-hour period.

Key highlights:

  • 81 cases reported between 10 and 25 August 2026.
  • Cases exceeded the outbreak alert threshold, resulting in the declaration of an outbreak.
  • Most cases are among children under 5 years of age.
  • Seven cases have been hospitalised, with one severe case reported and no deaths to date.
  • Stool samples have been collected and are awaiting laboratory results to identify the causative agent.
  • Community awareness, enhanced surveillance, and case management activities are ongoing.

title: PHL: Flood - 08-2026 - PHL: Enhanced by Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) (2026-08-29)
content:
Description

The Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) has intensified over the Philippines, bringing persistent and at times heavy to intense rainfall over western and northern Luzon, Metro Manila, and parts of MIMAROPA and the Visayas. The enhanced monsoon is being further influenced by an two LPAs east of Extreme Northern Luzon, which may develop into a tropical cyclone and is expected to continue enhancing the Habagat.

As of 29 August 2026, PAGASA has issued multiple heavy rainfall warnings, including Red Warning over parts of Metro Manila and Occidental Mindoro, with serious flooding and landslides possible in affected areas. PAGASA forecasts that enhanced monsoon rains will continue over western Luzon and may persist through the coming days, increasing the risk of flooding, flash floods, landslides, and disruption to communities and transportation.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 28 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,040 Palestinians have been injured in settler attacks, with 80 settler incidents resulting in casualties or property damage in the second and third weeks of August.
  • Three families in Qusra remained isolated following the establishment of a new settlement outpost in Area B around 9 August, while humanitarian access negotiations enabled partners to reach the families with assistance.
  • On 25 August, Israeli forces forcibly entered UNRWA’s Kalandia Training Centre in East Jerusalem, which Israeli officials indicated had been seized, putting the education of 340 Palestine refugee youth at immediate risk.
  • In Gaza, 58 per cent of the population is facing severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or access to essential services and non-food items, exposing them to serious health, safety and dignity risks.
  • Preparations for the rainy season are underway but are held back by restrictions on the entry of supplies access to land within Gaza and funding shortfalls.
  • Days of intensified airstrikes resulted in civilian casualties and damage to humanitarian structures and to critical supplies.

Overview

In a briefing to the Security Council on 26 August, the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process ad interim said that “tensions are rising and uncertainty deepens in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” While calling for steps towards recovery and a lasting political settlement, Dr. Alakbarov – who is also the Humanitarian Coordinator – said that people’s needs remain immense and urgent. He warned that humanitarian actors, especially international non-governmental organizations, “continue to face operational constraints related to access, supplies, and funding, with the 2026 Flash Appeal only 40 per cent funded.”

Speaking on the Gaza Strip, he said that people continue to endure intolerable conditions and immense hardship. He warned that amid Israeli airstrikes, drone attacks, ground operations, and persistent humanitarian challenges, people are losing hope. “Around two-thirds of Gaza remain inaccessible or subject to severe access restrictions, leaving civilians confined to overcrowded and insecure areas… Soon, winter will descend on Gaza.” Efforts to prepare for the rainy season “must be scaled up and facilitated. Plans are in place, but stocks of shelter and non-food items are depleted, access constraints on the entry of critical humanitarian items continue, and funding remains critically low.” Dr. Alakbarov called for the restoration of electricity, including by operationalizing the Gaza Power Plant.

Speaking on the West Bank, he warned that large-scale settler attacks “continue with virtually no accountability for these crimes. Israeli security forces have frequently failed to protect Palestinians from settler attacks and, in some cases, have reportedly facilitated or participated in such violence. Israel, as the occupying power, must ensure that the civilian population is protected, and perpetrators are held to account.”

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 11 to 24 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions. These practices have also disrupted access to essential services and constrained humanitarian operations, amid persistent funding shortages. According to the Education Cluster, on 23 August, Israeli forces entered a girls’ secondary school in Jericho, causing damage to parts of the building just weeks before the new school year is due to begin. In Masafer Yatta, community-supported clearance of rubble began at a mixed basic school partially demolished by the Israeli authorities on 4 August, while rehabilitation and alternative learning arrangements remain suspended due to the risk of further demolition.

In a significant development following the reporting period, on 25 August, Israeli forces forcibly entered the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) Kalandia Training Centre (KTC) in occupied East Jerusalem, after which Israeli officials indicated in public statements that the premises had been seized by the Israeli authorities. This marked the fifth unauthorized entry by Israeli forces into the Centre since May this year. UNRWA issued a statement condemning the unauthorized incursion, describing it as unacceptable and emphasizing that the KTC, as a United Nations facility, is protected by the privileges and immunities afforded to the agency under international law and that its inviolability must be fully respected. Later the same day, clashes erupted in the surrounding area, during which Israeli forces reportedly fired tear gas canisters and live ammunition, resulting in at least nine injuries. The UN Secretary-General condemned the actions in the strongest terms, including the unlawful entry, continued presence and unauthorized works on the premises, and reiterated that UN premises are inviolable and immune from interference. The UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process ad interim also condemned the unauthorized entry and unlawful seizure, warning that it would immediately deprive 340 Palestine refugee youth from the West Bank of their right to education, with thousands more at risk in the coming years. Established in 1952, the KTC is UNRWA’s oldest vocational training centre and has served Palestine refugees for more than seven decades, providing free vocational education and skills training to hundreds of students annually, many of whom come from refugee camps across the occupied West Bank and face significant socio-economic hardship.

Partners leading on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) continued to respond to acute and prolonged water insecurity. Following the technical breakdown at the Mekorot-operated Beit Iba well on 24 July, which disrupted water supply to communities in the northern West Bank, the WASH Cluster mobilized emergency water trucking to three communities in Nablus governorate – Tell, Qusin and Bizzariya – based on assessed needs and gaps in alternative bulk water supplies. Partners also continued water trucking to 10 communities in Masafer Yatta, more than 1,500 people displaced from Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps, and over 2,000 displaced people at the Arab American University displacement site in Jenin, where sewage desludging is also ongoing. Emergency water trucking continued in 15 additional locations, primarily supporting people recently displaced due to settler violence.

Humanitarian partners continued shelter and protection assistance. Between 10 and 23 August, Shelter partners provided shelter repairs, non-food items and cash assistance to 1,475 people from 348 households, primarily in Nablus, Ramallah and Hebron governorates. During the same period, partners addressing gender-based violence (GBV) maintained specialized services across 16 service delivery points and 40 safe spaces for women and girls, including psychosocial support, case management, emergency assistance and mobile outreach. Funding shortages, which have resulted in the closure of two Women and Girls Safe Spaces, alongside movement restrictions and settler violence, continued to constrain access to and delivery of GBV services. Mine action partners provided risk education on explosive ordnance, conflict preparedness and protection sessions to more than 2,000 people across six governorates. Since the beginning of 2026, child protection partners have provided mental health and psychosocial support to more than 57,000 children, including over 2,200 children with disabilities, and nearly 25,700 caregivers.

Casualties and Settler Violence

Between 11 and 24 August, members of Israeli forces shot and killed three Palestinians, including two boys, in three incidents in Jenin, Nablus and Hebron governorates. Two Palestinians, including one child, were killed during operations by Israeli forces on 21 and 23 August in Jenin city and Askar Camp, respectively. On 21 August, an Israeli settlement guard shot and killed a Palestinian boy and critically injured another Palestinian during an attack by more than 50 Israeli settlers on the Hamrush community near Sa'ir village in Hebron governorate. In the same incident, settlers damaged four residential structures and set fire to another structure, destroying about seven tonnes of stored fodder.

During the reporting period, over 100 Palestinians, including eleven children and nine women, and one off-duty Israeli soldier were injured. More than two thirds of Palestinian injuries occurred in the context of settler attacks, including 55 Palestinians injured by Israeli settlers. Recurrent attacks were reported in and around Al Mughayyir in Ramallah governorate, including along the village's only access road, where settler attacks repeatedly injured Palestinians, damaged vehicles and disrupted movement. On 20 August alone, 11 Palestinians were injured during an attack on the village. On the same day, another 11 Palestinians were injured during a night-time settler attack on the Deir Shams community near Adh Dhahiriya in Hebron governorate, during which more than 240 sheep were reportedly stolen and homes, vehicles and an animal shelter were damaged. On 23 August, a Palestinian child stabbed and injured an off-duty member of Israeli forces traveling with his family near Al Auja, in Jericho governorate. Following the attack, Israeli forces closed the village, raided several homes and a school, and detained a 16-year-old Palestinian boy in connection with the incident.

Since the beginning of 2026, 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,870 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank. Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,040 injured in the context of settler attacks. The frequency of injuries directly caused by Israeli settlers has risen sharply, from an average of one Palestinian injured every three days in 2020, to two per day in 2025 and more than three per day so far in 2026.

During the reporting period, OCHA documented 80 attacks by Israeli settlers that resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both. Incidents included recurrent attacks on some of the same communities, affecting Palestinians' access to homes, agricultural land and roads, as well as water and electricity infrastructure. Settler attacks also resulted in the displacement of three households: one family of six, including four children, after settlers set fire to their home near Yatta town of the Hebron governorate on 20 August, and two families comprising nine people, including two children, after settlers burned their residential and livelihood structures in Burqa, Ramallah governorate, on 22 August.

Access Restrictions Linked to Settlement Expansion

The establishment of Israeli settlement outposts, previously concentrated in Area C, has increasingly extended into Area B. According to Israeli group Peace Now, settlers have established at least 26 outposts in Area B of the West Bank over the past two and a half years, including 19 since the end of 2024, most of them in recent months. Peace Now estimates that settlers have taken control of more than 100,000 dunams (24,710 acres) in Areas A and B, including 55,000 dunams (13,591 acres) in Area B, and reports that violence and threats have been used to restrict Palestinian access to land and, in some cases, pressure families to leave their homes.

In Qusra, Nablus governorate, the establishment of a new settlement outpost in Area B around 9 August, near three Palestinian households in the Ras Al Ein area, was followed by increased presence of Israeli forces and settlers, damage to water and electricity infrastructure, and restrictions on Palestinian movement and access. On 15 August, after the municipality obtained Israeli approval to repair infrastructure damaged by settlers, settlers physically assaulted and injured two members of the repair team and Israeli forces detained four electricity workers, preventing the completion of repairs. On 23 August, municipality workers delivered food to the families, following access approval by Israeli authorities.

As of 26 August, the three families remained subject to severe access and movement restrictions, with two of the four roads connecting the area to the rest of Qusra under Israeli control: one through a permanent military checkpoint and another where Israeli forces have reportedly installed a road gate. One of the affected homes had also been occupied by Israeli forces for about 10 days. Following the withdrawal of Israeli forces on 23 August, the family was able to return to their home. During the period of the takeover, Israeli forces removed most of the family’s belongings from the house, many of which were reportedly damaged. Through coordinated access, humanitarian partners were able to reach the affected families with some essential assistance, including food, water, medicines and other basic supplies.

In Hebron governorate, on 12 August, a humanitarian assessment was conducted in Surif and Halhul following an increase in settler attacks and access restrictions in areas affected by the establishment and expansion of settlement outposts in Area C. In Al Quraynat area of Surif, home to about 65 Palestinian families, Israeli settlers established two settlement outposts in 2025 and mid-2026. Since January 2025, there have been 16 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage in the area, compared with eight such attacks in the preceding five years. The severity of incidents has also increased: since January 2025, one Palestinian has been killed and 20 others injured by Israeli settlers or forces during settler attacks, compared with seven injuries and no fatalities in the preceding five years. During the assessment, residents reported recurrent shootings, physical assaults and intimidation by settlers, damage to homes, agricultural land and livelihood assets, and increasing restrictions on their access to agricultural and grazing land.

In Halhul town in Hebron governorate, seven new settlement outposts have been established since May 2025. Palestinian residents reported that the establishment and expansion of these settlement outposts and associated restrictions have constrained their access to about 14,000 of 37,000 dunams (3,459 – 9,143 acres) they own, much of which is productive agricultural land. Farmers reported reduced agricultural production and income due to access restrictions, settler attacks and the designation of some farmland as “military zones.” The assessment also highlighted the impact on access to essential services and protection concerns. In Wadi Muhaisin, seven families comprising about 90 people face movement restrictions that disrupt their access to schools, health care, and other essential services. For the past eight months, Israeli forces have reportedly prevented residents from using a route near a closed road gate close to Karmi Tsur Israeli settlement, forcing schoolchildren and other residents to take a four-kilometre detour along narrow agricultural routes to reach schools and other essential services. Residents also reported settler harassment while travelling along these routes, alongside psychosocial distress among children, women and families exposed to recurrent violence and intimidation.

Operations by Israeli Forces and Access Disruptions

During the reporting period, OCHA documented at least 22 raids, search operations and other operations by Israeli forces involving detentions, temporary home evacuations and movement restrictions, including in Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm and Hebron governorates. On 13 August, amid the reported return of Israeli settlers to the former Ganim settlement east of Jenin city, which was evacuated in 2005, Israeli forces established checkpoints and closed sections of Road 60, cutting off direct access to Jenin city for about 10 villages comprising more than 20,000 Palestinians. On 17 August, Israeli forces temporarily evacuated for seven hours about 10 families from Jabal an Naser neighbourhood in Tulkarm, due to military activities near the adjacent Nur Shams refugee camp. Israeli military bulldozers excavated part of a road, damaging water and sewage networks, and carried out excavation works on Palestinian land before withdrawing. Families reportedly returned to their homes, and municipal crews repaired the damaged infrastructure once Israeli security forces withdrew from the area. A separate 10-hour operation in Qabatiya, in Jenin, involved searches of about 100 homes and the detention of more than 60 Palestinians. On 19 August, Israeli forces imposed a curfew for more than 12 hours affecting an estimated 40,000 Palestinians in Adh Dhahiriya town in Hebron governorate, where they detained and interrogated about 40 Palestinians and took over seven homes for use as interrogation sites, confining the affected families to single rooms.

Demolitions and Forced Evictions

During the reporting period, OCHA documented 22 incidents in which 79 Palestinian-owned structures were demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, five of which had been provided as humanitarian assistance following previous demolitions. The demolitions displaced 16 households comprising 73 people, including 34 children, and otherwise affected more than 280 people, including about 100 children. Three structures were demolished in Kafr Sur, in Tulkarm, in proximity to the Barrier and 76 structures were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, including 66 in Area C and 10 in East Jerusalem. Demolished structures included 15 residential structures and 64 livelihood-related, agricultural, and water and sanitation structures.

More than half of those displaced – 45 Palestinians, including 22 children – were in Beit Hanina, Jabal al Mukabbir and Silwan in East Jerusalem, following demolitions of residential structures carried out by Israeli forces or by owners following the receipt of demolition orders. In Jabal al Mukabbir, 22 people, including 13 children, were displaced in two incidents on 12 and 14 August; in Silwan, 13 people, including five children, were displaced in two incidents on 12 and 17 August; and in Beit Hanina, three refugee households comprising 10 people, including four children, were displaced on 19 August when the Jerusalem Municipality, accompanied by Israeli forces, demolished a two-storey residential building. Some affected families reported losing belongings and furniture during the demolitions, including in Beit Hanina, where residents reported being prevented from retrieving most of their belongings before the building was demolished.

Separately, on 18 August, Israeli forces forcibly evicted two Palestinian households comprising eight people from parts of their three-storey residential building in the Batn al Hawa area of Silwan, East Jerusalem, in favour of the Israeli settler organization Ateret Cohanim. The families had built and inhabited the building prior to 1967. Following Israeli court proceedings over claims that parts of the building stand on land owned by Jews prior to 1948, settlers took over the second-floor apartment and parts of the third-floor apartment rendering it uninhabitable, as well as the main entrance and part of a ground-floor apartment inhabited by two elderly women, one of whom has mobility challenges. The women were left without independent access to their home and now require coordination through the settler-controlled section to enter or receive visitors.

Since the beginning of 2026, 24 Palestinian households comprising 93 people, including 30 children, have been forcibly evicted from their homes following Israeli court decisions, most of them in Silwan. Approximately 200 Palestinian households of about 900 people across East Jerusalem remain at risk of forced displacement due to ongoing eviction cases before Israeli courts, the majority initiated by Israeli settler organizations.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and July 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank July 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 10-23 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical as military activities continued to result in civilian casualties, displacement, and damage to civilian and humanitarian infrastructure. Recent incidents affecting humanitarian facilities and warehouses have disrupted humanitarian operations and damaged critical infrastructure and supplies, while aid organizations continue to face severe access and security constraints.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 47 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 176 people were injured between 12 and 26 August. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,303 fatalities and 4,336 injuries, according to MoH. Children continue to bear a disproportionate impact of the violence, with at least four children reportedly killed and several others sustaining life-changing injuries across the Strip over the past five days, underscoring the continuing risks faced by civilians despite the ceasefire framework.

On 23 August, three UN warehouses in Deir al Balah were damaged following an airstrike on an adjacent location. One warehouse sustained significant structural damage, while the other two were affected to a lesser extent. No major loss of stored supplies was reported. On 24 August, warehouses operated by Ard El Insan Palestinian Charitable Association (AEI), also in Deir al Balah, sustained extensive damage following a strike on an adjacent residential building. According to AEI's initial assessment, virtually all stored nutrition supplies – including supplements and specialized products for children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers – were rendered unusable due to debris, dust, and blast damage. Not far from there, the windows of a guesthouse used by a humanitarian partner were shattered. Overall, at least four airstrikes hit near humanitarian facilities on 24 August – in Ash Shati’ Camp, Al Bureij, and two locations in Deir al Balah.

Meanwhile, on 24 August, severe damage to a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility in Deir Al Balah has disrupted access to safe drinking water for more than 4,000 people, including around 2,000 children. Emergency water trucking is ongoing. These but the incidents further undermine access to essential nutrition and safe water services for affected families.

Critical shortages of medicines, medical supplies and laboratory reagents continued to severely strain Gaza’s health system, threatening the continuity of lifesaving services. The Ministry of Health reported that central stocks of IV solutions had been depleted. While diagnostic cardiac catheterisation services have resumed, shortages of essential consumables continue to limit access to therapeutic procedures. More broadly, persistent shortages of medicines, dialysis supplies, laboratory reagents, oxygen equipment and other critical items, combined with restrictions and delays affecting the entry of health commodities, continue to undermine health care.

According to the latest classification by the Shelter Cluster, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people (94 per cent of Gaza's population) require shelter assistance and non-food items (NFIs). More than half of the population (58%) faces critical or catastrophic shelter needs, which means that they face severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or access to essential services and NFIs, exposing them to serious health, safety and dignity risks. Some 84 per cent of households experience severe living condition constraints, including inadequate protection from weather conditions. The findings highlight exposure to environmental hazards, deteriorating temporary shelters, and limited access to essential services and housing repairs.

While these findings stress the need for timely support in preparing for the rainy season, such efforts are held back because stocks of shelter materials and NFIs are largely depleted, due to Israeli access restrictions and funding shortfalls. Shelter response is also limited because much of the land suitable for the establishment of safer displacement sites is off limits for most Palestinians, as Israeli authorities continue imposing access restrictions on most of the Gaza Strip’s area (south, east and north of the “Yellow Line” and beyond). Without adequate support, hundreds of thousands of people, including those living in damaged homes, makeshift shelters and overcrowded displacement sites, will face heightened risks of flooding, illness, malnutrition and cold-related health complications, particularly among children, elderly people and other vulnerable groups.

Meanwhile, attempts by the de facto authorities to inspect humanitarian warehouses for alleged contraband continue. Between 27 July and 24 August, UN recorded at least four requests from the de facto authorities to search humanitarian warehouses, causing disruptions to humanitarian operations and breaching the inviolability of United Nations premises. No contraband was found.

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of truckloads successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, stood at 86 per cent, consistent with the previous reporting period. The Egyptian corridor continued to face the highest levels of truck returns and rejections, with an offloading rate of 76 per cent, consistent with the previous reporting period. The Ashdod route was the most utilized entry route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo during the reporting period, accounting for 45 per cent of all truckloads entering Gaza. By contrast, the use of the Jordan corridor declined compared with the previous reporting period. Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing point for cargo.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.
