title: Lebanon Situation Report - Update #16 (13 to 27 August 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

The humanitarian situation in Lebanon continues to be shaped by ongoing displacement, population movements and persistent insecurity in conflict-affected areas. As of 26 August, IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) identified 334,353 internally displaced persons (IDPs), including 19,543 individuals residing in 196 collective sites. A further 823,337 individuals were reported as residing in their areas of origin or habitual residence after previous displacement. During the reporting period, renewed hostilities highlighted the fragility of the security environment despite the ceasefire announced on 19 June. On 15 August, intensified airstrikes in Nabatieh Governorate reportedly prompted significant temporary population movements, with available reporting indicating that many of those who moved returned within a short period. Further strikes were reported on 26 and 27 August, underscoring the continued volatility of the security environment, although their implications for population movements were not yet fully reflected in the latest available displacement figures. Attacks affecting healthcare personnel and civilian infrastructure were also reported, further disrupting access to essential services and increasing protection concerns in conflict-affected areas. While large-scale displacement has continued to decline, many conflict-affected households continue to face significant challenges in rebuilding their lives and accessing essential services. Extensive damage to housing, water systems, electricity networks, health facilities, schools and agricultural land continues to constrain recovery efforts, particularly in South Lebanon. Many families remain unable to return to their homes and continue to rely on temporary accommodation arrangements while awaiting rehabilitation works and the restoration of basic infrastructure and services. Against this backdrop, humanitarian and recovery needs remain closely intertwined. Continued humanitarian assistance, alongside investments in shelter rehabilitation, restoration of basic services, livelihoods recovery, protection, and mental health and psychosocial support, will be critical to support safe, voluntary and sustainable solutions for displacement-affected populations and help conflictaffected communities recover from the impacts of continued hostilities.

title: UNHCR Ecuador: Operational Update No. 7 | July 2026
content:
Operational Update

Ecuador continued to operate in a complex protection environment marked by persistent insecurity, economic uncertainty and emerging climate-related risks. Despite the continuation of nationwide security measures and intensified law enforcement operations against organized crime, violence remained a significant concern in several parts of the country particularly in border areas and coastal regions. These conditions continue to affect forcibly displaced populations, who are often concentrated in urban and peri-urban areas where insecurity, limited livelihood opportunities and restricted access to services increase protection risks. Ongoing insecurity also constrained humanitarian access in some locations and increased operational challenges for humanitarian actors. Ecuador reopened the Macará-La Tina border crossing with Peru in Loja after a six-month closure implemented as part of efforts to combat organized crime and arms trafficking. The reopening restored an important route for cross-border mobility, family reunification and access to services for border communities while maintaining strengthened security controls. 2 At the same time, concerns grew over the country's energy outlook ahead of the dry season. Electricity demand reached historic levels, while authorities advanced contingency measures in response to forecasts indicating a potential moderate-to-strong El Niño event. The combination of possible energy shortages and climate-related impacts, including risks to agricultural production and livelihoods, could further affect vulnerable populations already facing displacement or protection risks. UNHCR continued working alongside the Government of Ecuador and local partners to support refugees, asylum-seekers and vulnerable host communities affected by violence and displacement. Through protection monitoring, legal assistance, case management, community-based protection activities and targeted humanitarian support, UNHCR helped people access safety, services and their rights, while strengthening the capacity of local authorities and communities to respond to growing protection needs and helping affected families rebuild their lives with dignity, stability and renewed opportunities for the future.

title: UNICEF Venezuela Situation Report No. 1 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Venezuela continues to face a complex humanitarian situation marked by socioeconomic vulnerabilities, pressure on essential services, and the impact of a water emergency in Sucre state and two severe earthquakes on 24 June.
  • By 30 June, UNICEF and partners had reached over 244,000 children under five with primary healthcare services and screened 146,534 children aged 6–59 months for wasting. WASH interventions expanded access to safe water for drinking and domestic use to 134,961 people.
  • More than 72,000 children, adolescents and caregivers received community-based mental health and psychosocial support, while 6,580 children accessed formal and non-formal education opportunities.
  • This Situation Report covers results under the original 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal up to 30 June 2026, prior to the HAC revision following the earthquakes, which increased the funding requirement from US$137.6 million to US$203.3 million.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 309: Week 4 - August 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained broadly stable during the fourth week of August, although price movements varied across food commodities, vegetables, fuel, and agricultural inputs. Most staple food prices changed only marginally, while vegetable prices declined. At the same time, diesel and fertilizer prices remained elevated, sustaining pressure on transportation and agricultural production costs. Overall commodity availability remained adequate, although regional trade conditions and higher fuel and input costs continued to weigh on market stability.

Food Items:

• National food prices remained relatively stable during the fourth week of August, with most staple commodities recording only modest weekly changes. However, several food items continued to trade above last year's levels, particularly rice, wheat, cooking oil, and potato.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and flour prices experienced negligible changes during the week. Compared with last year, wheat grain and low-price wheat flour remained 14% and 12% higher, respectively.

• Rice: The prices of rice categories showed mixed movements, with high-price Palawi rice declining slightly by 0.3%, while low-price Sholae rice increased by 1.2%. However, both varieties remained substantially above last year's levels, at 25% and 36% higher, respectively, and well above their three-year averages.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil and sugar prices increased by 0.6% and 0.8%, respectively, while pulses and salt declined slightly and bread prices remained unchanged. Year-on-year trends remained mixed, with cooking oil and sugar prices 11% and 8% higher, respectively, while pulses and bread were 14% and 3% lower than last year.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices continued to show divergent trends. Tomato, onion and potato prices fell by 4.6%, 2.2% and 0.7%, respectively. Despite the weekly declines, potato prices remained 50% higher than last year, while tomato and onion prices remain near to last year’s levels.

Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani strengthened slightly to AFN 64.8/USD, appreciating by 0.6% week-on-week. It remained 5% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, continuing to provide some support in containing imported commodity costs.

• Fuel: Diesel prices continued its upward trend and increased by 1.2% during the week to AFN 78.0 per litre. Prices are 17% higher than the same time last year and 20% above the three-year average, maintaining upward pressure on transportation and supply-chain costs.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices showed mix movements during the week, with DAP increasing by 0.4% while urea declined by 1.2%. However, fertilizer prices stand considerably above last year's levels, with DAP and urea prices 15% and 30% higher, respectively, continuing to raise production costs for farmers.

• Terms of Trade (ToT): The ToT, which reflects the purchasing power, remained under pressure for both labourdependent households and pastoralists during the fourth week of August. Nominal casual labour ToT declined by 0.8% week-on-week to 10.4 kg of wheat flour and remained 14% below last year, while unskilled labour availability fell by 2.8% to 2.0 days per week, remaining 16% below both last year and the three-year average. Similarly, pastoralist ToT declined by 0.7% week-on-week and 16% year-on-year, reflecting continued weakness in the purchasing power of livestock keepers.

title: Myanmar monthly food price report – July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Rice prices increased moderately in July 2026, with the national average rising by 3.6 percent month-on-month and 10.1 percent year-on-year. Regional price disparities persisted, reflecting differences in production conditions, market access, and transport costs.
  • Most export crop prices showed mixed movements. Maize prices declined following strong export activity earlier in the year, although prices remained well above year-earlier levels. Black gram and pigeon pea prices increased on expectations of stronger import demand from India, while green gram prices showed limited movements amid increasing quality requirements across export markets.
  • Most animal-sourced food prices remained substantially above year-earlier levels, while month-on-month movements were mixed. Chicken and egg prices increased notably amid higher feed costs, limited supplies of large-sized chickens, and reduced egg production associated with higher input costs and disease outbreaks. Mutton prices remained at record highs. Fish prices also remained above previous year, although increased catches following the resumption of fishing activities contributed to lower prices for some fish products.
  • The conflict in Iran and the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major transit route for global oil and fertilizer trade, are raising concerns for Myanmar’s agrifood system, which depends heavily on fuel for transportation, irrigation, mechanization, and processing. During the 2026 monsoon, some farmers reported cultivating smaller areas or reducing plowings because of higher fuel costs. Fertilizer prices also remain substantially above last year’s levels, while crop output prices have changed relatively little, reducing the profitability of fertilizer use and potentially leading to lower application rates and agricultural production.
  • Flooding has affected monsoon rice cultivation in some areas, while flood warnings have been issued for other parts of the country, including areas along the Bago and Sittaung rivers. While the reported impacts on rice cultivation remain geographically limited, continued monitoring of flood conditions will be important given potential implications for crop production, transportation, and food supply chains.

title: Vanuatu Pertussis Outbreak in Penama Province, Vanuatu: Situation Report 1 - 24-Aug-26
content:
Suspected case definition: A suspected case is any person with cough illness lasting >2 weeks, with at least one of the following symptoms; fits for coughing, OR; ‘whoop’ when breathing in, OR; vomiting after coughing fits.

Confirmed case definition: A confirmed cases is a person who meets at least of the following criteria: Isolatin of Bordetella pertussis bacteria from a clinical specimen; OR a positive PCR test for pertussis; OR a coughing illness in person epidemiologically link by time, person, place to a laboratory-confirmed case.

Mode of transmission: Spread from person to person through respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

Outbreak Threshold: Two epidemilogically linked cases occuring within one week.

title: Nepal Flash Floods: Rapid Situation Overview (27 August 2026)
content:
A series of flash floods struck the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa district, northern Nepal, on the morning of 26 August 2026, entering from the Tibet Autonomous Region of China at around 09:00 Nepal Standard Time (NPT) and surging downstream through the Trishuli River system into Nuwakot, Dhading and beyond. The border settlements of Timure and Syabrubesi, the Rasuwagadhi customs and border crossing, and roughly a dozen riverside settlements in northern Rasuwa took the earliest and heaviest impact, before the surge moved through Betrawati and Trishuli Bazar in Nuwakot, Galchhi and Dhunge Bazaar in Dhading, and onward past Muglin into the Narayani river system, where deaths were subsequently recorded as far away as Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahu and Nawalparasi East.

Casualty figures rose sharply and repeatedly through the day as search teams reached previously cut-off areas, and this report treats every figure below as provisional. By the morning of Thursday 27 August, the NDRRMA and Nepal Police put the confirmed death toll at 165, with 73 people injured, up from the roughly 160 (157 bodies recovered) reported late on Wednesday, and superseding Wednesday-evening figures of 95 from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) and 72 from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). Hundreds of people remain unaccounted for. As of a Nepal Police bulletin issued around 08:15 on Thursday 27 August, 826 people were listed as missing in Nepal alone: 579 travellers (466 foreign nationals and 113 Nepalis), 85 security personnel (44 Nepali Army, 28 Nepal Police and 13 Armed Police Force), 161 residents of Rasuwa and one of Nuwakot. Most of the missing foreign travellers were moving toward the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route through Tibet, and included at least 133 Indian pilgrims alongside citizens of Malaysia (55), the United States (47), Australia (34), the United Kingdom (33), Canada (24) and other countries. A further 85 security personnel (Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force), 60 hydropower-project workers, 26 bank employees and 15 customs officers were separately reported missing or out of contact A further 60 hydropower-project workers, 26 bank employees and 15 customs officers were separately reported out of contact. On the Chinese side of the border, state media (CCTV) reported 3 confirmed deaths and 558 people missing, 260 of them foreign nationals, around the Gyirong Port trade hub in Xizang (Tibet), bringing the combined Nepal-and-Tibet missing total to more than 1,300, though the two countries’ counts of foreign nationals may overlap.

The flood caused severe damage to infrastructure across a roughly 60-kilometer valley corridor. The Department of Roads confirmed that the entire 42-kilometer road linking Betrawati (Nuwakot) to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing had been destroyed at multiple points, including several concrete bridges, cutting Nepal’s principal overland trade and pilgrimage route to Tibet; a further 16-kilometer stretch toward the border, recently upgraded with Chinese government financing, was also swept away. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) reported damage to 14 hydropower projects with a combined capacity of approximately 748 MW (9 operational plants (354 MW) and 5 under construction (394 MW)) including the Rasuwagadhi, Chilime, Sanjen Khola, Upper Trishuli-1, Trishuli and Devighat plants and a 220 kV substation; the Ministry of Energy’s earlier same-day estimate had put the loss at 431 MW, illustrating how fast the damage assessment was still moving. Nine commercial bank branches were swept away, with 26 staff unaccounted for, and the Rasuwa customs office in Timure lost contact with 15 employees.

The trigger has not been officially confirmed. Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology and independent glaciologists advanced a preliminary hypothesis, based on satellite imagery shared by Chinese counterparts through the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), that an ice-and-rock avalanche blocked the Lhende Khola, a Bhote Koshi tributary on the Nepal-China border, roughly 20 km upstream of the Miteri Bridge, forming a temporary debris-dammed lake that subsequently burst The US Geological Survey initially logged a magnitude-4.4 earthquake at 08:37 local time shortly before the flood, but has since revised its analysis, concluding that the seismic signal was in fact a magnitude-5.2 glacial collapse, not a tectonic earthquake, based on nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves and satellite imagery. Meteorologists ruled out heavy local rainfall as the cause in Rasuwa itself, while noting that satellite data showed rainfall on the Tibetan side of the border. A broadly similar flood on the same river in July 2025 was ultimately attributed to the drainage of a supraglacial lake; ICIMOD scientists say such cascading glacial hazards are increasing at an “unprecedented” pace across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

The Government of Nepal has mobilized the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police, supported by military and private helicopters, for search, rescue and relief operations, and the Cabinet has ordered free medical treatment for the injured, financial assistance to bereaved families, and the reopening of roads, restoration of power and telecommunications, and provision of food and shelter for those displaced. Nepal has asked China and India for assistance; China has pledged relief funding, and India is sending humanitarian supplies, while Indian authorities in neighboring Bihar state have opened the Valmikinagar Barrage on the Gandak River as a precaution and prepared to evacuate up to 10,000–12,000 people downstream. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has released emergency funding to the Nepal Red Cross Society, which has begun distributing water, tarpaulins, blankets and first-aid supplies, though many of the worst-affected communities in Rasuwa remain difficult to reach because roads and bridges are destroyed. As of the data cut-off, no government or humanitarian body had published a consolidated total for people displaced, sheltering or in need, and this report treats that figure as a priority information gap for the days ahead.

title: WFP Nepal External Situation Report, 27 August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Northern Nepal was struck by a suspected Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) on the morning of 26 August after a sudden surge of water entered the Bhotekoshi River from the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, causing extensive damage across Rasuwa District and downstream areas of Nuwakot District. Preliminary assessments suggest a possible ice avalanche and damming of the Lhende River upstream.

• According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), 10,000 households require immediate relief. At least 157 deaths have been confirmed and nearly 245 people remain missing, including security personnel, customs officials, foreign tourists and residents, while search and rescue operations continue (RisingNepal).

• A significant number of tourists and trekkers are also unaccounted for in the affected area, both foreign nationals and Nepali citizens, many of whom may be in locations without communications as phone towers are impacted.

title: Regional External Update #39 West and Central Africa Region - Eastern DRC Situation - July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Persistent conflict and insecurity continued to drive a deepening displacement crisis in eastern DRC, with new internal displacement still outpacing returns in several affected areas. Smaller but steady cross-border movements into neighbouring countries also accumulated to more than 16,400 new Congolese arrivals since January 2026, adding pressure on host communities and overstretched services.

• The Ebola outbreak further exposed the deadly overlap between insecurity, displacement and weak basic services in the DRC, with more than 5,600 confirmed cases and over 2,700 deaths1 , over three months after the outbreak was declared a public health emergency of international concern. Uganda however declared itself Ebola-free on 28 July, but cross-border preparedness remained critical. UNHCR continued contributing to the Government-led response in displacement settings despite significant funding challenges.

• Despite the volatile context, voluntary returns maintained momentum, supported by health screening, water, sanitation and hygiene measures and cross-border coordination. By 31 July, around 51,000 Congolese refugees had self-organized their return from Burundi and 14,200 Government-UNHCR facilitated returns to the DRC had been recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: Syrian Arab Republic: Humanitarian Update No. 6 | May - June 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Flooding along the Euphrates River affected an estimated 13,000 families and displaced more than 1,700 households in north-east Syria, disrupting water infrastructure, damaging agricultural land and prompting a large-scale humanitarian response.
  • Returns continue to outpace recovery in Dar’a Governorate, where more than 32,000 returnees have been recorded in western Dar’a since December 2024, placing increasing pressure on health, water and education services.
  • Explosive ordnance contamination remains a major obstacle to recovery, with 104 incidents recorded during May and June, resulting in 40 deaths and 96 injuries.
  • Humanitarian partners reached an average of 2.4 million people per month during the first half of 2026, delivering assistance through 299 organizations in 4,377 communities across Syria.
  • OCHA facilitated and participated in more than fifteen field missions, assessments and monitoring visits across 11 governorates helping inform humanitarian planning, recovery efforts and support for return-affected communities.
  • Through Syria Humanitarian Fund (SHF) support, protection and psychosocial services are helping children and adolescents affected by conflict and displacement rebuild confidence, resilience and a sense of safety.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #51 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 24 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • World Humanitarian Day was marked by the Humanitarian Coordinator visiting Tebnine (18 August) and a Town Hall with humanitarian partners (19 August). Discussions highlighted the continued challenges facing frontline responders and essential service providers operating in conflict-affected areas.
  • Continued military activity across southern Lebanon is undermining civilian safety and return prospects. Airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions, and land-clearing operations continued across South and Nabatieh governorates. Military activity also damaged civilian infrastructure, including a public water reservoir in Mansouri (Tyre District), while a suspected explosive remnant of war in Mayfadoun (Nabatieh District) reportedly killed three people and injured another.
  • Humanitarian partners reported increasing access constraints affecting assessments, monitoring activities, service restoration efforts, and referral pathways in hard-to-reach areas, limiting the delivery of assistance and support to conflict-affected populations.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains volatile, with continued military activity, prolonged displacement, and challenging return conditions sustaining significant humanitarian and protection needs. Israeli military activity continued across South and Nabatieh governorates during the reporting period, including airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions, and land-clearing operations affecting communities in Nabatieh, Marjaayoun, Bint Jbeil, Jezzine and Tyre districts. The most intense incidents were reported around the Ali al-Taher heights (Nabatieh District, Nabatieh Governorate), where strikes and shelling persisted throughout the reporting period. Additional demolitions were reported in Aita al-Shaab (Bint Jbeil District), Houla and Khiam (Marjaayoun District), and Majdal Zoun (Tyre District), while artillery fire also affected the outskirts of Houla (Marjaayoun District) and Rashaya al-Fakhar (Hasbaya District). Continued insecurity, destruction of civilian infrastructure, and movement restrictions continue to expose civilians to protection risks, hinder humanitarian access, and constrain safe and sustainable returns.

Military activity continues to affect civilian infrastructure and access to essential services. In Mansouri (Tyre District, South Governorate), land-clearing operations and shelling reportedly damaged or destroyed a public water reservoir serving the community, raising concerns over access to water. In Ain Arab (Nabatieh Governorate), Israeli forces reportedly installed an iron gate restricting access to part of the village, further limiting access and return prospects. Extensive damage to housing, roads, water networks, electricity systems, and other public infrastructure continues to be reported across conflict-affected areas of southern Lebanon.

The security situation remains particularly volatile in Nabatieh Governorate despite continued return movements. The escalation around the Ali al-Taher heights that began in mid-August continued throughout the reporting period, with additional strikes reported around Nabatieh, Kfar Rumman and Nabatieh al-Fawqa (Nabatieh District), where houses were reportedly destroyed. While no new displacement orders were reported, ongoing insecurity continues to impede returns and contribute to concerns over renewed displacement among returning families.

Explosive ordnance contamination remains a significant protection concern. On 19 August, an explosion involving a suspected explosive remnant of war in Mayfadoun (Nabatieh District) reportedly killed three people and injured another. The incident underscores the continuing threat posed by unexploded ordnance (UXO) and explosive remnants of war (ERW) to civilians living in or returning to conflict-affected communities. Contamination continues to affect residential areas, agricultural land, access routes, and public infrastructure, restricting movement and delaying recovery efforts.

Population movements continue, though displacement and return trends are showing signs of stabilization. According to the latest Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), 348,898 people remained displaced across Lebanon as of 19 August, a decrease of less than one per cent compared with the previous reporting period. At the same time, 817,458 people had returned to their communities, although the pace of returns continues to slow. The majority of displaced people originate from conflict-affected districts in South and Nabatieh governorates, particularly Bent Jbeil, El Nabatieh, Sour, and Marjaayoun.

Collective shelter populations continue to decline. As of 24 August, 21,000 people remained accommodated in 209 collective shelters, a decrease of three per cent compared with the previous reporting period. However, most displaced people continue to reside outside collective shelters, with 72 per cent living in rented accommodation and 12 per cent in host community arrangements. Protracted displacement, rising living costs, and declining economic opportunities continue to place significant strain on affected households and host communities.

Return movements remain concentrated in southern Lebanon but continue to face significant challenges. Sour and El Nabatieh districts account for the largest numbers of returnees, while returns remain constrained by insecurity, damage to housing and infrastructure, limited access to essential services, and UXO contamination. Humanitarian actors continue to emphasize that returns should not be equated with a reduction in humanitarian needs.

Humanitarian and protection needs remain acute among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities. Key concerns include explosive ordnance contamination, barriers to accessing services, economic hardship, housing insecurity, documentation challenges, psychosocial distress, and heightened protection risks. Women, girls, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities remain particularly vulnerable. Declining household resources, rising living costs, and limited livelihood opportunities continue to erode coping capacities and deepen humanitarian needs.

Recent consultations with local authorities and communities in conflict-affected areas highlighted that restoring basic services remains a key prerequisite for sustainable return. Priority needs identified include reliable water and electricity supply, rehabilitation of schools ahead of the academic year, livelihood support, agricultural recovery assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and strengthened municipal capacity to restore local services. Communities also emphasized the need for longer-term recovery investments, including support to small businesses, agriculture, solar energy systems, water infrastructure, and employment opportunities.

Humanitarian access remains complex and unpredictable, particularly in areas of South and Nabatieh governorates affected by ongoing military activity. Insecurity, access restrictions, damaged roads, telecommunications disruptions, UXO contamination, and evolving security conditions continue to affect humanitarian operations, monitoring activities, and service delivery.

Access to essential services remains under pressure. In addition to conflict-related damage, humanitarian partners have raised concerns regarding potential disruptions to water and wastewater services following electricity supply cuts by Électricité du Liban (EDL) affecting entities with unpaid bills. The South Lebanon Water Establishment remains particularly vulnerable due to reduced operational capacity and financial constraints. Any interruption in electricity supply could affect water pumping, treatment, and wastewater facilities in South and Nabatieh governorates, with implications for public health and continuity of water and sanitation services.

Funding constraints continue to hamper the response at a critical stage. According to Financial Tracking Service, as of 24 August, the 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal requiring US$639.9 million have only received US$332.4 million (52 per cent) one week before the end of its six-month timeline. Humanitarian actors warn that declining resources may place essential activities, including food assistance, cash-for-rent support, protection services, operational coordination, and nutrition interventions, at risk in the coming months. Humanitarian partners continue to emphasize the importance of sustained de-escalation and cessation of hostilities, respect for international humanitarian law, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, support for safe, voluntary and dignified returns, UXO clearance, restoration of essential services, and predictable funding to sustain humanitarian and early recovery efforts.

title: Qatar Charity – Emergency Response Plan (ERP) - Nepal Flash Flood Response 2026
content:
August–November 2026 | Total Planned Response: USD 1,069,000

1. Executive Summary

On 26 August 2026, an ice-and-rock landslide in the upper transboundary watershed near the Nepal–China border triggered a major debris-laden flash flood through the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. As of 27 August, at 09:00 Nepal time, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), provisional figures report 10,000 households require immediate relief, 165 bodies recovered, 247 people out of contact, 73 injured, and extensive infrastructure damage, including 35 motorable bridges and 45 suspension bridges swept away and approximately 40 km of paved road damaged. Evacuation orders and downstream alerts remain active because the upstream blockage lake may not have fully drained. QC has approved a USD 69,000 quick life-saving intervention for immediate food and emergency shelter assistance. An additional USD 1,000,000 is urgently needed to expand the relief response and support priority early recovery interventions, bringing the total planned intervention to USD 1,069,000.

2. Funding and Budget Overview (USD 1,069,000)

Funding Window

Allocation (USD)

Purpose

QC Quick Life-Saving Intervention

69,000

Immediate food and emergency shelter assistance

Expanded Relief and Early Recovery

1,000,000

Scale-up of multi-sector relief and priority early recovery interventions

Total Planned Allocation

1,069,000

Immediate response, expanded relief, and early recovery

3. Qatar Charity Response

A) Quick Life-Saving Food Assistance – Part of the USD 69,000 Immediate Allocation

QC will provide rapid food assistance to evacuated, displaced, stranded, and highly vulnerable households in affected districts, selecting modalities according to access, market functionality, cooking capacity, and coordination findings:

  • Ready-to-eat meals and food for people in evacuation sites, temporary shelters, transit locations, and rescue staging areas.
  • Household food parcels where families retain safe cooking capacity and access to fuel.

B) Quick Life-Saving Emergency Shelter Assistance – Part of the USD 69,000 Immediate Allocation

QC will distribute context-appropriate emergency shelter and household items to evacuated and displaced families in safe temporary sites, host arrangements, and accessible affected communities, including:

  • Blankets, sleeping mats, and family household items
  • Hygiene kits

C) Expanded Relief and Early Recovery Package (USD 1,000,000)

Additional funding is required to expand the response across priority sectors according to verified needs, coordination findings, operational feasibility, Interventions may include:

  • Scale-up of food assistance, emergency shelter, core relief items, WASH, health, and essential service continuity.
  • Improvement of safe temporary accommodation and evacuation sites, including lighting, privacy, accessibility, and drainage.
  • Early recovery support, including shelter repair, drinking-water system restoration, community infrastructure rehabilitation, livelihoods recovery, and targeted cash or voucher assistance where appropriate.

Detailed sector allocations, outputs, and beneficiary targets under the USD 1,000,000 expansion will be finalized following rapid multi-sectoral assessments, government and cluster coordination, partner capacity review and market analysis.

4. Geographic Prioritization

QC will prioritize the most severely affected and operationally accessible areas along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani corridor, subject to government guidance, verified needs, safety, and partner presence:

  • Rasuwa: Rasuwagadhi, Timure, Syaphrubesi, and other affected or isolated communities
  • Nuwakot and Dhading: riverbank settlements, evacuation sites, and access corridors
  • Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun, Nawalparasi East, and Nawalparasi West: downstream affected locations based on verified impact and unmet needs

5. Response Coordination:

QC will coordinate its response efforts closely with the relevant Government of Nepal counterparts, including national and district authorities, as well as UN agencies, international NGOs, local organizations, and other humanitarian partners operating on the ground. This coordination will help align interventions with national priorities and sector mechanisms, avoid duplication, address identified gaps, facilitate information sharing and referrals, and promote a coherent, complementary, and accountable response.

Implementation Timeline (90 Days)

Hours 0–72 / Week 1: Coordination with national and district authorities; rapid assessment; partner mapping; immediate procurement and distribution of food and shelter support to accessible sites.

Weeks 2–8: Expanded multi-sector implementation; temporary shelter; post-distribution monitoring; adaptive targeting as access and official figures evolve.

Weeks 9–12: Early recovery priorities, service restoration support, transition or handover, final monitoring, reporting, and lessons learned.

Annex: Key References and Planning Assumptions

  • Nepal Flash Floods Situation Report No. 01, 27 August 2026, 11:00 hrs Nepal time.
  • Government of Nepal, NDRRMA Bhote Koshi Flood Emergency Status Report #05, 27 August 2026, 09:00 hrs.
  • Department of Hydrology and Meteorology technical report on the 2083 Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani Flood.
  • All figures, geographic priorities, targets, modalities, and budgets remain provisional and require validation through government coordination, field assessment, partner due diligence, market analysis, and internal approval.

title: Nepal: Deadly Flash Floods - August 26, 2026, No. 1
content:
Key figures

• 157+ deaths1
• 400+ missing
• 10,000 households in need

Highlights

• 26 August 2026: A glacial lake outburst flood on the Bhote Koshi River struck around 09:00am local time, sending a wall of water through communities without warning
• The government has declared Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading disaster crisis zones following extreme flooding in the three districts
• Buildings, roads, homes, and bridges have been swept through and destroyed
• 12 power plants damaged causing significant disruption to electricity supply
• Search operations are under way on both sides of the border
• The death toll is expected to rise significantly in the coming days
• Current affected areas include Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan

Situation Overview

On 26 August 2026, a massive flash flood surged down the Bhote Koshi River from the Tibet Autonomous Region in China into Nepal's Rasuwa district before cascading downstream through Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan. Assessments are still going on to determine the cause of the flooding. Initial assessments point to a glacial lake outburst flood, potentially triggered by an earthquake recorded that morning ~100 km north-northwest of Kathmandu. Entire settlements, including Timure, Syaphrubesi, Hakubesi, Mailung, and Shantibazar in Rasuwa, and Betrawati and Trishuli Bazaar in Nuwakot, have been inundated or sustained significant damage. The flooding also damaged the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border, causing casualties and missing persons on both sides of the border. Evacuation orders are in place along the Trishuli River corridor covering parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan. The Nepal Army and other security forces are conducting emergency search, rescue, evacuation, and relief operations, including helicopter airlifts of survivors and deployment of medical teams. Access to several affected areas remains constrained by damaged roads and high water levels.

title: Syrian Arab Republic - Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update - Round 20 (24 August 2026)
content:
Following the ceasefire in Lebanon announced on 17 April 2026, cross-border movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) have continually declined. Observed cross-border mobility is increasingly characterised by more gradual and stabilised patterns. After reaching a peak of 153,087 arrivals on 27 April, DTM estimates that around 27,712 Syrian and Lebanese nationals have since returned to Lebanon.

From 2 March to 24 August, DTM identified 125,375 arrivals across 1,172 locations in all 14 governorates in Syria. Syrian nationals accounted for the overwhelming majority of arrivals, with Lebanese nationals representing less than 1 per cent. Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded 707,425 movements into Syria over the same period, of which approximately 98 per cent were Syrian nationals and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. In addition, 3,470 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, highlighting the continued use of Syria as a route for onward regional movement.

The Arida border crossing remains closed following the temporary closure from 6 August due to technical works on the Lebanese side. Consequently, Arida movement figures are available only up to 5 August. Key informants (KIs) cited persistent access constraints for travellers, with those previously using Arida having to rely on alternative crossings located further from Tartous Governorate, increasing travel times and associated costs.

The situation remains fluid, and DTM continues to monitor developments.

title: Doo Tha Htoo District Short Update: Experiences and testimonies of two civilians who were forcibly recruited by the Burma Army (June 2026)
content:
This Short Update describes events that occurred in Hpa-an Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, in 2026. In 2024 and 2025, the Burma Army arbitrarily arrested and recruited two young men from Yangon and Tanintharyi divisions as soldiers. These two young men shared what they experienced and the human rights abuses that they had seen when they were forcibly recruited, as well as how they escaped from the Burma Army. Since the 2021 coup, the Burma Army has arbitrarily arrested and forcibly recruited many villagers in Karen State.[1]

“They [the Burma Army] try to spread propaganda. Every day, they say good things about themselves to make us believe them. It is like brainwashing. They try to put false information into our brains. They use all kinds of methods to [make people] obey their orders. They threaten us that they will shoot us dead if anyone runs away. When I was attending military training, someone tried to run away. Finally, they were able to arrest him. Then, they asked all trainees to beat him. 200 trainees beat him up. After that, they detained him. It was very bad. We could not even recognize his face [as a result of the beating]. They made him an example so that other trainees would not dare to run away.”

- Maung[2] Q---, a former Tatmadaw[3] soldier who escaped after being forcibly recruited

On 1 February 2021, the Burma Army forcibly seized national power [in a military coup] after accusing the National League for Democracy (NLD),[4] which had won a landslide victory in the 2020 general election, of voting fraud. The people did not accept this action. As a result, widespread protests occurred across the country.[5] In response, the Burma Army tried to crack down on protestors by using police force, but the protests continued. Finally, they used violence and lethal weapons to suppress and crack down on the protestors, which resulted in deaths and injuries. Therefore, young people and politicians bear no more patience with the actions of the Burma Army.

To continue to resist against this injustice, educated young people and politicians have sought refuge in areas, controlled by ethnic armed organizations (EAOs), which have been fighting against the dictatorship for many years. As the Burma Army continued to oppress, arrest, and imprison protesters, youths and politicians who sought refuge in ethnic areas gathered to take up arms to fight back the Burma Army. As a result, weekly military training courses were provided to youths and politicians in many places in ethnic areas. Then, the People’s Défense Force (PDF)[6] was established. The number of PDF troops increased year by year, and they joined the EAOs in various regions as they fought back against the Burma Army. The combined forces of the PDF and EAOs fought the Burma Army with a strong desire to win. As a result, the Burma Army lost many of their army camps in different areas.

This became a threat to leaders of the Burma Army. The army became increasingly demoralized and its strength declined. To address this situation, the Burma Army’s leaders issued a conscription law [in 2024] as an emergency [measure]. On the other hand, the number of young people who joined the Burma Army after the 2021 coup decreased significantly because the Burma Army has been unjustly arresting and imprisoning protesters; therefore, the people do not support them. After the Burma Army issued the conscription law, many young people sought ways to escape military service by going abroad or fleeing to the EAOs in ethnic areas.

When they Burma Army implemented this law, they extorted, threatened, and imprisoned people whether or not they were on the conscription list for military service. In addition to these unjust actions, many soldiers from the Burma Army were killed in battles. It does not matter how quickly they were replaced; they have not been replaced [quickly] enough. Therefore, the Burma Army has been using force and violence against the will of the people, such as arresting passengers and travellers, and even entering civilians’ homes to arrest without warning or prior notice. Among them, Maung K--- and Maung Q--- were also forcibly recruited. In April 2026, these two men escaped to ethnic areas in Hpa-an Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, controlled by the Karen National Union (KNU).[7] They surrendered to Brigade (1) of the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA).[8]

First incident: Maung K--- (people’s militia); Military ID number: XXX [Censored for security purposes]

Maung K--- is a villager from Kk--- village, Kk--- village tract,[9] Longlon Township, Tanintharyi Division. One evening in September 2025, at 5 pm, he returned home from his work. When he was about to eat dinner, a car full of soldiers from Light Infantry Battalion (LIB)[10] #401 came to his house and they entered his house. Then, they arrested him. At the time he was arrested, it was a time when the Burma Army had begun to recruit new soldiers for the 17th batch of People’s Military Service Training. When soldiers from LIB #401 arrested Maung K---, they hit his face twice with the butt of MA-1 gun. Then, they took him to LIB #401 army camp in Dawei Town.

Maung K--- told KHRG about his experience when he was arrested, saying: “I went to work in the village. I came back home at around 5 pm. Then, they entered my house. They arrested me. […] I had not taken a shower yet. I was about to eat dinner. Then, they pointed their guns at me, and they arrested me. […] Then, they hit me twice with a gun. After that, they dragged me to their car. Then, they took me to LIB #401 army camp in Dawei Town. […] At first, I did not know why they arrested me. I also did not expect that they would arrest me. I was just busy with my work all day. So, I did not know why they arrested me.”

Maung K--- was detained at LIB #401 army camp in Dawei Town for four days. After that, he was sent to a recruitment centre in Myeik Town [Mergui-Tavoy District] by a military ship. He was held in the centre for over a week. Then, he was again transported to a higher military training school (#12) in Palaw Town [Mergui-Tavoy District] by a military ship. He had to attend a military training in the school for four months from September 2025 to January 2026. After he attended the military training for four months, he was asked to take a break for two weeks. After this, he was sent to Light Infantry Division (LID)[11] #44 army camp in Kyaikto Town, Mon State [in Doo Tha Htoo District], with a military ship. He had to attend a military refresher training in the LID #44 army camp for two weeks. Then, he was sent to the frontlines in the Kone Tai area in Kawkareik Township, Karen State [in Dooplaya District]. He was assigned to serve as a security guard at the frontlines.

He stayed at the frontlines in the Kone Tai area for two months. After that, he was sent to a checkpoint at the entrance of Hpa-an Town [Doo Tha Htoo District]. This checkpoint is controlled by combined forces of the Burma Army and Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA).[12] Then, he was again sent to Pein Net Taw army camp in Doo Tha Htoo District with a guide from the DKBA. Again, he was sent to Lay Kay army camp and Win Tar Pan army camp in Bilin Township, Doo Tha Htoo District, as [part of] reinforcements. When he was sent to those army camps with the Burma Army’s troops to help them as reinforcements, along the way, the KNLA attacked the Burma [Army] troops. As a result, almost everyone from the troops was killed or injured. Therefore, Maung K--- was afraid to continue the journey, and he decided to run away for the survival. Then, he surrendered to KNLA Battalion #1 on 20 April 2026. As he surrendered, the KNLA took care of him and kept him in a safe place. Maung K---‘s [Burma Army] military trainer was Major Min Maw Than.

Maung K--- and many other soldiers did not want to join the Burma Army. He told KHRG about his experience and perspectives. “Many people want to run away if they have a chance. […] We do not have fighting experience at the frontlines. When the fighting happened, I did not shoot a gun. I just lay down and stayed like that. Some people died of hunger at the frontlines. Some people died as they stepped on landmines. I have seen this situation. That is why I was afraid to continue our journey. Then, I decided to surrender.”

Maung K--- worked as a masonry worker to support his family. He is Bamar and Buddhist. He is 23 years old and he is married. His wife was also in the house when he was arrested. His wife’s name is Ma G---. According to Maung K---, Ma G--- did not even have a chance to talk to her husband when he was arrested and taken away. She felt really sad about what happened to her husband.

Second incident: Maung Q--- (Tatmadaw); Military ID number: XXX [Censored for security purposes]

Maung Q--- is from Thingangyun Township, Yangon Division. On one day in April 2024, he was sleeping on a street, as he was drunk. Two unknown people arrested him. These two people worked as recruiters for the Burma Army. Then, they put him on a bus and drove him to a military training school in Toungoo Town, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District. When he arrived there, it was a time when the Burma Army had begun to conduct the 3rd batch of People’s Military Service Training.

According to Maung Q---, all kinds of people from different areas and backgrounds, including criminals, were arrested, and they were sent to recruitment centre #4 in Toungoo Town. The Burma Army forcibly recruited them and often tortured them. Maung Q--- testified that they were asked whether they wanted to be a soldier or not when they were in the recruitment centre. The Burma Army hit and beat those who answered that they did not want to be a soldier. They tortured them until they had to confess that they wanted to be a solider. After staying in the recruitment centre for 15 days, the Burma Army reached the number of people that they wanted to be conscripted. Then, they [the forcibly recruited individuals] were sent to military training school #6 in Pathein Town [Ayeyarwady Region]. Maung Q--- had to attend the military training there for five months, from 1 May 2024 to 28 October 2024.

Maung Q--- told KHRG: “They [the Burma Army] try to collect [arrest] people. Many people from different areas were arrested. Some prisoners were even arrested. They were taken out from the cell. They were asked whether they would continue to stay in jails or whether they would join the army. Some prisoners said that they wanted to join the army. Then, they were handcuffed when they were sent to the recruitment centre. There were all kinds of people, including criminals. Some of them were people with mental disabilities. Some of them were over 40 years old. Then, they [the Burma Army] took pictures of them for their records. After that, they questioned and interrogated them. During the interrogation, they [the Burma Army] asked whether they [the arrested people] agreed to join the army or not. If people said that they did not agree, a gang of soldiers beat them and hit them. They beat and hit them until they had to say that they agreed. They beat and hit them very harshly. If anyone tried to run away, they tied them with ropes. When they got 200 people, they sent them to a military training school in Pathein Town with military trucks. Along the journey, they asked them again whether they agreed to join the army or not. If they said that they did not agree, then they beat and hit them again. If you say you don’t agree, they beat you and they ask again. They will keep doing that until you agree.”

After Maung Q--- attended the military training, he was sent to LIB #1 army camp, under the command of LID #44, in Thaton Town, Mon State [Doo Tha Htoo District], along with around ten other trainees. He stayed at LIB #1 army camp for over 20 days. Then, he was sent to Thay Baw Boh army camp, Thay Baw Boh village tract, Kaw T’Ree (Kawkareik) Township, Dooplaya District. This army camp is located near the Thoo Mweh River along the Thai-Burma border. He stayed at the camp for five months. In May 2025, combined forces of KNLA and PDF troops led by Bo[13] Da Baw attacked and occupied the army camp. During the attack, 46 Burma Army soldiers, including Maung Q--- and the Operations Commander, surrendered to the KNLA. Then, the KNLA took them on a boat across the river, and they sent them to Thai authorities as a way to avoid detaining them.

However, the Burma Army and Thai authorities negotiated with each other. Finally, Thai authorities sent the surrendered [soldiers] back to Burma. Then, the surrendered [soldiers] were sent to LIB #545 army camp in Myawaddy Town [Dooplaya District]. LIB #545 is under the command of Military Operations Command (MOC)[14] #12. Maung Q--- stayed at LIB #545 army camp for three months. Then, he was sent to LIB #1 army camp in Thaton Town again. Then, he was sent to Kq--- village, Kawkareik Township. He stayed in the village for almost three months. After this, he was sent to Lay Kay army camp and Win Tar Pan army camp as [part of] reinforcements with a guide from the DKBA.

Along the journey, Maung Q--- and his troops faced a food shortage. The Burma Army’s soldiers were dying every day because of severe hunger. According to Maung Q---, his commander’s management was very poor for the military operation. Therefore, many soldiers from the troop died. Maung Q--- could not even continue on the journey as he became weak because he did not get to eat food for several days. Finally, he ran away alone, and he went to places that he thought he might be able to get water. While he was running away, he encountered KNLA troops. He explained everything to the KNLA about what happened to him. Then, the KNLA provided him food and kept him in safe place. Maung Q---‘s [Burma Army] upper leader was Lit. Colonel Kyaw Thu.

Maung Q--- is 30 years old. He is single. He worked as a ship worker to support his livelihood. Maung Q--- tried to think about escaping before he was sent to the frontlines, but it was not easy for him to escape. He told KHRG: “They [the Burma Army] tied those who ran away with ropes. Then, they hit and beat them. So, it is not easy to run away. I cannot imagine what would happen to me if they catch me.”

Further background reading on the situation on forced recruitment in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Forced to Harm: Impacts of the State Administration Council (SAC)’s forced recruitment and enactment of the conscription law in Southeast Burma (January 2024 – February 2025), March 2025.
  • “Taw Oo District Situation Update: SAC shelling, drone attacks, forced recruitment, threats, and other military activity, causing casualties and livelihood challenges in Htaw Ta Htoo and Daw Hpah Hkoh Townships (November 2024 to January 2025)”, May 2025.
  • “Mergui-Tavoy District Short Update: Forced recruitment of villagers by an SAC-affiliated militia causing displacement in Ler K’Saw Township (December 2023 to March 2024)”, April 2024.
  • “Taw Oo District Short Update: SAC forced recruitment and extortion of villagers, and resultant displacement in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (January to February 2024)”, March 2024.

Footnotes:

[1] The present document is based on information received in June 2026. It was provided by a community member in Doo Tha Htoo District who has been trained by KHRG to monitor human rights conditions on the ground. The names of the victims, their photos and the exact locations are censored for security reasons. The parts in square brackets are explanations added by KHRG. This document combines several received reports with the following KHRG internal log numbers: #26-163-D1, #26-163-A1-I1, and #26-163-A2-I1.

[2] ‘Maung’ is a Burmese male honorific title used before a person’s name.

[3] The terms Burma military regime, Burma Army, junta, Tatmadaw, and SAC are used interchangeably throughout this report to describe Burma’s armed forces. Villagers themselves commonly use Burma Army, Burmese soldiers, or alternatively the name adopted by the Burma military regime at the time –from the 2021 coup to July 2025, the State Administration Council (SAC). On 31 July 2025, the military junta changed its name to State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC).

[4] The National League for Democracy (NLD) is the political party that governed Burma/Myanmar from 2016 to January 2021. Led by Aung San Suu Kyi, the NLD won landslide victories in the 2015 and 2020 General Elections. The NLD government was deposed by the Burma Army in the February 2021 Myanmar coup d'état, after which elected President Win Myint and State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi were detained, along with ministers, their deputies and members of Parliament.

[5] On 2 February 2021, healthcare workers at state-run hospitals and medical facilities across Myanmar spearheaded what is being referred to as a Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) consisting of labour strikes in protest against the 1 February 2021 military coup. The movement quickly spread to include civil servants from all sectors of the government who are walking off their jobs as a way of non-recognition and non-participation in the military regime. Because of the popularity of the movement, and its seminal role in wider protests across the country, some people have begun using it as a catch-all phrase to include other protest forms like boycotts and pot-banging.

[6] The People’s Defence Force (PDF) is an armed resistance established independently as local civilian militias operating across the country. Following the 1 February 2021 military coup and the ongoing brutal violence enacted by the junta, the majority of these groups began working with the National Unity Government (NUG), a body claiming to be the legitimate government of Burma/Myanmar, which then formalized the PDF on 5 May 2021 as a precursor to a federal army.

[7] The Karen National Union (KNU) is the main Karen political organisation. It was established in 1947 and has been in conflict with the government since 1949. The KNU wields power across large areas of Southeast Myanmar and has been calling for the creation of a democratic federal system since 1976. Although it signed the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in 2015, following the 2021 coup staged by Burma Army leaders, the KNU officially stated that the NCA has become void.

[8] The Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) is the armed wing of the Karen National Union.

[9] A village tract is an administrative unit of between five and 20 villages in a local area, often centred on a large village.

[10] A Light Infantry Battalion (LIB) comprises 500 soldiers. Most Light Infantry Battalions in the Tatmadaw are under-strength with less than 200 soldiers, yet up-to-date information regarding the size of battalions is hard to come by, particularly following the signing of the NCA. LIBs are primarily used for offensive operations, but they are sometimes used for garrison duties.

[11] A Light Infantry Division (LID) of the Tatmadaw is commanded by a brigadier general and consists of ten light infantry battalions specially trained in counterinsurgency, jungle warfare, search and destroy operations against ethnic insurgents. They were first incorporated into the Tatmadaw in 1966. LIDs are organised under three Tactical Operations Commands, commanded by a colonel, three battalions each and one reserve, one field artillery battalion, one armoured squadron and other support units. Each division is directly under the command of the Chief of Staff (Army).

[12] The Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA) was re-formed on 16 January 2016 as a splinter group from the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (2010 – present) and is also referred to as Na Ma Kya (‘Deaf Ear’). During fighting between the Tatmadaw and DKBA Benevolent throughout 2015, there was internal disagreement within the DKBA Benevolent, which resulted in a number of commanders being dismissed in July 2015. These former commanders then issued a statement in January 2016 declaring the formation of a new splinter group. This DKBA Buddhist (2016 – present) should not be confused with the DKBA Benevolent (2010 – present) from which it broke away in January 2016, or with the original DKBA (1994 – 2010) which was broken up in 2010 into the BGF and the DKBA Benevolent. Importantly, the DKBA Buddhist did not sign the preliminary or nationwide ceasefire with the Myanmar government, whereas the DKBA Benevolent has signed both agreements.

[13] ‘Bo’ is a Burmese honorific title meaning ‘officer.’

[14] Military Operations Command (MOC) is comprised of ten battalions for offensive operations. Most MOCs have three Tactical Operations Commands (TOCs) made up of three battalions each.

title: Taw Oo District Situation Update: Healthcare, education, and military activities in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (September 2025 to February 2026)
content:
This Situation Update describes events occurring in Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaunggyi) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District from September 2025 to February 2026. Throughout the reporting period, challenges to healthcare remained largely the same, with an increase in reported “flu” cases in February 2026. Small clinics administered by the Karen Department of Health and Welfare (KDHW) continued to provide treatment and medicine. However, one clinic reported inadequate medicine supplies and referred patients with serious illnesses to Toungoo Town for further treatment. In terms of education, bunkers were built within four school compounds through the Karen Human Rights Group (KHRG) small grant program. Meanwhile, in October 2025, Burma Army soldiers forcibly cut down villagers’ bamboos and trees in Ag--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract, to repair army fences and as a result damaged villagers’ plantations. On 15 November 2025, the Burma Army shelled Al--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract, damaging a church’s window and a villager’s house. In November, there was also fighting between the Burma Army and Company #3, under Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) Battalion #5. On 13 and 14 November 2025, fighting broke out between Burma Army soldiers and Company #3 at Ai--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract, killing two volunteers from Company #3. Then, on 28 November 2025, Company #3 attacked a truck carrying Burma Army trainees from Bayint Naung Army Camp on a highway between Thandaunggyi Town and Toungoo Town, killing one Burma Army soldier and injuring 19 others.[1]

Healthcare challenges

Within the six months [September 2025 to February 2026], nothing much had changed compared to before. In February 2026, the number of sick people, especially people infected with “the flu”, increased. “The flu” is a mild disease as it only causes fever. Thus, when patients took medicine that reduces fever, they felt better.

Clinics in the [Day Loh Mu Nu Lar] village tract,[2] Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaunggyi) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District were operating the same as before [prior to September 2025]. There is a clinic located near Aa--- village, Ab--- village, and Ac--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract. Previously, Company #3 under KNLA [Karen National Liberation Army][3] Battalion #5 used to have its base near this clinic’s location [in the surrounding area, not inside the clinic compound]. Later, Company #3 relocated to another location, but the clinic remained at the same location. The clinic was not big, yet when villagers were infected with diseases, they usually went to the clinic to receive treatment. The clinic usually provided medicine and injections to patients. [It is] unknown [to KHRG] what kind of medicine was available at the clinic. The clinic is administered by the KDHW [Karen Department of Health and Welfare].[4]

There is also a clinic named Ad--- clinic in Klay Loh Mu Lar village tract, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. The clinic is not big, and it had inadequate medicine [in quantity]. Ad--- clinic is administered by the KDHW, and it was expensive to receive treatment in the clinic [because while KDHW clinics provide fee-free treatment, villagers had to pay the cost of medicines]. Because the clinic had inadequate medicine, it ordered medicine from Toungoo Town, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. Patients with advanced diseases in Ad--- clinic were sent to Toungoo Town [to receive further treatment]. Sometimes, villagers [from Klay Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract] sought help from a doctor named Naw[5] A---, who lives in Am--- Town, Htaw Ta Htoo (Htantabin) Township, Taw Oo District. She worked as a doctor in a government hospital when the situation was good [before the 2021 military coup[6]]. When needed, Ad--- clinic sought help from Dr. Naw A---.

There is a clinic in the compound of Ae--- school, which is located in Day Loh Mu Htaw village tract, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. The clinic is not big, and it is administered by the KDHW. When villagers got sick, they went to the clinic to receive treatment. Nothing had changed for this clinic [compared to before September 2025].

Bunkers built within school compounds

In 2025, four schools [in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township] received a small grant from KHRG. These were three high schools named Ae--- school, located in Klay Loh Mu Htaw village tract, Ad--- school, located in Klay Loh Mu Lar village tract, and Af--- school, located in Ag--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lah village tract, as well as a middle school named Ah--- school, located in Day Loh Mu Htaw village tract. Due to the small grant program, bunkers were built within each school’s compound to protect teachers and students from shelling and air strikes. [The bunkers were built by parents and volunteers.] Nothing had changed other than that [in terms of education in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township, compared to before the reporting period].

Political situation and military activities

When the Burma Army[7] were repairing fences and their army camps, they cut bamboos and trees from villagers’ plantations, which were grown for building villagers’ houses and huts. On 2-3 October 2025, approximately 20 soldiers of the SAC [State Administration Council],[8] who lived in Ag--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract, brought two guns along with them and cut trees and bamboos from the village’s plantation called Ak---. The plantation was owned by Saw[9] E---, and his plantations like cardamon, dog fruits trees, and turmeric plants were damaged. When asked, the soldiers responded that their leaders are Min Zaw Htun and Daw Na, and they got permission to cut trees and bamboos from the plantations, from the former [Ag---] village head, Saw F---. However, villagers were not informed about the cutting trees. The soldiers were cutting bamboos since May 2025.

On 15 November 2025, Saturday, at 7 am, the Burma Army conducted shelling into Al--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract, damaging a church’s window and a house of a 35-year-old man who has three sons, Saw D---.

[Meanwhile,] on 13 and 14 November 2025, fighting took place between the Burma military regime and Company #3, under KNLA Battalion #5, at Ai--- village, Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract. Due to the fighting, two volunteers serving with Company #3, Saw B--- and Saw C---, were killed. During these six months [September 2025 to February 2026], the [Burma Army’s] military activities increased near Ai--- village.

[Later,] on 28 November 2025, security guards operating under Company #3 attacked a truck carrying [Burma Army] military trainees from Bayint Naung Tat Myo Town, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township, near the upper part of Ai--- village, while it was travelling on the highway between Thandaunggyi Town and Toungoo Town, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. Due to the attack, one Burma [Army] soldier was killed and 19 sustained injuries. This information was provided by the commander of Company #3.

On 29 November 2025, soldiers from the Burma military regime, based at 13 Miles gate [a checkpoint located in P’Shaw Loh village tract, Daw Hpa Hkoh Township] confiscated civilians’ trucks and villagers were taken hostage.

Further background reading on the situation in Taw Oo District in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Stolen Childhoods: Violations of children’s rights, urgent needs, and local agency in rural Southeast Burma during the conflict, October 2025.
  • “Taw Oo District Situation Update: Burma Army activities caused livelihood, fuel, education, and healthcare challenges in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (January to March 2026)”, July 2026.
  • “Taw Oo District Incident Report: Burma Army soldiers fatally shot a 17-year-old boy in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (May 2025)”, June 2026.
  • “Taw Oo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling and air strike injured two children, damaged villagers’ houses, and caused displacement in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (July 2025)”, June 2026.

title: WFP Togo Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Togo has experienced relatively strong economic and agricultural performance in recent years, with real GDP growth over six percent since 2023, supported by public investments and policy measures.

• Favorable harvests and market supply have contributed to generally adequate food availability with staple food prices remaining below the previous year and five-year average in May 2026, supporting food access, including for vulnerable households.

• However, localized climate-related shocks such as land degradation, soil erosion and irregular rainfall continue to constrain agricultural productivity and undermine resilience in affected areas.

• Additionally, in the Savanes region, the spillover effects of the Sahel crisis have led to an influx of over 55,000 refugees and asylum seekers and more than 10,000 internally displaced persons according to the latest governmental data, increasing pressure on markets, services, and natural resources in areas hosting large numbers of displaced populations.

• Sustained investment in climate adaptation, food systems and social protection is needed to address persistent vulnerabilities and support long-term food security. WFP supports the Government’s response through an integrated approach combining emergency assistance, resilience-building and system strengthening under the Country Strategic Plan.

title: WHO Afghanistan Emergency Situation Report No 66 (July 2026)
content:
Highlights

Over 155 900 returnees entered Afghanistan in July, with 62% of whom arrived from Pakistan.

Three hundred eighty health workers were trained, and 240 medical kits were distributed to strengthen the health system.

CCHF cases decreased by 37.5% compared to June levels; however, monitoring needs to continue to ascertain seasonality of this trend.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, August 27, 2026 - September 2, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is strengthening. Abnormal heat continues to threaten many parts of northern and eastern Africa, Central Asia, Hispaniola, Central America, and northern South America. Dryness is worsening in Central America, Hispaniola and Venezuela.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is anticipated across the Sahel region of West Africa and extending into Eastern Africa, while dryness persists in much of Eastern Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.

2) Severe rainfall deficits across large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have led to abnormal dryness. As a result, conditions have been upgraded to "Drought" across southern South Sudan and parts of Ethiopia’s northern, eastern, and central regions. An abnormal dryness polygon also expanded west to parts of Chad.

3) Southeastern Mali and central and eastern Liberia remain under abnormal dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall.

4) Persistent heavy rainfall continues to pose an elevated risk of flooding across southeastern Nigeria and the western part of Cameroon. Heavy rainfall and associated high runoffs elevate risk of flooding in Guinea and surrounding areas.

5) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected across parts of northern Algeria, parts of Sudan, South Sudan, northwestern and eastern Ethiopia, and western Eritrea.

6) Moderate to heavy rainfall over the month, along with a forecast of moderate to heavy rainfall, maintains a high alert for flash flooding in western Ethiopia. Flooding has been reported in Tawila town in western Sudan, which displaced hundreds of people and destroyed several homes.

title: Epidemiological Update Avian Influenza A(H5) in the Americas Region - 26 August 2026
content:
Avian influenza A(H5) is a highly contagious viral disease that primarily affects poultry and wild birds, with the ability to sporadically infect mammalian species, including humans. Since 1996, the A/goose/Guangdong/1/96 lineage has caused recurrent outbreaks in bird populations, as well as hundreds of human cases and deaths resulting from exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. Currently, the A(H5N1) subtype and other avian influenza A(H5) viruses have been identified in birds and mammals across multiple geographic regions worldwide.

Between 2021 and March 2026, more than 600 species of wild and poultry birds and more than 100 species of mammals have been reported as affected by avian influenza viruses with zoonotic potential, such as A(H5Nx). In May 2026, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), and the World Health Organization (WHO) determined that the global public health risk associated with highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAI) A(H5) belonging to the Gs/Gd lineage remains low. Similarly, for people with occupational or frequent exposure, the risk was estimated to be low to moderate.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 82, as of 2025 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Insecurity is jeopardizing the delivery of humanitarian assistance in Vakaga Prefecture.
  • CERF has allocated US$3 million to support Ebola prevention efforts.
  • More than 800 households receive food assistance in Ouham-Fafa Prefecture

GENERAL CONTEXT

Vakaga Prefecture - North-East

  • The deterioration of the security situation in Am-Dafock and surrounding areas, combined with recent population movements, including arrivals from Sudan, is increasing pressure on available resources and exacerbating vulnerabilities among affected populations. It is widening the gap between humanitarian needs and response capacity. Humanitarian actors present in Birao and Am-Dafock are providing assistance in the health, water, protection and food security sectors. However, the response remains constrained by persistent insecurity along major supply routes, ongoing military operations and the remoteness of the prefecture. Secondary population movements, particularly of people leaving Am-Dafock in search of safety and livelihood opportunities, are further complicating needs assessments and the delivery of assistance.

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture - South-East

  • Since the death of the village chief of Guinikoumba in June and abuses committed by armed actors along the Zemio-Dembia road, around 3,655 people have fled the villages of Tabane, Bogou, Bangassou-Issa, Barh and Guinikoumba. Some remain in the bush, while others have sought refuge in Dembia. In Guinikoumba, the entire population of approximately 1,100 people has moved to Dembia. This situation could hamper ongoing humanitarian operations along the road, including the construction of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure funded by the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF).

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Countrywide

  • In response to the risk of cross-border spread following confirmed Ebola virus disease cases in provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) bordering the Central African Republic (CAR), the Emergency Relief Coordinator, through the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), announced on 21 August an allocation of US$3 million to support prevention efforts in CAR. The funding will help strengthen disease surveillance, isolation capacities, community engagement and access to water. To date, no Ebola cases have been confirmed in the Central African Republic.

Food Security

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture - North-West

  • Between 15 and 21 August, 875 vulnerable households received food security assistance in Batangafo and Benzambé. Plan International and its partners distributed food commodities, including cereals, pulses, oil and salt, to 667 households, including 493 in Benzambé and 174 in Batangafo. The assistance targeted households hosting people displaced by armed attacks in Benzambé and arson incidents carried out by armed men in the localities of Nganda, Ndoubamoudou and Bezanga. In addition, the NGO Welthungerhilfe, with funding from the World Bank, provided 208 households in Batangafo with breeding animals for small livestock production to support income-generating activities, livelihoods and food security

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 15, Data as of 23 August 2026
content:
Event description

More than three months into the response, the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains characterized by sustained transmission, high mortality and continued geographic expansion. The epidemiological picture is increasingly heterogeneous, with persistent transmission in established hotspots in Ituri, intensifying transmission in parts of Nord-Kivu and Haut-Uélé, and continued geographic expansion through the emergence of cases in previously unaffected health zones. Since External Situation Report #14, a total of 563 new confirmed cases and 302 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 5 584 confirmed cases,including 2 680 deaths. The number of affected health zones has increased from 55 to 57 across six provinces, with Viadana in Bas-Uélé and Mutwanga in Nord-Kivu being the most recently affected health zones.
